After Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Following the inauguration of the new US government, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—shifting from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—which could have profound impacts on the global economic landscape. It is worth noting that with the accelerating pace of US interest rate hikes strengthening the US dollar and the possibility of the US adopting trade protectionist measures, the risks faced by emerging market economies have intensified. The HKD exchange rate remained largely stable, while the HKD interbank offered rate rose in line with the US dollar interbank offered rate. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained good, and overall loan growth rose further in the second half of 2016. Following the implementation of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment but has recently rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should prudently assess the impact of the US interest rate hike pace potentially being faster than expected, as well as the broader uncertainty of US policy, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and the potential impact on Hong Kong interest rates. After Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only were the election results unexpected to the market, but the corresponding market reactions were also surprising. In particular, expectations that measures introduced by Trump—such as tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation—would drive US economic growth propelled global stock markets higher. Following the inauguration of the new US government, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—shifting from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—which may have profound impacts on the global economic landscape. However, the tax cuts expected by the market may fail to provide the anticipated stimulus to US economic growth. Specifically, as current US economic activity is close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a slight cyclical stimulus to US economic growth while exacerbating the upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the Federal Reserve will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen significantly, partly reflecting market expectations that inflation risks are increasing. At the same time, the rise of trade protectionism will result in a "lose-lose" situation for the US and other parts of the world. Increased trade barriers will lead to market distortions that damage overall interests, hinder global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and bring downside risks to the global economic outlook. Concurrently, political instability remains a major risk and adverse factor, especially for the European economy, where the recovery remains weak. As for emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows caused by the accelerating pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar has risen. This could drag down economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, in anticipation of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns over soaring energy prices, the market has repriced inflation risks, leading to a comprehensive and significant rise in long-term bond yields across both advanced economies and several emerging market economies. Topic 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. Research results show that since the "taper tantrum" of 2013, the impact of the US Treasury market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions will have a significant impact on advanced economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, with the recovery of exports, economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, but market volatility—such as the depreciation of regional currencies and rising sovereign bond yields caused by concerns over policy changes by the new US government—only gradually stabilized toward the beginning of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces are both rising. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility may lead to tightening financial conditions. At the same time, the United States may implement protectionist policies, which could affect regional economies, though the actual impact remains unclear at present. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved business spending in the private sector. Although the economy continues to show signs of recovery, the growth outlook for the Mainland still faces uncertainties. Particularly with the government's determination to curb rising property prices, if the real estate market continues to cool, the property sector's contribution to growth may decrease this year. Concurrently, the continued progress of economic structural adjustments and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the short-term economic outlook. Externally, although the RMB remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressure increased toward the end of 2016 due to the appreciation of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of recovery in private sector economic activity, some concerns remain in the market regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy, especially given that M1 growth accelerated while M2 growth slowed. Topic 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Topic 3 (see page 27) explores factors that may cause the divergence in M1 and M2 growth. Research findings indicate that there is no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap; the primary reasons for M1 growth being significantly faster than M2 are that recent monetary easing has lowered the opportunity cost of holding liquid currency, and rising economic uncertainty may have increased the demand for precautionary money. Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarterly real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Locally, growth in private consumption continued to strengthen, while robust infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter boosted investment growth. Externally, growth in goods exports rose with improved regional trade flows, while services exports grew steadily with the recovery of trade-related and transport services. As growth in goods and services imports was faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half. With the rise in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate fell slightly to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. Protectionist rhetoric from the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. With the US dollar facing appreciation pressure and expectations of an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to provide less support for the real economy, and may lead to tightening local financial conditions in the event of tail risks. Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of the Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index to assist in monitoring local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarterly inflationary momentum accelerated slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising house rents. As import prices remained stable, local cost pressures were moderate, and expected inflationary pressures remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the HKD exchange rate remained broadly stable, though it weakened intermediately after the US interest rate hike in December. The Linked Exchange Rate System was not triggered. With the appreciation of the US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate of the HKD rose further. Due to the large monetary base, the Hong Kong interbank interest rate remained relatively low, but it has risen since October due to year-end funding demands and the recovery of US dollar interest rate hikes. Consequently, the average mortgage rate rose slightly to 2.07% in January 2017, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared to a growth of 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by the strengthening of local economic activity and the rising financing demands of multinational corporations at year-end. Domestic loan growth accelerated slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decrease in the first half. By currency analysis, HKD loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded a growth of 3.2% as mainland borrowers gradually reduced the repayment of foreign currency loans. The funding position of banks remained generally robust. The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio fell slightly to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting that deposit growth exceeded loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, and the USD loan-to-deposit ratio fell significantly to 63.8% due to strong growth in USD deposits. Due to the strength of the US dollar, both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore RMB funding pool (including customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances) further consolidated with other offshore RMB markets, and the volatility of the Hong Kong interbank interest rate for offshore RMB increased significantly. Nevertheless, the banks' RMB liquidity management remained robust, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system maintained a high level. Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is likely to continue facing headwinds brought by the uncertainty of the RMB exchange rate trend. As global market conditions improved, the Hong Kong stock market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election produced unexpected results, the market was only briefly impacted. This was mainly because investors were optimistic about the Trump administration's fiscal stimulus measures, which drove global stock markets upward. While benefiting from this, the Hong Kong market remained cautious amidst the optimism, possibly due to concerns over an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges facing the mainland's economic outlook, an unclear RMB policy, and capital flow controls. Looking ahead, although the Hong Kong market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation can provide support for the market. Although HKD bond yields rose rapidly at the end of last year and the spread with US Treasuries widened rapidly, the HKD bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB bond market recovered in the second half after contracting in the first half of 2016, but the new bond issuance for the full year still decreased compared to the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies, both the HKD and offshore RMB bond markets will face pressure. As US trade policies remain unclear, the RMB exchange rate may still fluctuate, and the prospects of these two bond markets in the next six months will still be plagued by significant uncertainties. Following the government's introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment but has recently rebounded. Given that the market became exuberant again, the government raised the stamp duty uniformly to 15% in November. Transaction volumes in the primary and secondary markets both fell in the following two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting developers increasing the launch of primary properties. At the same time, property prices continued to rise to new highs, but the momentum has slowed.

Policy uncertainty in the US has increased following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President. While markets have focused on the short-term benefits of a potential large-scale fiscal policy and pro-business measures, the US economy is already operating near its economic potential. Fiscal stimulus may only provide a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth, but it would further exacerbate the upside risks to inflation. More importantly, risks to emerging market economies are rising with the pressure of capital outflows from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures would threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have recently increased. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, and downside risks to economic growth have risen. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016, amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. The Mainland economy continues to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. With the government determined to curb rising property prices, the contribution of the real estate sector to economic growth may also decrease this year if the property market continues to cool. On the external front, although the Renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 with the appreciation of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly with markets anticipating that Trump's policies of tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating major stock markets to rise (Figure 2.1). Consequently, market expectations for US inflation and US interest rate hikes have warmed, leading to a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Figure 2.1 Stock Market Indices of Selected Advanced Economies However, the market-anticipated Trump tax cuts may not have the positive impact on US economic growth that the market expects. Although a shift in economic policy to rely on fiscal easing would help alleviate the heavy burden on monetary easing, the timing of implementing fiscal easing at the current stage of the US economic cycle is debatable. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, and the unemployment rate in February also met the Fed's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier will be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labor or capital may lead to a decrease in tax revenue (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with reduced excess capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited, may push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may also exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. Even with the increased risk of rising US inflation, the Federal Reserve has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and has tended to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting the increased risk of US inflation. Since the US election, although market forecasts for future federal funds rates have been revised upwards to near the Fed's median forecasts for 2017 and early 2018, they are still well below the Fed's long-term forecast (Figure 2.2). Therefore, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger significant market volatility. While financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of potential expansionary fiscal policies and pro-business measures to drive stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further rise in US national debt. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfill its election promises and adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Figure 2.2 Future Federal Funds Rate Forecasts: Fed vs. Market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and headwind to the European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Eurozone has gradually improved, with real GDP growing at a moderate 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly lower than the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, economic activity in the Eurozone is still only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels, relative to the stronger recovery in the US economy (Figure 2.3). Since the Brexit decision last summer, there have been concerns that the Eurozone will eventually disintegrate. Although the economic and political situation in Italy seems to have stabilized after the formation of a new government and the implementation of bank rescue measures, upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment could become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have widened, particularly in peripheral countries, which could create a vicious cycle for the real economy and put pressure on real business investment in the Eurozone. Figure 2.3 Real GDP of Major Advanced Economies In Japan, real GDP has been revised upwards in recent quarters, with the annualized growth rate increasing to 1.6% year-on-year in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger-than-expected economic recovery. However, partly due to structural problems in the labor market, wage growth has been slow, leading to weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen means that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation from the previous appreciation of the yen is about to begin to subside. Coupled with the stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates an improved short-term inflation outlook, and while "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, in the face of long-term and structural headwinds, growth is likely to remain slow, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the level at the launch of Abenomics in early 2014. Therefore, the risk that the inflation rate will fail to reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% remains. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits from faster US economic growth through trade channels may be smaller due to reduced US imports after the global financial crisis and the potential implementation of protectionist policies by the US. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will lead to tighter financial conditions, exacerbating downside economic risks. This could drag on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, market expectations of a large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risks, causing a significant and widespread increase in long-term bond yields in advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained vitality, with a small increase in regional GDP and rising inflation. Real GDP Growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable due to steady private consumption in many regional economies. At the same time, exports generally rose slightly from their lows in 2015. This benefited not only from the stabilization of growth in China but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (e.g., Malaysia and Indonesia), the rebound in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained momentum due to growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — As commodity (especially oil) prices have rebounded, producer price inflation has generally shown an upward trend. While this will push up industrial costs and even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may be boosted by the reduced risk of long-term deflation. The acceleration of producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which the increase in producer prices is passed on to consumer prices, which is inconsistent across economies. Consensus forecasts for the Consumer Price Index indicate that while inflation in many regional economies will remain slightly below the central banks' 2017 inflation targets, it will rise to levels closer to the targets (Figure 2.4). With the exception of Indonesia, central banks in the East Asian region have generally maintained an accommodative monetary policy with unchanged interest rates, while Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Figure 2.4 Headline CPI Inflation, Forecasts, and Central Bank Targets in East Asia Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign Exchange Markets — After the US presidential election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies have depreciated less or even appreciated slightly since the US election (Figure 2.5). Figure 2.5 Spot FX Depreciation against the US Dollar and Changes in the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate after the US Election Bond and Stock Markets — Asset prices fell briefly after the US presidential election but then stabilized. The spread between sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasury bonds widened. However, as markets stabilized, yields in some regional economies declined but have not yet returned to pre-election levels (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the spread has narrowed from pre-election levels. Figure 2.6 Spread between 10-Year Sovereign Bonds and US Treasury Bonds Portfolio Investment Flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. Inflows were recorded again in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth in the region is expected to remain stable, but at a pace still below the historical average. Financial markets are likely to remain volatile due to increased uncertainty about US government policy and the potential policy response from the Federal Reserve. A sharp rise in the US dollar and yields could attract capital from the region to the US, leading investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, especially those with already high valuations. The tightening of financial conditions in this situation would also put repayment pressure on companies with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. At a macro level, a general rise in global interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which would not only drag on aggregate demand in the short term but could also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, the region's exporting countries face the potential threat of protectionist policies from the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Figure 2.7), especially in the region's major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. Over the past two decades, the US has seen a significant loss of jobs in these industries as imports have increased. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose a significant risk to the region's exporting countries.

Accelerated growth in private consumption and robust property and construction activities drove a slight acceleration in Hong Kong's economic growth in the second half of 2016. Due to an increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth in 2017 is expected to be moderate. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Private consumption growth accelerated, becoming the main driver of GDP growth, partly due to improved consumer confidence and a robust labor market. Property and construction activities also became robust, supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport. However, weak corporate capital expenditure narrowed the contribution of overall investment expenditure to GDP growth. Externally, both imports and exports accelerated in growth following the rise in regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).22 Trade-related and transport services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports  The labor market remains tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at 3.4% in the first three quarters, before falling slightly to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates in several major industries declined in the second half, including retail, accommodation, and food services, partly due to a recovery in the slowdown of the retail sector. Total employment reached a new high of 382.4 thousand in February 2017, while the labor force participation rate remained steady at approximately 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment  Real economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. Regarding external factors, global economic and trade growth may continue to be moderate due to the uncertain global macroeconomic and financial environment. Additionally, a strong US dollar leading to a rise in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar will suppress Hong Kong's export performance. Regarding domestic factors, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, weighed down by rising interest rates. With the increase in housing supply and the planned commencement of several infrastructure projects, property and construction activities should grow steadily, but a sluggish business atmosphere and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth for 2017 to be between 2 and 3%, while the average forecast by private-sector analysts is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is constrained by numerous uncertainties, with the impact from the external environment being particularly significant. Policy uncertainties from the new US administration will make the global economic outlook uncertain, and potential trade protectionist policies may create resistance to global trade flows. The progress of Brexit and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect capital flows for the Hong Kong dollar. Furthermore, the normalization of US interest rates will tighten local currency conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has seen an uptick in quarterly momentum in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the basic Composite Consumer Price Index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The basic inflation rate, reflecting inflationary momentum on a three-month basis at an annual rate, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before falling slightly to 2.4% in January. The main reason for the rise in inflationary momentum is the increase in trade goods prices and housing rents (Chart 3.5). In particular, trade goods price inflation rose from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, primarily driven by basic food and footwear prices. At the same time, since the third quarter, the housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) has risen as the decline in private residential rents narrowed and public housing rents were adjusted upward in September 2016, but it subsequently slowed slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by main components Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rental In the short term, local cost pressures will remain mild due to weak import prices, and inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. Imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7) as the strong Hong Kong dollar offsets the impact of rebounding global commodity prices to some extent. On the local side, the output gap is estimated to remain close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thus curb inflation in the services component. Despite a tight labour market, wage growth has been slight in recent quarters, with real wages per capita rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 and falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Given the continued uncertainty in the external environment, which has led to cautious business sentiment, the rise in labour costs should be somewhat restrained. Additionally, as retail sales have performed poorly in recent months, the expected increase in retail property rents will be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the earlier softening of private residential rents will gradually emerge, also helping to ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate for the full year of 2017 is expected to decline; the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate for the full year to be 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real wages per capita The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation rises more rapidly in the United States under the Trump administration, it could lead to a faster pace of US interest rate hikes than expected, which may push up local mortgage rates and increase downward pressure on property prices and housing rents. At the same time, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak while simultaneously weakening local attractiveness to visitors. On the upside, if global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. Furthermore, the upwardly adjusted statutory minimum wage will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may cause inflation to rise further, but the substantial impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite volatility in financial markets, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained largely stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in tandem with US dollar rates. Partly due to an improving local economic environment, overall lending continued to grow modestly. Looking ahead, with the pace of US interest rate normalisation accelerating, uncertainties surrounding the policy direction of the new US administration, and ongoing political risks in Europe, fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar funding flows may increase. Despite financial market volatility, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar stayed largely stable (Chart 4.1). Although market turbulence triggered by the November US presidential election led to broad declines in Asian currencies, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13–14 December 2016 heightened market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened alongside other Asian currencies; however, as market expectations of a March 2017 US rate hike gained momentum from mid-February, the currency began to show signs of weakening. During the review period, the exchange rate peg was not tested (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and funding flow indicators Chart 4.2 Funding flow indicators Driven by a stronger US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index rose 4.9% between August and December before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). Given the minimal impact from narrowing inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the real effective exchange rate index closely mirrored the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment saw net outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics indicate that non-resident investments in equities and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and a surge in initial public offerings (Table 4.A). Nevertheless, driven partly by Hong Kong banks’ increased purchases of US Treasury bonds, resident investments in debt securities experienced substantial outflows, outweighing non-resident inflows. Consequently, cross-border portfolio investment recorded a net outflow in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds revealed that portfolio outflows in the final quarter of 2016 were largely attributable to the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election and expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, which exerted downward pressure on both Hong Kong and other Asian financial markets (Chart 4.4). However, recent data indicate that portfolio inflows into Hong Kong resumed in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to investors’ optimism regarding expansionary US fiscal policies, which boosted global financial market performance. Chart 4.4 Market survey on equity and bond-related funding flows Looking ahead, fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar funding flows may intensify. An accelerated pace of US interest rate normalisation would heighten the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar funding flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the UK’s Brexit process, and upcoming elections in EU member states could further amplify funding flow volatility. Additionally, rising demand from mainland Chinese investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert upward pressure on the currency. Although northbound trading initially outpaced southbound trading following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, it is expected that two-way equity investment flows between the mainland and Hong Kong under this scheme will gradually increase. Despite rising US interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and more recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable; driven by growth in certificates of indebtedness and government-issued currency in circulation, it rose a further 1.7% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.5). Given that the exchange rate peg was not tested, the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Amidst this, the issuance of an additional HK$49 billion worth of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes was undertaken to meet the substantial demand from banks for liquidity management purposes. Consequently, the Aggregate Balance contracted while the outstanding volume of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose accordingly. Chart 4.5 Composition of the Monetary Base Driven by a gradually strengthening local economy, the growth rate of Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. The growth rate of Hong Kong dollar M3 increased from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits posted a relatively rapid growth rate of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), primarily driven by heightened local economic activity and increased trading demand stemming from a rebound in initial public offering activities. An analysis of corresponding assets reveals that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflects rises in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6); these developments respectively indicate monetary expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds into the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Movements in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding assets On the other hand, growth patterns for foreign currency deposits remained varied. Following a 10.2% increase in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded an even higher growth rate of 12.8% in the second half, driven by a stronger US dollar (Chart 4.7). In contrast, deposits denominated in other foreign currencies contracted further by 10.3%, largely due to a decline in Renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits held by authorized institutions rose by 6.2% in the second half of 2016, resulting in an annual growth rate of 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, wholesale funding costs for banks climbed in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained relatively low, they still rose somewhat, partly driven by year-end financing demand and the upward trend in US dollar interbank rates. In the second half of the year, the overnight and three-month Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) climbed by 54 and 46 basis points respectively to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Concurrently, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards in tandem with the US dollar yield curve; the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by approximately 90 basis points, closing at 1.93% at the end of December. Moving into early 2017, reduced financing demand led to a general decline in Hong Kong dollar interbank rates, while long-term Hong Kong government bond yields also dipped slightly following a fall in US Treasury yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank rates and 10-year government bond yields Thanks to the substantial deposit base within the banking system, retail-level interest rate hikes remained relatively modest. The average cost of funds for banks, measured via the composite rate, stayed low; in January 2017 it edged up by just 6 basis points to 0.32% compared to seven months earlier (Chart 4.9). With financing costs remaining relatively stable and competition in the mortgage market intensifying, the average interest rate on newly issued mortgages fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 as HIBOR rose. Chart 4.9 Composite rate and average interest rate on newly issued mortgages Looking ahead, the pace of local interest rate hikes will hinge on the speed of US interest rate normalisation, the scale of capital outflows, and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on local interest rates, coupled with an appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar’s real effective exchange rate relative to the US dollar, may diminish the extent to which local financial conditions continue to support the real economy. Topic 4 discusses the compilation of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index intended for monitoring local financial conditions. Driven by stronger local economic activity and heightened cross-border financing demand, total lending expanded by 4.2% in the second half of the year following a 2.2% increase in the first half (Chart 4.10). With economic growth momentum gaining further traction, domestic lending growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half of the year, after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting heightened financing needs among multinational corporations at year-end. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans posted robust growth of 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also saw a modest 3.2% increase, as mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments on their foreign currency-denominated loans. Overall, total lending grew by 6.5% in 2016, up from 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 shows loan growth broken down by economic sector. Domestically, loan performance varied across sectors in the second half of the year (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial services firms and the information technology sector posted double-digit growth, reflecting stronger financing demand driven by their relatively favorable growth prospects. Loan growth also accelerated in the construction and property development sectors, in tandem with rising private construction activity. Conversely, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and to the manufacturing, wholesale, and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 depicts domestic loan growth by individual sectors. Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half of the year, compared to just 0.5% in the first half. Partly reflecting an improving economic climate, personal loans—including credit card balances and other loans for personal use—rose by 7.2% (Chart 4.11). Residential mortgage lending also picked up, growing at 3.1%, largely driven by robust residential property transactions between July and October. Consequently, the ratio of household debt to GDP climbed from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 illustrates the ratio of household debt to GDP and its components. Bank funding conditions remained largely stable. With deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at end-June 2016 to 77.1% by year-end (Chart 4.13). Meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% by year-end; notably, the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped sharply to 63.8% due to robust growth in US dollar deposits. Chart 4.13 displays loan-to-deposit ratios. Given expectations of rising interest rates and rapid shifts in the macro-financial environment, credit growth is expected to remain uncertain in the near term. The HKMA’s “Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook” indicates that loan demand will likely stay weak in the short term. The appreciation of the US dollar led to a weakening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates (Chart 4.14). For most of late 2016, the offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore rate, closing the year at an annual low of 6.98 per US dollar. In December, liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market tightened once again, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary financing needs ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks bolstered their liquidity buffers amid worsening market sentiment, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate surged to 61.3% on January 6, 2017. The subsequent rise in offshore renminbi financing costs prompted liquidation of short positions, prompting a rebound in the offshore renminbi exchange rate in early January 2017; the offshore premium over the onshore rate also reappeared. Since mid-January, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilized somewhat, with liquidity conditions gradually improving; the overnight and three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rates fell to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively by end-February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared to the same period in 2015 due to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment provisions. The capital position and asset quality of the banks also remained robust. Although Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBORs) rose significantly following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity situation in the banking sector remained good. The funding costs of retail banks remained stable and at low levels under a massive retail deposit base. However, banks should prudently assess the impact of the US interest rate hike pace potentially being faster than expected, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and the subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. Furthermore, given the continued rise in leverage levels of non-local enterprises, a sharp rise in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in the asset quality of banks. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical buffer capital ratio requirement will be increased to 1.875% from 1 January 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.1). The factors for the improvement in profitability were the growth in net interest income and non-interest income, and the reduction in loan impairment provisions. For 2016 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose from 1.05% in 2015 to 1.10%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Hong Kong's wholesale funding costs rose significantly following the resumption of interest rate hikes in the US in December 2016. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose significantly by 33 basis points in December 2016; however, it remained at a low level by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates However, the overall impact of the US interest rate hike on the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained slight. This is because the primary source of funding for retail banks is retail deposits, and even with the interest rate hike, retail deposit rates remained stable and at low levels. In this situation, the composite rate reflecting the average funding cost of Hong Kong dollars for retail banks remained at a low level of about 0.26% for more than a year, rising only slightly by 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016. On a broader level, the total funding costs for Hong Kong dollars and US dollars of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar picture. Although the average funding costs for non-deposit market Hong Kong dollars and US dollars of banks rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in average deposit funding costs in the retail market was smaller, rising by only 11 basis points. Overall, the average total funding costs for Hong Kong dollars and US dollars of licensed banks rose by 17 basis points (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Funding costs and tenors of Hong Kong dollars and US dollars of licensed banks The magnitude and speed of the rise in HIBORs exceeded the funding costs of Hong Kong banks, which may benefit some retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted mortgage loans based on HIBOR in recent years, and the rise in interest rates for such loans may help expand their overall net interest margin. However, the improvement in net interest margin may be partially offset by fierce competition in the mortgage market. In fact, there are signs that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. In the long term, as the US will further hike interest rates, banks may soon face pressure from rising retail deposit rates, which will affect the funding costs of banks and have a more significant impact on the net interest margin. The capital levels of the banks remain strong and are far above the international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a high level of 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was common equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital levels of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated status. 2. Locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital adequacy framework "Basel III," which took effect on January 1, 2013. Therefore, capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards cannot be directly compared with data as of December 2012. Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirements of "Basel III," the liquidity situation of the banking industry remained good during the reporting period. Although the average liquidity coverage ratio of Category 1 institutions dipped slightly from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016 to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016, it remained at a high level (Chart 5.6). Meanwhile, the average liquidity maintenance ratio of Category 2 institutions remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remain far above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking industry is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks caused by potential outflows of Hong Kong funds. Chart 5.6 Liquidity coverage ratios Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for retail banks. The proportion of customer deposits in the total liabilities of banks rose from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks Due to the similar growth rates of the total amount of loans and advances and the total amount of deposits of retail banks during the reporting period, the loan-to-deposit ratio calculated in all currencies remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). During the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratios calculated in HKD and foreign currencies also remained largely unchanged. Chart 5.8 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of retail banks Although the interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks rose slightly, it remained at a relatively low level. Estimates show that under a hypothetical shock of a comprehensive 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.9). However, given that the pace of US interest rate normalization may be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of bank accounts and transaction accounts, presented as a percentage of the total capital base of the bank. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail bank loan portfolios remained robust, with the total specific classification loan ratio and the overdue and restructured loan ratio remaining at low levels of 0.72% and 0.53% respectively at the end of December 2016. Both ratios remain at low levels when measured against historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks Although current asset quality remains robust when measured against historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to monitor the peripheral environment; as the assessment in Theme 5 shows that loans used by the banking industry outside of Hong Kong have grown rapidly since the global financial crisis, reflecting that the asset quality of banks is more susceptible to the peripheral environment. Expectations for short-term credit growth vary. The "Credit Situation Outlook Survey" by the HKMA in December 2016 showed that although most surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next 3 months, the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next 3 months rose slightly to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk of unsecured personal loans remained manageable, with the annualized credit card charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio falling to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio for credit card lending and bankruptcy petitions The banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained robust, with the delinquency ratio remaining at 0.03% at the end of December. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio for new mortgages in the fourth quarter of 2016 was 51.3% (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio is significantly lower than the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing the seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt service ratio for new mortgages rose from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (red line in Chart 5.12), primarily reflecting a slight increase in the average amount of new mortgage loans (Chart 5.13). The continued implementation of interest rate normalization in the United States may further increase the personal debt burden. A sensitivity test shows that if interest rates rise by 300 basis points while other conditions remain unchanged, the index could rise significantly to 67.3 within 4 quarters. 48 Banks should remain vigilant regarding the risk of a continuous increase in the personal debt burden. Chart 5.12 Average LTV ratio for new mortgage loans and personal debt burden Chart 5.13 New mortgage loans of surveyed authorized institutions The pace of US interest rate hikes remains a major factor affecting the credit risk of corporate loans. However, the actual impact on the asset quality of individual banks depends on the characteristics of their corporate loan portfolios. In particular, our assessment based on the accounting data of non-financial companies listed in Hong Kong found that the trends in leverage ratios for local and non-local corporates showed significant differences after the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates being more susceptible to debt service issues. 50 Banks should assess the impact of interest rate hikes on the credit risk of non-local corporate loans. Specifically, corporate leverage measured by the weighted average debt-to-equity ratio rose after the global financial crisis, with the increase primarily driven by non-local corporates.
