As markets reevaluated inflation risks in the United States, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the start of the year. In February, global equity markets tumbled sharply from their late-January peaks, erasing all the significant gains recorded earlier in the year. Meanwhile, the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equities had posted steady gains amid low volatility, driven by market expectations of continued robust economic growth coupled with low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations now face risks stemming from tightening global monetary conditions, rising protectionist sentiments, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar weakened, yet financial markets continued to function smoothly. In the latter half of 2017, overall lending continued to expand, albeit at a slower pace. Following a modest slowdown last year, both property price growth and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may further increase fluctuations in capital flows to Hong Kong. Given ongoing uncertainties in financial markets, the continued normalization of US monetary policy, and persistent geopolitical risks, banks must remain vigilant against heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given the ongoing rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt, banks should assess how any faster-than-expected interest rate hikes might affect asset quality. After remaining at low levels for over two years, the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) saw global financial markets become volatile once again at the start of the year. Global equity markets dropped sharply from their late-January peaks; the S&P 500 index fell by more than 10% at one point, completely offsetting the substantial gains recorded in early January. This shift in market sentiment was triggered by indications that the global economic recovery might exert upward pressure on US wages and prices, which had remained low for a long time, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its interest rate hikes. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note also climbed to a four-year high. The sustained rise in global equities over the past two years was underpinned by market expectations of continued favorable economic conditions. In the latter half of 2017, global economic growth momentum strengthened, with economic activity rebounding in both advanced and emerging economies. Toward year-end, the US Congress passed a tax reform package featuring tax cuts and comprehensive revisions to corporate and individual tax regulations, fueling market optimism that the robust US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical support in the short term. Despite this uptick in economic activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would stay low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets posted notable gains in 2017; US equities, in particular, repeatedly hit new record highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth figures for January, global equity markets reevaluated inflation risks. Beyond the short-term market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, where the economy has now reached its production potential, the anticipated cyclical boost to domestic demand resulting from tax cuts could accelerate inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Meanwhile, since tax cuts are expected to widen the fiscal deficit, the US may issue more Treasury bonds in the future; this is likely to exert upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve proceeds with its balance sheet normalization efforts. Outside the US, stronger growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to anticipate that their respective central banks might scale back their quantitative easing programs. Should this materialize, it would result in a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Additionally, policy and event risks stemming from international and geopolitical tensions could also dampen the global growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined toward protectionist trade measures aimed at shielding domestic industries from competition. Recent examples include announcements of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminum. These actions raise concerns that trading partners might respond with retaliatory measures. Additionally, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could disrupt global trade and heighten volatility in global financial markets. Given these uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, it remains doubtful whether current elevated valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. On a fundamental level, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical upturn in global demand and expectations of US tax cuts—which are set to widen fiscal deficits—will push up the natural interest rate (R*). Moreover, the Fed’s ongoing balance sheet normalization is expected to raise term premiums, potentially driving long-term interest rates higher and exerting downward pressure on asset valuations. In East Asia, economies in the region are also enjoying a favorable environment characterized by solid growth and moderate inflation. Supported by strong economic performance and optimistic prospects, capital inflows have accelerated, driving financial markets higher. However, this positive outlook faces downside risks stemming from several factors: tightening global liquidity due to synchronized monetary policy normalization by major central banks; the US government’s inward-looking trade policies; heightened geopolitical tensions; and the potential shortage of offshore US dollar liquidity resulting from US firms repatriating profits en masse under a one-time “deemed repatriation” provision introduced as part of recent tax reforms. Should any shocks occur in credit or financial markets, capital flows could reverse abruptly, with industries and economies carrying higher leverage levels being most vulnerable to tighter financial conditions. On the Chinese mainland, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by steady consumption, robust infrastructure investment, and a rebound in industrial spending toward year-end. Meanwhile, signs of the emergence of a “new economy” have become increasingly evident; over recent quarters, sectors such as high-value-added manufacturing and services have demonstrated strong expansion momentum. Looking ahead, near-term growth prospects remain positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the “new economy” can offset short-term headwinds to growth stemming from further implementation of structural reforms. In 2018, mainland authorities announced their intention to maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance, which could help mitigate any adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in advancing structural reforms and containing systemic risks. Notably, following the introduction of tighter regulatory measures, the mainland’s property market showed signs of cooling, particularly in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, banks’ exposure to firms in overcapacity sectors remained under control, as lending standards were tightened; shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging efforts. Beyond these positive developments, our analysis suggests that capital allocation efficiency on the mainland appears to have improved. Specifically, borrowing constraints on state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capabilities seem to have tightened, possibly due to reduced support from local governments (see Topic 2 on page 28 for details). Regarding external factors, capital outflow pressures remained moderate throughout most of 2017, aided by stabilizing economic conditions and reduced risk levels. In Hong Kong, the economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP expanded by 3.8% for the full year, marking the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favorable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow robustly in the latter half of the year. Overall investment spending also rebounded, driven by increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance further improved, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net goods exports continued to weigh on GDP growth, while net services exports made a positive contribution. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018, supported by private consumption, construction and real estate activities, as well as exports. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates are ultimately set to rise, Topic 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage burdens on private consumption. Both government forecasts and market consensus project real GDP growth of 3–4% and 3.0% respectively for 2018. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the Chinese mainland’s economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, as well as trends in the local asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to 2.9%, a near 20-year low, domestic inflationary pressures remained under control. That said, there have been slight signs of rising quarter-on-quarter inflation recently, with both traded goods and services prices increasing. Looking ahead, underlying inflation is likely to edge up to a still-moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of recently signed increases in private residential rents. Tightening liquidity conditions—driven by funding demands from new share offerings and seasonal factors—and increased unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions contributed to a strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar spot rate between September and November 2017. Since December 2017, however, the currency has weakened again as liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities picked up. At the start of 2018, despite volatility in global financial markets, particularly equities, the Hong Kong dollar largely remained stable. It weakened further in early March 2018, yet the currency peg was not tested. From September to December 2017, upward pressure emerged on Hong Kong dollar interbank rates, primarily due to funding demands from new share offerings and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management toward year-end. In December, the average overnight and 3-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively compared to six months earlier, reaching 0.25% and 1.26%. After a slight dip in early January 2018, HIBORs generally stabilized, remaining unaffected by recent global market corrections. Despite intense competition in the mortgage market, the average interest rate on newly issued mortgages rose to 2.16% in December, tracking the upward trend in short-term HIBORs. Meanwhile, retail banking funding costs remained generally low following a brief uptick in October due to new share offerings; the composite rate stood at 0.38% in December. Moving forward, as US monetary policy continues normalizing, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; any sharp shifts in global market sentiment could also increase capital flow volatility. Throughout 2017, total bank lending grew steadily by 16.1%. After a robust 10.2% increase in the first half, the growth rate slowed to 5.3% in the second half, with declines observed in both domestic lending and lending for use outside Hong Kong across most sectors. Growth in foreign currency lending slowed partly due to rising US dollar funding costs, while Hong Kong dollar lending continued to expand rapidly, supported by a favorable local economic environment and relatively low funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar lending outpaced deposit growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% by year-end—the highest level since March 2015. Conversely, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% by year-end due to relatively sluggish growth in foreign currency lending. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilizing between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, both the onshore and offshore renminbi rates strengthened starting from December. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool—which includes total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit—rebounded slightly in the second half of the year after a minor decline in the first half, broadly reflecting shifts in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. Regarding other offshore renminbi activities, although renminbi lending continued to decline, the volume of renminbi trade settlements processed by Hong Kong banks rose in the latter half of the year. Meanwhile, the average daily turnover on the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the ongoing implementation of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalization of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 shows no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects drove global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States, a wave of selling and heightened volatility swept across global equity markets in February, marking an end to the relative calm seen over the previous two years. Looking ahead, the risks of tightening global financial conditions, along with various policy and event-related risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. In a tight labour market environment, U.S. tax cuts may accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to hasten its pace of monetary tightening. As the Fed proceeds with balance sheet normalization, increased issuance of U.S. Treasury bonds to fund these tax cuts could exert upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, supported by robust export performance and steady domestic demand. Despite this optimistic outlook, multiple downside risks remain, including the possibility of more pronounced global monetary tightening than anticipated, as well as U.S. protectionist trade policies and geopolitical tensions. Should these risks materialize, they could also heighten the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face the dual challenge of mitigating risks to economic growth while limiting the impact of prolonged easy financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In mainland China, economic performance remained strong in the second half of 2017. Over this period, some progress was made in advancing structural reforms and curbing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist; these will depend in part on how effectively the rapid growth of the “new economy” can offset any short-term drag on growth stemming from further structural reforms. With economic conditions stabilizing and risks subsiding, capital outflow pressure remained moderate throughout most of 2017. As the cyclical economic uptrend has gained momentum since late 2016, both advanced and emerging economies experienced accelerated growth in 2017. Among major advanced economies, the U.S. saw solid gains in investment and exports, driven by improving private-sector sentiment and a substantial depreciation of the U.S. dollar; the eurozone and Japan also experienced broad-based cyclical recoveries. Emerging economies also benefited from stabilizing global commodity prices and rising import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, following U.S. tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive further boosts from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. Given this ongoing cyclical uptrend and the expansionary effects of U.S. tax reform, the International Monetary Fund projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1: Projections for real GDP growth. With stronger growth momentum in the eurozone and Japan, expectations of a narrowing divergence in global monetary policies, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, helped to increase risk appetite and spur capital inflows into emerging economies, thereby putting downward pressure on the U.S. dollar. Despite three interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve and the commencement of balance sheet normalization, the U.S. Dollar Index still fell by nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite overall acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below central bank targets, leading markets to anticipate that global interest rates would stay low well into the future (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global stock markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly hitting new highs. This drove the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio up to 33.8 in January 2018—the highest level since the dot-com bubble at the start of 2000. Figure 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies  However, since the second half of 2017, concerns have grown that tax cuts would widen fiscal deficits and fuel inflation, prompting a steady rise in US long-term Treasury yields. This has cast doubt on whether the ever-rising asset market valuations can be sustained. When the US reported that average hourly wage growth in January 2018 exceeded expectations, markets re-evaluated inflation risks, triggering a correction in global stock markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index tumbled more than 10% from its January 26 peak, erasing all its gains from the start of the year; it remained under pressure after the US government announced new trade protection measures in early March. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note also climbed to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply; the CBOE Volatility Index briefly hit a two-year high of 37.3, signaling an end to the period of low volatility seen over the previous two years (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 CBOE Volatility Index (VIX)  Looking ahead, following the recent short-term stock market volatility, inflation risks in the US, upward pressure on long-term Treasury yields, and possible monetary tightening by other major central banks could all contribute to a tightening of global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, regarding inflation risks in the US, the recently enacted tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. Key measures under the reform include: (1) lowering corporate and individual income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time “deemed repatriation” rule designed to reduce US firms’ incentives to keep overseas earnings abroad. Although it remains unclear how these tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, given that the US economy is already operating at its production potential, the cuts could push output beyond that potential level, leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. Should inflation pressures rise more sharply than anticipated, the Federal Reserve might accelerate its pace of monetary tightening. Currently, financial markets anticipate a more gradual trajectory for the federal funds rate than what the Fed itself projects. Nevertheless, if inflation were to rebound unexpectedly, there is a risk of a sudden revision upward in rate-hike expectations (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4 Federal funds rate projections  Second, given that the tax reform is likely to exacerbate fiscal deficits, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase going forward. As the Fed continues its balance sheet normalization program, this is likely to push up term premiums; under such circumstances, higher Treasury issuance could intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Additionally, since the second half of 2017, inflation expectations in the US have been on the rise, driven by growing optimism over the likelihood of tax reform being enacted (Figure 2.5). Consequently, after remaining at low levels for most of 2017, the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note has risen by over 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting concerns over rising Treasury supply and heightened inflation expectations. Figure 2.5 5-year and 10-year forward inflation expectations  Furthermore, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), which constitutes a major component of long-term interest rates, will indeed remain low over the long term, as most analysts anticipate. Although estimates of R* vary, there is broad consensus that it has declined substantially since the global financial crisis (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, given that (1) an anticipated rise in fiscal deficits may lead to a decline in the national savings rate, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment for capital expenditure could boost the investment rate, the R\* level in the United States may be at risk of rising in the future. An increase in R\* coupled with expectations of Fed balance sheet normalization is likely to push up term premiums, potentially signaling higher long-term interest rates and exerting downward pressure on asset market valuations. Figure 2.6 shows the estimated R\* level in the U.S. based on the Laubach-Williams model.  Thirdly, stronger growth momentum in the Eurozone and Japan has led markets to anticipate that their respective central banks might scale back monetary easing measures. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Eurozone, all member economies are experiencing broad-based cyclical expansion (Figure 2.7). In Japan, the economy has also accelerated its recovery; real GDP posted positive growth for the eighth consecutive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan continue to signal their intention to maintain accommodative monetary policies amid subdued inflation, the improving economic outlook in both regions—along with Japan’s tightening labor market—has led some market participants to predict further tapering of quantitative easing programs in the near future. Figure 2.7 illustrates real GDP trends in select Eurozone countries.  Policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent global economic recovery and trade rebound. The U.S. government appears inclined toward inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries; recent examples include the imposition of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines in January 2018, followed by tariffs on steel and aluminum announced in early March. These measures raise concerns over potential retaliatory actions by trading partners. Meanwhile, negotiations between the UK and other EU members regarding post-Brexit trade arrangements remain fraught with uncertainties. Should these developments lead to heightened trade frictions, global trade flows and overall production efficiency could be adversely affected. Additionally, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions—such as military conflicts on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East, or latent risks of terrorist attacks—could increase volatility in global financial markets.  In East Asia, growth momentum further strengthened in the second half of 2017, resulting in a robust full-year performance. Real GDP growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, marking the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained a key growth driver, while domestic demand provided steady support (Figure 2.8). The accelerating recovery of advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in mainland China, and rebounding global demand for technology products all contributed to export growth in the region. Figure 2.8 depicts domestic demand and export trends in East Asia.  Inflationary pressures have remained subdued thus far. In the latter half of 2017, overall inflation in East Asia eased due to declining food price inflation and stable energy prices (Figure 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation—excluding food and energy—remained low across multiple economies, reflecting sluggish wage growth. Driven by robust domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained steady growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. However, the economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiments, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although domestic inflationary pressures are expected to stay moderate, certain upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy continued to grow in the latter half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the 3rd and 4th quarters, a figure comparable to the average 0.9% growth rate recorded in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared to the first half of the year, private consumption remained robust and continued to serve as one of the main drivers of GDP growth. This steady consumption growth was fueled by favorable employment and income conditions, continued optimism among consumers, and the positive wealth effect stemming from rising asset prices. Although activity in the property and construction sectors slowed down, corporate capital expenditure increased, resulting in a notable rise in overall investment spending in the final quarter after three quarters of relatively stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance further improved, aided by stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods continued to weigh on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution by major expenditure components   Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports    The sustained economic momentum also led to job creation in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by approximately 0.7% to exceed 385 million people during this period, with the most significant increases observed in the construction, financial and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. Given that real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labor productivity showed further signs of improvement. Growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Externally, Hong Kong’s export performance is anticipated to benefit from improved global economic prospects and a continued recovery in inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is projected to keep expanding, primarily due to favorable labor market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to rise eventually, Special Topic 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage burdens on private consumption. As for domestic fixed capital formation, activity in the property and construction sectors should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and ongoing infrastructure projects. Although an improving economic environment is likely to stimulate business capital expenditure, the potential rise in interest rates may exert a negative influence. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2018 to range between 3 and 4%, while international institutions and private-sector analysts project growth between 2 and 4%. Nonetheless, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains contingent upon various uncertainties and risks, including the external environment outlined in earlier sections, the performance of the Chinese mainland economy amid tightening financial conditions, and trends in local asset markets. Domestic inflationary pressures remained under control in the second half of 2017; however, month-on-month inflation momentum showed slight signs of picking up in recent months. Year-on-year, the underlying composite CPI rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, figures comparable to the average annual increase of around 1.7% recorded in the first half of the year. That said, the three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Both prices of traded goods and services contributed to this rise. The rebound in newly signed private residential rents since mid-2016 may also have contributed to inflationary pressures to some extent (Chart 3.4). Meanwhile, labour cost pressures have remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 shows various indicators of consumer price inflation; Chart 3.4 depicts the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents; Chart 3.5 shows unit labour cost and average wages per employee. Given that global inflation remains moderate and local cost increases are steady, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to stay mild in 2018, though the underlying inflation rate is likely to gradually rise from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, owing to the transmission effect of rising newly signed private residential rents, inflationary pressures may intensify in the second half of 2018. Consensus market forecasts put overall inflation at a modest 2.2% for 2018, while the Government projects the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is benign, upside risks persist. Externally, any unexpected surge in global inflation or commodity prices could heighten local inflationary pressures. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently; the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, marking the first time in almost 20 years that it dropped below 3% (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; should the labour market tighten significantly, this could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the global financial crisis in 2008, interest rates remained low, leading to a rise in mortgage debt among Hong Kong households. As US interest rates undergo normalisation, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow suit, thereby increasing future mortgage repayment burdens and dampening household consumption. Hence, this special study examines how rising mortgage burdens affect private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage burden is defined as the proportion of mortgage repayments—comprising interest payments and principal amortisation—to household income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage burden in transmitting interest rate shocks to private consumption. Apart from the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect and collateral effect stemming from asset price movements as described in standard economic theory, interest rate shocks also influence private consumption under conditions of mortgage burden by altering the amount of interest payments and consequently household disposable income. This impact intensifies as outstanding mortgage debt rises. Additionally, principal amortisation amounts vary with outstanding mortgage debt levels, thereby affecting disposable income and private consumption as well. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To gauge the impact of mortgage burden on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt-to-Income Ratio (OMDSR) based on total outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike existing mortgage burden indicators applicable solely to newly issued mortgages, OMDSR encompasses all outstanding household mortgage debt, which bears a closer relationship to overall private consumption. Drawing broadly on methodology employed by the Bank for International Settlements, we calculated OMDSR using a standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt represents total outstanding residential mortgage debt in the banking sector, Yt denotes total income of owner-occupier households (measured by multiplying median income of such households by their total number), while rt and st stand for average interest rate and term of outstanding mortgages respectively. To assess whether OMDSR reliably measures mortgage burden across the entire household sector, it is advisable to compare it against two commonly used burden indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median debt servicing ratio (DSR) of mortgage payments and loan repayments relative to household income, as estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios showed a downward trend, which aligns with the concurrent decline in overall household mortgage borrowing and the significant drop in mortgage interest rates following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997. Despite a substantial rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, largely due to the HKMA’s macroprudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which helped contain overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the lengthening of terms for newly issued mortgages contributed to a reduction in actual mortgage payments. Figure B3.2 OMDSR and median debt-servicing and repayment-to-income ratios  We also compared the OMDSR with the DSR calculated by banks, which represents the actual debt-servicing ratio of new mortgage applicants. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR remains lower than the banks’ DSR, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. This is partly because the OMDSR encompasses both existing and new mortgages; since existing mortgages were taken out when property prices were lower, their monthly payments are naturally lower than those of new mortgages. Consequently, the OMDSR—which reflects the overall burden of all outstanding mortgage payments—is lower than the DSR calculated solely for new mortgages. Moreover, the higher level of banks’ DSR stems from their compliance with HKMA prudential regulations, which require them to factor in non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the DSR. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks’ DSR remained stable, thanks to the HKMA’s macroprudential oversight of mortgage lending, including the imposition of caps on banks’ DSR levels, which in turn helped stabilize the OMDSR (Chart B3.3). Overall, the OMDSR closely mirrors commonly used debt burden indicators; however, it offers greater timeliness and captures the overall burden of all outstanding mortgage debt rather than just that of newly issued mortgages. Therefore, we believe the OMDSR serves as a reliable gauge for assessing how mortgage payments affect private consumption. To evaluate this relationship, we estimated an error-correction model following the methodologies outlined by Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-term relationship between real private consumption—measured by real average household consumption per capita—and its determinants is captured via an error-correction term within the short-term equation. Drawing on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we identified real income (measured by median household income adjusted for the Composite Consumer Price Index), real housing and financial wealth (measured by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, also adjusted for inflation), and the OMDSR as the key long-term determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but the growth rate slowed compared to the first half of the year. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, the Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly, the volatility of capital flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate briefly strengthened between September and November 2017, remaining at a level around 7.80. This was mainly due to increased funding demand from IPO activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management at month-end and year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions, thereby slowing down interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. As the tight liquidity situation in the Hong Kong dollar eased and commercial demand for the US dollar rose at year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (especially stock markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This is broadly in line with the trend of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners is very small and has a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to closely track the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded an inflow in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics show that equity portfolio investment by both residents and non-residents recorded an inflow in the third quarter, reflecting an improved economic outlook in the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt portfolio investment by non-residents recorded an inflow in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflow from debt investment by residents. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, due to optimistic views on the economic outlook and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that despite the correction in global financial markets, equity investment still recorded inflows, while bond investment recorded a slight outflow (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalisation process continues, the negative interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to an increase in arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking for the Hong Kong dollar being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given the uncertain pace of US monetary policy normalisation and the rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, the volatility of Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully guarantee the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the US Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base further increased by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly due to the growth of Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the total amount of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained basically unchanged in the second half of the year, at about HK$1,226.8 billion. Among them, the Aggregate Balance shrank, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased accordingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet the huge demand from banks for liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite the stock market correction, the monetary base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of the Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half of the year to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7). Among them, demand deposits grew faster in the second half of the year, partly due to the buoyant asset market and rising investment demand. An analysis of the counterpart assets shows that the growth of HKD M3 was supported by the strong growth of Hong Kong dollar loans on the one hand (Chart 4.6), and dragged down by the net outflow of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction of banks' net foreign currency assets on the other. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKD M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half of the year to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after a continuous decline for more than two years, rebounded significantly in the second half of the year, with an increase of 8.4%. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in RMB deposits. Due to the slowdown in the growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits, total deposits of authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half of the year, while the growth rate in the first half was 5.6%. For the full year of 2017, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, which was broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth From September to December 2017, the increased funding demand from IPO activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management at month-end and year-end put upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months ago, the overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, to 0.25% and 1.26% in December (on a monthly average basis). The negative interest rate spread between the 1-month to 3-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates also narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, which was broadly in line with the trend of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half of the year, the 3-year Hong Kong government bond yield rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the 10-year Hong Kong government bond yield rose less, by 33 basis points, to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, Composite Interest Rate and average mortgage rate for new loans Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates fell in early January. Since then, despite the correction in global and local stock markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have remained broadly stable. The overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose along with the surge in Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, banks' funding costs generally remained low due to the still large deposit base. Despite fierce competition in the mortgage business, the average mortgage rate for new loans gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the rise in the 1-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. On the other hand, the Composite Interest Rate, which measures the funding cost of retail banks' Hong Kong dollars, although briefly rising in October due to increased funding demand from IPO activities, remained soft for most of the second half of the year, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, and other major economies may also start interest rate normalisation, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase the volatility of capital flows. However, the large Hong Kong dollar monetary base can serve as a buffer to help moderate any excessive rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and access to the discount window also help to curb excessive volatility in interbank offered rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate was as high as 10.2% in the first half of the year, but slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, the growth of both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed down. Analysed by currency, due to the favourable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans only rose slightly by 0.1%. Among them, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to the rise in US dollar funding costs. For the full year of 2017, total loans recorded a strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth The growth of loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) fell from 9.4% in the first half of the year to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major industries (Chart 4.11). The loan growth for the construction and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half of the year, partly because authorities required banks to strengthen risk management of loans to property developers starting from June 2017. Despite further improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and the transport industry only recorded relatively slight increases, while loans for the wholesale and retail trade sector recorded a decrease. In contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related enterprises remained strong, which to some extent reflected the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11 Local loan growth by individual industry Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with a 5.0% increase in the first half. Within household debt, the growth of personal loans (including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes) further accelerated, with an increase of 12.4% in the second half of the year. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management clients with financial assets as collateral. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth of client assets managed by banks. The risks of such collateralised loans are manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidance to banks on the risk management of personal loans in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting limits on loan tenors and borrowers' debt-to-income ratios. On the other hand, although residential property transactions increased, the loan-to-value ratio of new mortgages fell, and the growth rate of residential mortgage loans slipped slightly to 3.8% in the second half of the year. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Driven primarily by growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained robust. Following strong credit growth in the first half of 2017, credit expansion slowed down in the latter half; nevertheless, asset quality remained solid by historical standards. Despite a marked rise in Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBORs), the cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks stayed low, thanks to persistently low retail deposit rates. However, banks should remain vigilant against risks stemming from heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows associated with the normalization of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the ongoing rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt, banks must assess how any greater-than-expected interest rate hikes might affect asset quality. To strengthen banks’ resilience against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% effective 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks rose by 13.6% year-on-year. This was largely attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan loss provisions, which offset the decline in non-interest income. Nevertheless, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets for retail banks dipped slightly from 1.17% in the first half of 2017 to 1.15% in the second half. Even so, the return on assets for the second half of 2017 remained above the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the full year 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets climbed to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks In the fourth quarter of 2017, the net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks widened further to 1.5% from 1.34% in the same quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Empirical evidence indicates that this improvement in NIM aligns with the rise in average interest rates on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans within the syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average interest rates on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans Since September 2017, HIBORs have risen across the board, driven mainly by liquidity demands related to initial public offerings and year-end funding needs of banks, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Overall, the average aggregate cost of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding for licensed banks climbed by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). The aggregate capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remains well above international minimum standards, reflecting the robust capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector. As of end-December 2017, the total capital ratio rose to 19.1% from 18.7% at end-June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 16.6%, of which 15.4% comprised common equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.6 Capital levels of locally incorporated authorized institutions    The HKMA recently released a consultation paper seeking views on rules under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance governing the loss-absorption capacity of authorized institutions. While enhancing such capacity benefits society by reducing the likelihood of financial crises, it inevitably entails costs. Topic 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of these loss-absorption requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing such requirements would yield net benefits for the Hong Kong economy. Measured against Basel III’s Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirements, the banking sector’s liquidity position remained sound throughout the review period. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions climbed from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), comfortably exceeding the statutory minimum of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the 25% minimum requirement. The ample liquidity levels of authorized institutions suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector can withstand any liquidity shocks arising from potential outflows of funds from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Stable Liquidity Coverage Ratio    The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), another Basel III liquidity standard, came into effect in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. This requirement aims to mitigate medium- to long-term funding risks by mandating that banks maintain sufficient stable funding sources to support their operations. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of at least 100% at all times. 57 Customer deposits remain the primary funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure within the banking system. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits expanded at a quicker pace than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 65.5% at end-June to 63.1% at end-December. Overall, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio increased from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of a rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. Nevertheless, given expectations of continued interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve and the normalization of its balance sheet, banks should evaluate how this situation affects their interest rate risk management. After two years of decelerating growth, total loans still posted a solid increase of 16.1% for the full year 2017. For retail banks, these ratios also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans used outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may become more sensitive to external conditions; therefore, banks should closely monitor their credit risks.
