The HKMA’s “Opinion Survey on the Outlook for Credit Conditions” conducted in December 2017 revealed that 29% of surveyed authorized institutions anticipated an increase in loan demand over the next 3 months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5. A). During the review period, credit risk associated with personal loans remained low. Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios stayed robust, with the default rate remaining at a low 0.03% at end-December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio for newly approved mortgages further declined from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This ratio is considerably lower than the 64% recorded prior to the implementation of the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures by the HKMA in September 2009.

The global economy maintained growth, but the growth momentum weakened due to persistent trade frictions, tightening financial conditions, and other specific and cyclical headwinds that increased uncertainties. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," leading investors to rule out further interest rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data, especially data that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy, such as rising US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the Hong Kong Dollar triggered the weak-side exchange guarantee in March, HKD trading continued to remain smooth and orderly. In the second half of 2018, the growth in total loan amounts narrowed slightly, reflecting a decline in credit demand under headwinds such as the ongoing US-China trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with a significant drop in transaction volumes and a decline in property prices, followed by signs of stabilization in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking industry faces multiple headwinds due to increasing uncertainties in the external environment. If these uncertainties intensify and persist over the long term, they could significantly suppress business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on bank profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potential deterioration in the external environment on the credit risks of their related corporate loans. In the second half of 2018, the global economy maintained growth. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major Eurozone countries saw slower growth and low inflation. Slowing global trade and a significant drop in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. Given the slowing global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively compared to its October 2018 forecasts. Due to the dimming growth outlook and escalating trade frictions, global stock markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, sparking market concerns that the US was facing an imminent recession. However, US economic fundamentals remain robust, and the possibility of a recession in the short term is low. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation provided the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, the Fed's policy stance of being data-dependent also signaled that financial markets might be more sensitive to subsequent data, particularly data such as rising US inflation that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy. At the same time, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China, as well as between the US and the EU, remain uncertain. In the UK, it remains unknown whether a solution to avoid a "hard Brexit" can be achieved. In East Asia, while the financial markets have stabilized due to the slowing rise of the US dollar and market expectations that the Fed will pause rate hikes, a deteriorating external environment could drag down economic growth in the region. In fact, the weakening momentum of global trade has already weighed on the economic growth of several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures have also eased. While this shift may alleviate the policy dilemma for regional central banks between supporting growth and curbing inflation, financial imbalances such as high debt levels of private institutions in some countries in the region remain severe. As detailed in Topic 1 (page 16), another challenge facing the East Asian region is that if the Federal Reserve's monetary policy undergoes unexpected changes, the resulting impact could affect the sovereign bond markets of emerging market economies (including East Asian economies). In Mainland China, growth further slowed in the second half of 2018 due to increasing uncertainties in the external environment and slightly slowing domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain as the US-China trade negotiations remain unresolved. The significant contraction in shadow financing activities has led to increased financing difficulties for private enterprises (especially small companies) over the past few quarters, which, coupled with weakening economic confidence, may also exert pressure on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers need to continue to strike a balance between stabilizing the economy and containing potential systemic risks by adopting loose but targeted measures (e.g., targeted RRR cuts). At the same time, the authorities are also taking more supply-side measures to enhance productivity growth (e.g., promoting competition among companies with different ownership types), as well as providing a better social safety net for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0–6.5%. In 2018, risk-off sentiment dominated the mainland financial markets. Bank asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage levels of listed non-financial companies rose slightly. However, bank loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, and the risk exposure of their off-balance sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments helped protect the banking system from potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage levels of listed companies in overcapacity industries—one of the main sources of bank credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Topic 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors that prompted the recent improvement in the business performance of overcapacity industries. Compared with the first half of 2018, Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half. The quarter-on-quarter growth rate of local GDP stagnated, and the year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging down the full-year economic growth from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect impacts of the US-China trade conflict. The slowdown in private consumption may reflect the increase in economic uncertainties and the wealth depreciation effect brought about by the adjustment of local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong's merchandise exports also performed poorly, especially after the US and China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Topic 3 takes a closer look at the impact of the US-China trade conflict on Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance and will explore the short-term outlook and its associated risks. Due to the slowdown in global economic growth, economic growth in 2019 is expected to slow down further. Under the mutual influence of multiple factors, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Locally, with low unemployment rates and increased household income, private consumption is expected to continue to support economic growth, but the outlook for overall investment expenditure may become more uncertain. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2019 to be between 2 to 3%, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts average 2.3%. These forecasts are affected by the various uncertainties and risks mentioned above. Local inflation rose slightly in the second half of 2018 but remained at a moderate level. The slight rise in inflation was partly affected by the growth in local private residential rents signed earlier. At the same time, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in over 20 years, the growth in total employment showed signs of slowing down. Looking ahead, as the momentum of local economic growth weakens, local inflation pressure in 2019 is expected to remain moderate. After the weak-side convertibility undertaking was triggered in late August, the HKD exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side convertibility undertaking was triggered again four times in total (as of March 19) in March 2019. The HKD exchange rate rose in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades under tightening liquidity. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) depreciated against the US dollar due to the rebuilding of carry trade positions. Despite the weak-side convertibility guarantee being triggered again in March, HKD trading continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner. Due to the triggering of the weak-side convertibility guarantee, the total balance decreased slightly to HK$709 billion (as of March 19). The HKD interbank offered rate rose significantly in the second half of 2018, primarily reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong bank interbank offered rates rose by approximately 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December (on a monthly average basis). Entering 2019, the HKD bank interbank offered rate fell overall due to waning seasonal demand. The composite rate measuring the average HKD financing cost for retail banks rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. Given the rising financing costs, following the upward adjustment of the US Federal Funds target range at the end of September, retail banks raised their prime lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. By the end of January 2019, the average lending rate for new mortgages followed the prime lending rate to rise to approximately 2.45%. Due to continued uncertainties related to China-US trade frictions and Brexit negotiations, capital flow volatility may intensify. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between the HKD and the USD may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to capital outflows. In this situation, capital outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side convertibility guarantee are normal operations under the linked exchange rate system. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (RMB) exchange rates have faced depreciation pressure due to market concerns over escalating China-US trade frictions. However, under the optimistic sentiment driven by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US, the CNH and RMB exchange rates stabilized in November. Although China-US trade frictions persist, they have not yet had a significant impact on the liquidity situation in the offshore bank interbank market. The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong bank interbank offered rate remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month offshore renminbi interbank offered rate hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily transaction volume of the renminbi real-time payment settlement system remained at a high level and further increased to RMB1.0101 trillion in 2018. Despite concerns over China-US trade frictions, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to continue expanding, driven by the opening of the mainland's capital account, the development of stock and bond connectivity, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives. The local stock market took a roller coaster ride over the past six months. At the beginning of the review period, the market fell sharply due to the continued tightening of US monetary policy, significant disagreements between both sides in China-US trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in the mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance; meanwhile, during the trade war truce, China took more measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the US filed a highly political lawsuit against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides displayed a friendly posture, indicating a determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local stock market rebounded rapidly at the beginning of this year. However, as both sides discuss the details of the agreement (if any), the future remains quite uncertain, and the future developments of the US federal government's lawsuit will complicate the situation, particularly in the high-tech sector. The HKD debt market grew slightly last year. Yields fell, and as the end of the year approached, expectations that the pace of normalization of US monetary policy would slow down strengthened, leading to improved performance. Consequently, fund flows into bond funds reversed and increased slightly in the second half of the year. The issuance of the offshore RMB market in Hong Kong rebounded significantly after decreasing for three consecutive years. However, as mainland companies continue to deleverage, total issuance remains less than maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remains full of challenges, and its prospects depend on global economic developments, particularly those in the mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum weakened amid the combined impact of special and cyclical headwinds, with the slowdown particularly evident in regions outside the US. In view of the dimmer growth outlook, the Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, stressing that decisions would be “data-dependent” and that “patience” was needed, and it no longer provided forward guidance on further rate hikes. As the Fed’s policy stance has turned more data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data releases and may perceive monetary policy as increasingly uncertain. At the same time, heightened uncertainties surrounding global trade policies and rising geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook.  In East Asia, financial markets have generally stabilised since end-2018, as signs of a slowdown in the US rate hike cycle emerged and the US dollar became more stable. However, amid a deteriorating external environment – including the unresolved US–Mainland China trade conflict and weaker growth in advanced economies – the region may face a broad-based slowdown. On the Mainland, growth momentum weakened further in the second half of 2018, and uncertainties over the growth outlook increased in the face of the US–Mainland China trade conflict and financing difficulties for small firms. In response, policymakers introduced more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support the private sector and small enterprises. Confronted with these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to contain systemic risks and supporting corporates and the real economy.  In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to register broad-based growth. However, although the US economy remained generally solid, some signs of deceleration emerged. There were also clear indications that growth momentum outside the US had slowed. A number of country-specific shocks – including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian sovereign bond yields amid a fiscal standoff with the EU, and social unrest in France – weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, global import growth experienced a cyclical slowdown, posing headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also posed new challenges for oil-exporting emerging market economies.  Reflecting the weaker growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund in January revised down its forecast for global growth in 2019 by 0.2 percentage point to 3.5%. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices of selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volumes and industrial production in emerging market economies  In the fourth quarter, as global growth momentum weakened, uncertainties about trade policies intensified, concerns mounted over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Fed signalled that monetary policy tightening would continue, global equity markets underwent a sharp correction. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, triggering concerns among some market participants that a US recession might be imminent (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Yield spread between 10-year and 3-month US Treasuries and the probability of a US recession  That said, the probability of a US recession in the near term is very low. The US economic fundamentals remain solid, especially with a tight labour market that is expected to continue supporting private consumption. At the same time, it is estimated that the US output gap only turned positive again last year, suggesting that the likelihood of the economy overheating to an extent that would prompt the Fed to aggressively tighten monetary policy is low. However, perhaps taking into account the significant tightening in financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data-dependent, and noted that moderate inflationary pressures allowed them to remain “patient” when considering future adjustments to monetary policy. In addition, after its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee stopped providing forward guidance on further rate hikes, and announced that it “is prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalization in light of economic and financial developments.” This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World (excluding the US) Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index  Despite the Fed’s recent “dovish” signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains highly uncertain and will depend on inflation and other developments. So far, inflationary pressures have been moderate, giving the Fed room to proceed with monetary normalisation gradually. In recent years, inflation expectations have remained stable, supporting the view that the Fed “can be patient” (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell pointed out in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slower growth outside the US and uncertainties about trade policies. In light of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations  Nevertheless, the tight labour market is expected to continue to support overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which usually implies that inflation could pick up going forward (Chart 2.6). Hence, markets may be overly optimistic in essentially pricing out the possibility of Fed rate hikes in 2019 (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds target range staying unchanged versus at least one rate hike in 2019  All in all, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy mistakes, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data-dependent as part of a risk-management strategy. This implies that financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data releases, especially those that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy.  Uncertainties also surround the monetary policy paths of other major central banks. In the euro area, the European Central Bank ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, in January the ECB downgraded its assessment of near-term growth, describing the risks to the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside.” The implications of this downgrade for monetary policy remain to be seen.  In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its recent policy meeting that, with downside risks increasing, it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary. However, there may be significant headwinds to further monetary easing, as its effectiveness is increasingly being questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment over a prolonged period have become more apparent. For example, as persistently low yields have continued to weigh on profitability, the capital ratio of regional banks has fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. As a result, the BOJ has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term.  Apart from uncertainties about the global monetary policy outlook, the outcomes of upcoming trade negotiations and rising geopolitical risks are also two major sources of risk facing the global growth outlook. In early December, the US Government announced that it would refrain from increasing tariffs on imports from Mainland China for 90 days, and extended this deadline again in late February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. At the same time, trade negotiations between the US and the EU have made little progress so far. As the outcomes of these negotiations remain highly uncertain, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also highly salient. In the US, disagreements between the two parties over funding for border security led to a partial shutdown of the federal government for 35 days from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be short-lived, the strained relationship between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives may lead to more policy gridlocks going forward.  In the UK, after the May Government’s Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, the risks associated with Brexit and its spillover effects surged, and it remained uncertain whether any plan could be put in place at the last minute to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit”.  Elsewhere, heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East – such as the renewed US sanctions on Iran – could also add uncertainty to oil prices and in turn affect the global growth outlook.  In East Asia, after repeated bouts of volatility in the first three quarters of last year, financial markets largely stabilised in the fourth quarter. The US dollar has been broadly stable since October, and signs that the Fed would be patient about further rate hikes have eased depreciation and capital outflow pressures on East Asian economies. A number of regional currencies edged up against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, and portfolio investment flows reverted to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: currency indices and capital flows  Despite the stabilisation in financial markets, there has been a growing number of signs that the region may face a broad-based slowdown. Weaker global trade momentum caused by the US–Mainland China trade conflict has dampened export growth in the region, leading to slower real GDP growth in most East Asian economies in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices (which reflect short-term external trade performance) of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices in several regional economies have fallen into contraction territory since the fourth quarter, pointing to a further weakening of short-term growth momentum (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 New export orders indices in Markit PMIs of East Asian economies  Against the backdrop of slowing growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: headline inflation and oil prices  With recent inflationary pressures and upward pressures on the US dollar both remaining moderate, East Asian central banks are under less immediate pressure to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy trade-off between supporting economic growth and containing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private sector indebtedness in some East Asian economies remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face challenges from financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

Hong Kong’s economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting a slowdown in private consumption growth and weaker export performance amid the Sino-US trade dispute. With global growth decelerating, real GDP growth in 2019 is also expected to slow down. The growth outlook for Hong Kong is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the performance of the Chinese mainland economy. Inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain moderate in 2019, though both upside and downside risks exist. Economic activities in Hong Kong weakened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, they failed to sustain the strong momentum seen in the first half of the year; the quarter-on-quarter growth rate of GDP turned slightly negative in the latter half of the year (Table 3. A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed down, with the growth rate in the fourth quarter standing at 1.3%, below the trend level. This dragged down the full-year growth rate from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Calculated based on the volume index of GDP compiled on an expenditure basis and seasonally adjusted. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution by major expenditure components  The weakening of economic activities was mainly due to consumption and exports being adversely affected, directly or indirectly, by the Sino-US trade conflict. Perhaps because of heightened economic uncertainties and the wealth-reducing effect stemming from adjustments in local asset prices, the growth rate of private consumption slowed down (Chart 3.1). Total investment expenditure declined significantly amid fragile business confidence. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after the US and China imposed additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, since the total value of imports fell at a faster pace than that of exports, the net trade balance still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Topic 3 will examine Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance in greater detail and discuss its short-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports  With economic activities weakening, the growth of employment also appeared to slow down in the second half of 2018. At the end of 2018, the total number of employed persons rose by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000, a lower rate than the 0.8% increase recorded in the first half of 2018. Owing to sluggish growth in both output and employment, labour productivity remained largely unchanged, showing no signs of substantial improvement. Given the further slowdown in global economic growth, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to decelerate in 2019. Amid external headwinds, Hong Kong’s export performance is likely to remain under pressure. Domestically, although a low unemployment rate and rising household incomes will continue to support private consumption, the growth rate of private consumption is expected to slow down, partly due to waning consumer confidence and the wealth-reducing effect stemming from earlier adjustments in asset prices. As for fixed capital formation, the outlook may become even more uncertain. While housing and construction activities are expected to grow steadily with increased housing supply, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment amid heightened economic uncertainties. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index have continued to hover in contraction territory; forecasts derived from this index suggest that the year-on-year growth rate of GDP will further decelerate in the short term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2019 to range between 2 and 3%, while the latest growth estimates by private-sector analysts fall between 1.5 and 2.7%. The growth outlook for Hong Kong is influenced by multiple uncertainties and risks outlined in the previous two chapters. Although inflationary pressures have been gradually building up in recent months, they remain at a moderate level. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 2.8% in the third quarter and 2.9% in the fourth quarter of 2018, both figures higher than the average 2.4% increase recorded in the first half of the year. Inflation momentum, as reflected by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, has also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). This modest uptick in inflation momentum was driven by rising prices in certain services. The recently signed increases in private residential rents and the accelerating rise in dining-out prices continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures remained largely moderate over recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various indicators of consumer price inflation   Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rental rates   Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and average wage    Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019, primarily reflecting weakening domestic growth momentum. Nevertheless, the earlier uptrend in private residential rents will continue to feed into consumer price inflation. Consensus forecasts put overall inflation for the full year at a modest 2.2%, while the Government projects the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. Both upside and downside risks exist to these inflation outlooks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate has stayed at around 2.8%, the lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). Should the labour market deteriorate unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap could turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. Conversely, any easing of Sino-US trade tensions that leads to better-than-expected domestic economic performance could push up local inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate    Sino-US trade tensions escalated in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the United States imposed 25% tariffs on imports from mainland China worth $34 billion and $16 billion respectively. On 24 September, the US further raised tariffs to 10% on imports from mainland China valued at $2,000 billion; mainland China promptly imposed 5–10% tariffs on US goods worth $600 billion. Subsequently, both sides entered negotiations to avert further tariff hikes. Given Hong Kong’s long-standing role as a re-export hub between these two economies, the imposition of tariffs inevitably has a direct impact on Hong Kong via trade channels. Hence, the Sino-US trade dispute carries important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomic and financial stability. This special feature reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and explores its short-term prospects. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify trade items directly affected by the tariff hikes, thereby examining their impact in greater detail. To analyse the effects of the tariffs, we first selected six groups of Hong Kong re-export data, each affected by one of the rounds of tariff hikes described earlier. In the first two rounds, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactured products, while mainland China targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round, the scope of affected goods expanded to include more consumer products. For simplicity, we refer to goods affected by these three rounds as List 1, List 2, and List 3 respectively. Having gathered this more detailed trade data, we focused on analysing year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports, adjusting for seasonal factors. Readers should also exercise caution when interpreting September 2018 data, as trade activity that month was somewhat disrupted by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings presented here should be regarded merely as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariff hikes. Shortly after additional tariffs were imposed on Hong Kong re-exports originating from mainland China and subject to such duties, the volume of related goods re-exported from mainland China via Hong Kong to the United States appears to have declined significantly or seen a slowdown in growth (Chart B3.1). For instance, the growth in re-exports under List 1 and List 2 slowed down in the first month following the tariff imposition, while List 3 even recorded negative growth. Moreover, all three lists showed negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from mainland China to the United States via Hong Kong in 2018  In contrast, the performance of goods re-exported from the United States to mainland China via Hong Kong, which also originate from the US and are subject to tariffs, varied (Chart B3.2). Re-exports under List 1 appeared to drop sharply in the months following the tariff implementation, though they rebounded toward the end of the year. Re-exports under List 2 remained largely in negative growth territory throughout the year, while List 3 showed relatively stable growth. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the United States to mainland China via Hong Kong in 2018  Front-loading: Due to the time lag between the announcement and actual implementation of tariffs (or simply the threat of such tariffs), firms may increase shipments of affected goods prior to the expected effective date. Indeed, various data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behavior is quite common. Some private sector analysts also attribute part of the strong overall trade figures prior to tariff implementation to this phenomenon. More detailed trade data reveal signs of front-loading for certain tariffed goods, but this appears to apply only to goods re-exported from mainland China to the United States (Chart B3.1). The growth rates of List 1 and List 2 re-exports both rose in the months preceding their respective tariff implementations. On the other hand, the growth rate of goods re-exported from the United States to mainland China (Chart B3.2) shows no clear evidence of front-loading behavior by firms. Re-exports from Hong Kong not affected by tariffs: It is worth noting that re-exports from Hong Kong directly affected by additional tariffs account for only about 4–5% of total re-export volume. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, we must also examine re-exports unaffected by these tariffs. We found that such re-exports recorded negative growth in both November and December 2018 (Chart B3.3). Meanwhile, the growth rate of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) declined more sharply starting from the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of tariffs. The slowdown in growth of non-tariff-affected re-exports partly reflects weakening external demand. Given ongoing trade tensions, heightened uncertainty, tighter global financial conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, external demand may continue to weaken more broadly. In particular, trade disputes have dampened global economic sentiment and activity, as evidenced by corrections in major equity markets. Consequently, import demand from other economies has declined, adversely affecting Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong’s re-exports in 2018  Even if Sino-US trade tensions ease, Hong Kong’s short-term prospects for merchandise trade remain challenging. Global growth is expected to slow down in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further dampen Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that firms of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with the trade sector experiencing particularly low sentiment levels. Other trade-related sectors such as logistics may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Business outlook survey for Hong Kong’s import and export sectors

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting a tightening of liquidity driven by expected seasonal funding demands, which led to the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the HKD exchange rate gradually softened due in part to the repatriation of funds from new share capital raising by corporations and the market's re-establishment of carry trade positions, triggering the weak-side currency intervention (CU) in March. Nevertheless, HKD trading remained smooth and orderly. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demands, before retreating in January 2019. Looking ahead, capital flows for the HKD may be more volatile given uncertain factors such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization. If the HKD-USD interest rate differential remains large, market carry trade activities may persist, causing the HKD to remain relatively weak over the coming period and potentially triggering the weak-side CU again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Following the weak-side CU trigger in late August, the HKD exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the HKD triggered the weak-side CU again in March 2019, totaling 4 times (as of March 19) (Chart 4.1). The HKD exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades under tightening liquidity, but gradually fell thereafter in October. The HKD stabilized again after November due to the tightening of liquidity driven by year-end funding demands, leading to the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting the repatriation of funds from new share capital raising by corporations and the market's re-establishment of carry trade positions. As the HKD-USD interest rate differential widened after the year-end, it triggered carry trade activities by market participants buying US dollars and selling HKD, driving the HKD gradually weaker and triggering the weak-side CU again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side CU, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance has remained at a level of approximately HK$760 billion since August (Chart 4.2), slightly decreasing to HK$709 billion after the weak-side CU was triggered in March (as of March 19). The capital outflow of HKD from April 2018 to date accounts for only a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion inflow since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Capital flow indicator The nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the HKD broadly tracks the movements of the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). Since the inflation rate gap between Hong Kong and its trading partners is very small, the impact on the HKD real effective exchange rate index (REER) is limited, and the trend of the HKD REER broadly follows the NEER. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates The latest balance of payments statistics show that securities investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amidst a weak market sentiment and heightened stock market volatility, the outflow of equity securities investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting the inflow of securities investment by non-local residents in the third quarter (Table 4. A). In contrast, debt securities investment by local and non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, capital flow volatility may intensify given uncertain factors such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between the HKD and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the LERS, the HKD exchange rate may weaken and could potentially trigger the weak-side CU again. Capital outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side CU are normal operations under the LERS. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalization process and the multiple triggering of the weak-side CU between April and August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decrease from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while certificates of indebtedness, banknotes and coins issued by the government, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) increased slightly. The HKD Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$709 billion (as at 19 March). Chart 4.4 Composition of the Monetary Base As for the broader HKD money supply indicators, the growth rate of the money supply generally slowed down in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. HKD broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year and only increased slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As a major component of HKD M3, HKD deposits remained relatively stable compared to the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among HKD deposits, current and savings deposits declined, partly due to a decrease in investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth due to upward adjustments in deposit rates. Corresponding asset analysis shows that the growth of HKD M3 slowed down due to changes in bank capital and reserves (included in "Net other items"). Chart 4.5 HKD M3 and changes in corresponding assets The growth rate of foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half of the year. Due to the increase in deposits attracted after banks raised the preferential deposit rate for US dollars, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half of the year, thus becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits grew slightly by 1.4% in the second half of the year, with RMB deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with AIs grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Although the HKD Monetary Base and deposit scale remained sizeable, the HKD interbank offered rate began to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting the US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demands occasionally pushed up short-term interbank offered rates, leading to greater volatility in the latter compared to long-term interbank offered rates (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong interbank offered rates averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than the average values in June. Entering 2019, the HKD interbank offered rate fell overall as seasonal demand subsided. The average values of the 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong interbank offered rates fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 HKD and USD interbank offered rates The HKD yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly following the movements of the USD yield curve. Compared to the end of June 2018, the yields of 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite rate and new mortgage average lending rate During the review period, the composite rate, which measures the average HKD financing cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit financing costs, the composite rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before falling back to 0.83% in January 2019 (Chart 4.8). Given the rise in financing costs, retail banks raised their prime lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points after the US Federal Funds target range was adjusted upward in September. However, retail banks did not make further adjustments to prime lending rates after the US Federal Funds target range was adjusted upward again in December. On the other hand, the average lending rate for new mortgages followed the prime lending rate and was approximately 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the trend of US interest rates, capital flows, and local financial market activities (such as new share subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of HKD interest rates. Given that the HKD monetary base remains large and the banking system holds a large amount of foreign currency fund certificates, the pace of the rise in HKD interest rates should be relatively moderate as banks can use foreign currency fund certificates as collateral to borrow HKD funds at the discount window. Against the backdrop of intensifying China-US trade frictions, the offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (RMB) exchange rates have depreciated against the US dollar since early 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, under the optimistic sentiment driven by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US, the CNH and RMB exchange rates stabilized in November. At the same time, the spread between onshore renminbi and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Currently, ongoing China-US trade frictions have not yet had a significant impact on the liquidity of the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained largely stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of the review period, rising occasionally only due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, which may reflect the recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of the progress of China-US trade negotiations on the liquidity of the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019 remains to be observed. Chart 4.10 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) grew slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4. B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. The growth rate of corporate customer deposits was faster than that of individual customer deposits. However, the balance of certificates of deposit further declined by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to a decrease in the issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively larger number of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Benefiting primarily from increased net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared to the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained robust. Reflecting upward pressure on Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBORs) and retail deposit rates under the normalization of US interest rates, the overall HKD funding costs of retail banks rose significantly, but remained at relatively low levels. Under an uncertain external environment, bank lending contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilizing since November, and asset quality remains robust by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking industry will face multiple headwinds due to continued uncertainty in US-China trade relations, a global economic slowdown, uncertainty regarding the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels, banks should remain vigilant regarding the impact of a potential further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared to the same period in 2017, while the return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly benefited by the substantial growth in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the increase in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, and the return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% for the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks The NIM of retail banks roughly reflected further US interest rate hikes and a decline in HKD liquidity among Hong Kong banks after the weak-side swap guarantee was triggered in August 2018; funding costs for Hong Kong banks continued to experience upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally increased time deposit rates to secure long-term stable funding, retail HKD deposit rates also rose during the review period. Additionally, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their prime lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given that both wholesale and retail funding costs rose, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at relatively low levels by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) Year-end figures. (b) Period average figures for new loans. On a broader level, the overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to show an upward trend. In the second half of 2018, the average overall HKD and USD funding costs of banks rose by 36 basis points, while they rose by 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Funding costs of licensed banks in HKD and USD The cumulative increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in overall funding costs for Hong Kong banks, which may have a positive impact on mortgage loans based on HIBORs for retail banks, as the industry has actively promoted such loans in recent years. However, future improvements in NIM may become more limited, as most mortgage loans based on HIBORs have already reached the cap rates based on prime lending rates. Since the timing of future prime lending rate increases remains uncertain, the continued upward trend in bank funding costs under the normalization of US interest rates may weigh on the overall NIM. Looking ahead, increasing uncertainty in the external environment may cast a shadow over the profit prospects of banks. Particularly against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, continued uncertainty in China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this situation lead to a significant decline in lending and a deterioration in asset quality, it could place a burden on bank profitability. The capital base of the Hong Kong banking industry remains substantial, far exceeding international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the aggregate total capital ratio of locally incorporated AIs further rose to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Aggregate position. 2. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards cannot be directly compared with data as of December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced non-risk-based leverage ratio requirements to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a robust level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum level of 3% (Chart 5.6). The average LCR of Type 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average liquidity maintenance ratio of Type 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Aggregate position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The average NSFR of Type 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average core funding ratio of Type 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and robust funding positions of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking industry is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Against the backdrop of continued uncertainty over China-US trade conflicts, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of recovery since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, the total amount of loans and advances of all authorized institutions in the second half of 2018 decreased by 0.9% after an increase of 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to the slowing growth of local loans (including loans and trade financing used within Hong Kong) and a decrease in the amount of loans used outside Hong Kong. Local loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while the amount of loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% during the same period, compared to growth of 5.3% and 5.2% in the first six months, respectively.
