On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to the slowing growth of private loans (including credit card advances and other private purpose loans) offsetting the rapid growth of residential mortgage loans (Table 5. B). As the growth rate of Hong Kong's nominal gross domestic product (GDP) was slower than the growth rate of personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose slightly from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

Since the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic in early 2020, both demand and supply have been adversely affected, posing challenges to the global economy unlike those seen in previous crises. Although major central banks and several governments introduced stimulus measures starting in early March to mitigate the economic impact of the pandemic, financial markets remained volatile and global financial conditions tightened. Despite uncertainties in both external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and orderly. With a relatively strong Hong Kong dollar, stable total reserves, and modest growth in total deposits, no significant outflows of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the banking system were observed during the review period. After a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, the growth rate of total loans slowed down in the second half. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trend has been somewhat erratic. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the ongoing rise in corporate leverage and household debt levels, banks should prudently assess how the asset quality of their loan portfolios might be affected under these heightened risks. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown initial signs of stabilization, aided by intensified monetary easing by major central banks, easing Sino-US trade tensions, and a reduced risk of a “no-deal” Brexit. However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has raised market concerns and triggered substantial volatility in global financial markets. To address evolving pandemic risks, several major central banks slashed interest rates and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp declines in equity markets. Looking forward, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic is expected to dampen global economic activity, with the extent of its impact depending on its severity and duration. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners may tighten once again, while trade negotiations between the UK and the EU following Brexit could prove difficult. Weak global demand continues to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 Exports from the region to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and mainland China remained sluggish in the second half of 2019. Although several major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, it remains to be seen whether the technology sector cycle will experience a broad-based rebound. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One Sino-US trade agreement announced in December 2019; the trade truce has, to some extent, reduced global trade uncertainties. That said, East Asia will continue to grapple with weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region’s economies may face further pressure amid persistently sluggish growth. Travel bans imposed by various economies in the region could adversely affect Asia’s tourism sector, particularly economies heavily reliant on tourism-related exports. Given the region’s close integration with mainland China’s supply chains, the manufacturing sector may also be impacted by the outbreak. In mainland China, economic growth continued to decelerate in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One Sino-US trade agreement helps alleviate external uncertainties for the mainland economy, downward pressures remain due to the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 identified economic stability as a key priority for 2020, while also emphasizing the need to control financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts predict that mainland China’s economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to roll out targeted monetary and fiscal policies aimed at supporting the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial firms may have experienced a decline in shareholders’ equity in recent years, which is regarded as a sign of “regression in the private sector.” Topic 2 examines the factors driving changes in the equity of mainland Chinese industrial firms using data from listed companies in 2018. It finds that private or small-sized enterprises are not inherently more prone to downsizing or “regression.” While negative profitability emerged as the primary driving factor, other elements—particularly structural factors—also warrant attention (for details, see Topic 2). Economic activity in Hong Kong contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the local economy had entered a recession. Consequently, the economy as a whole shrank by 1.2% in 2019, a marked deterioration from the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018 and the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in domestic demand, especially a decline in private consumption, was the main factor behind the GDP drop in the latter half of 2019. Local social unrest severely disrupted consumer activity, dampening economic prospects and eroding both consumer and business confidence. Amid renewed Sino-US trade tensions, a global economic slowdown, and a sharp decline in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained weak. Given these significant headwinds, the government introduced multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To provide banks with greater capacity to bolster the local economy and help smooth out economic cycles, the HKMA announced on October 14 that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio would be lowered from 2.5% to 2.0%. This adjustment allowed banks to release an additional HK$2,000–3,000 billion in lending capacity, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The economic outlook for 2020 is expected to remain challenging, and the recent pandemic has introduced notable downside risks. Since sectors such as retail, hospitality, food services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the impact of social unrest, the pandemic will deal them a double blow. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures outlined in the 2020/21 Budget will provide relief to households and businesses, especially SMEs; these include one-off cash payments to adult permanent residents and 100% government-guaranteed low-interest loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 2. On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, thereby granting banks even more room to support the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing heightened short-term pressures due to the pandemic. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak amid fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government spending will help sustain economic growth, public investment is expected to remain relatively subdued following the completion of several major infrastructure projects. Externally, the Phase One Sino-US trade agreement is anticipated to exert a modestly positive effect on the local economy in the short term. 3 However, sluggish global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average projection among international institutions and private analysts stands at -1.5%. This bleak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including global economic slowdown, Sino-US trade relations, mainland China’s economic performance, and local social unrest. The labor market faced mounting pressure in the latter half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index posting a year-on-year drop. Specifically, the unemployment rate climbed from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social unrest and the pandemic on retail, hospitality, and food services. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further amid weak economic prospects and the coronavirus outbreak. Topic 3 will delve into recent labor market developments and short-term prospects in greater detail. Local inflationary pressures accumulated through the third quarter of 2019, primarily driven by rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually subsided. Given the weak economic conditions, stabilization of private residential rents, and moderate import inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the near term. Market consensus forecasts place overall inflation in 2020 between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government projects core inflation at 2.5%. Supported by heightened demand for Hong Kong dollars linked to equity-related activities, including initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. In December, this upward trend intensified, partly due to robust IPO activity and partly because year-end liquidity tightening prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar slightly weakened toward the end of February. Overall, during the review period, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly, with no trigger of the exchange rate peg mechanism. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at approximately HK$540 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demands and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Topic 4 examines how market expectations regarding future IPO activity influence the 3-month Hong Kong interbank rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% by end-January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued efforts to raise preferential deposit rates to attract funds. As some banks raised their maximum lending rates tied to the prime rate, the average interest rate on newly issued mortgages climbed to around 2.6% in October; however, following a subsequent cut in the prime rate starting November, this average dipped slightly to roughly 2.5% by January 2020. With a relatively strong Hong Kong dollar, stable total reserves, and modest growth in total deposits, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the banking system were observed during the period. Nevertheless, we must monitor the potential impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus pandemic amid an uncertain external environment. Hong Kong boasts substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system; the HKMA possesses the capability, resources, and resolve to handle capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability. During the review period, market optimism over a Sino-US trade deal bolstered both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates; however, since late January 2020, the outbreak of the coronavirus has exerted downward pressure on these rates. In late 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore rate; by end-January 2020, the discount briefly widened, though the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi funding pool recovered slightly after a slight decline in the previous review period. As of end-January 2020, outstanding renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit totaled RMB637.4 billion. Other renminbi-related activities in Hong Kong also expanded, with strong growth seen in renminbi bank lending and trade settlement. The daily average transaction volume on the Renminbi Real-Time Payment System throughout 2019 remained robust at RMB1,133.9 billion. Despite prevailing external uncertainties, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from continued mainland China capital account liberalization, increased international investor allocation to renminbi assets, and deeper regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area plan.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases has dashed hopes for a recovery. Investors' concerns about a global recession have deepened, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To counter the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have launched stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, the downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand in the second half of 2019 cast a shadow over the outlook for the region's economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag on the region's economic growth in the short term, with the tourism industry being particularly hard hit. On the other hand, the East Asian region also continues to face challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has helped to temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures remain in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a global economic slowdown. The monetary and fiscal policies adopted by the authorities will provide some buffer. Amidst ongoing trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was still sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilising in the last quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier easing policies of the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions after the signing of the “Phase One” trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index However, since the end of January, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases and the subsequent economic impact have caused market concern, leading to a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in the global supply chain, disruptions to its production activities and a drag on its economic growth due to the epidemic will have significant spillover effects, potentially affecting the entire world (Chart 2.3). Since the end of February, the surge in coronavirus infection cases outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose a risk of directly dragging down local economic activities. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China by Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, and some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face huge selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which in turn may exacerbate the downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index In addition to the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased after the China-US Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to be smooth, thus sustaining post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp fall in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 due to sluggish global demand. Exports from the East Asian region to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downward cycle of technology products in the region is bottoming out, including reports from major regional electronics companies of improved earnings at the end of 2019,6 it remains to be seen whether there will be a substantial rebound in the region's technology product exports. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise Exports to Major Destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also plagued investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which could affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. In order to support economic growth in a mild inflation environment, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting them in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation The outbreak of the coronavirus has led to concerns that the region's economies may come under further pressure amid continued weak growth. As many economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies that are more dependent on tourists and tourism service exports from Mainland China being more affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). The continuation and intensification of the epidemic will also affect the region's supply chains, which are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists In the short term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Referring to the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be short-lived, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. At the same time, East Asian economies are also facing multiple headwinds. First, although corporate earnings are expected to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), the loose global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. As a result, the region's stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents Second, the weakness in corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the region to repay their debts. Although lower local interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. In addition, as mentioned in Special Topic 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into the region's financial markets, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector may also increase, although this impact may be limited to financially sound companies and their long-term borrowing. Third, in terms of external factors, East Asian economies may also face increased risks in the face of increasingly protectionist US trade policies. Despite recent progress on the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, trade tensions between the two countries persist as fundamental trade issues between them remain. As can be seen from the increasing trade surpluses of many economies in the region with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek more supply channels outside the China-centric supply chain to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had increased to approximately US$1670 billion. If the trade surplus with the US continues to expand, the relevant Asian economies may become the next target of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed huge tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Goods Trade Surplus with the US Over the past decade, the increasing integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (often referred to as passive funds), but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors that the relevant economies would not have been able to attract or reach otherwise, these funds help to promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. As a result, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of their markets. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are concerns that such fund investments may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, leading to high leverage levels in the relevant companies. 10 In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, even more vulnerable. 11 This special topic assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to the relevant bonds according to the weight of the constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may give the issuers of the index constituent bonds less incentive to act in the interests of the fund investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, this behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies Using the weights of companies from various emerging market economies in a mainstream index that tracks emerging market economy corporate bonds as an estimate of their bonds' investment by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investment will push up the long-term (but not short-term) leverage ratios of the relevant corporate bond issuers. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base due to passive bond funds is also beneficial to the development of companies in emerging market economies. We also find that the above-mentioned effect is only significant for companies in emerging market economies with stronger fundamentals (especially those with stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher financial distress costs, highly leveraged or less solvent companies seem less likely to fall further into a debt trap due to investment from passive bond funds. In conclusion, the above research shows that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase the solvency risk of the corporate sector in emerging market economies.

Due to weakened private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and lackluster export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the coronavirus pandemic has also recently introduced substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, such as the slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, economic performance in Mainland China, and developments in local social events. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate may rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, though the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Year on year, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the 3rd and 4th quarters respectively (Table 3. A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, a sharp contrast to the 2.9% growth in 2018, and also marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution by major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% respectively in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Locally, private consumption was the main factor dragging down real GDP in the 3rd quarter. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, which in turn weakened the economic outlook and hit consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract significantly starting from the third quarter. 33 Due to increasing economic uncertainties and a deteriorating business atmosphere, total investment expenditure remained weak, dragging down real GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 Externally, as China-US trade frictions intensified, global economic growth weakened, and visitor arrivals to Hong Kong plummeted, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to remain sluggish (Chart 3.2). 35 Under the impact of a sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down real GDP in the third quarter but supported real GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partially reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports  Given the huge headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and industries severely impacted, such as retail, catering services, transport, and tourism. 36 To provide banks with more room to increase support for the local economy and help mitigate economic cycles, the HKMA announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical buffer capital ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby allowing banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$2,000 billion to HK$3,000 billion for enterprises, including SMEs. Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the pandemic has also recently brought significant downside risks. As some industries have yet to recover after the destruction caused by social events, the pandemic will bring a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 fiscal budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including one-off cash payments to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans for businesses under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" with 100% government guarantee. 37 The HKMA further lowered the countercyclical buffer capital ratio of banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks more room to increase support for the local economy, especially for industries and individuals facing greater pressure in the short term due to the pandemic. Based on the composition of the local GDP, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively sluggish as some major infrastructure projects are completed. In terms of external factors, the first phase of the US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's foreign trade performance. In particular, the outbreak of the coronavirus may lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (e.g., the tourism industry), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real local GDP growth for 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Meanwhile, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services industries rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the heavy impact caused by social events. 39 As economic momentum weakened, the total number of employed persons fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among these, the decline in the number of employed persons mainly came from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction industries. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to climb further. Topic 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term prospects of the labour market in greater detail. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to accumulate until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum also gradually eased. On a year-on-year basis, the basic Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, and the increase slowed slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The basic inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum on a 3-month annualised basis, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The easing of inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures on several items comprising the CCPI. In terms of traded goods, the rise in fresh pork prices meant that basic food inflation remained significant, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and on durable goods remained mild. In terms of services, as the growth in rents for newly signed private residential leases slowed down earlier, the growth of the rental component of the CCPI also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures rose slightly but remained at a mild level in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting CCPI inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the short term. Locally, the weak economic conditions and the widening output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to slow down, the housing rent component of inflation should ease further. Externally, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate for 2020 to be between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government projects the underlying inflation rate to be 2.5% and the headline inflation rate to be 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On one hand, given that the estimated output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe economic deterioration than expected (for example, due to the continued coronavirus pandemic) could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, a more severe disruption in the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the significant economic slowdown in Hong Kong, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8–2.9% in the first 9 months of 2019. It was only as social events continued that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Due to the impact of the coronavirus pandemic, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this background, this special report analyzes recent developments and the short-term outlook of the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market remained largely stable (with almost no change in the unemployment rate) in the first three quarters of 2019, and what implications this has for future developments. The article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator because it takes time to adjust labor demand costs. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature explains why the unemployment rate remained low at about 2.9% even when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Regarding labor demand (Figure B3.1), although tensions in China-US trade and local social events dealt heavy blows to employment in trade and retail and tourism-related industries respectively, some major industries were still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in the finance, business, public administration, and social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Although the economy entered a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities in fintech development and new share issuances were very active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the finance and business services industries. Furthermore, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to economic cycles. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many industries is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of the public administration, social and personal services sectors to economic cycles is more neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows down, employment in these industries may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Figure B3.2: Changes in employment by industry in 2019. Regarding labor supply, the labor force participation rate fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer for the rising unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted significantly in the second half of the year, the decrease in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although the number of employed persons decreased during the economic recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure on the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Some changes in the structure of the labour market leading to changes in the unemployment rate (Chart B3.3) are also noteworthy. In particular, the increasing proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have fallen to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second largest group in the total employed population (approximately 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the higher proportion of part-time workers among the current employed population.

Since October, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been trending upward, with this upward momentum intensifying in December. As a result, the exchange rate has remained on the strong side of the exchange rate guarantee band in recent months. The robust demand for the Hong Kong dollar stems partly from equity-related activities and partly from the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened toward year-end. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and orderly. Despite the uncertain external environment, where the coronavirus outbreak could potentially heighten capital flow volatility through its impact on market sentiment, Hong Kong’s substantial foreign exchange reserves and sound banking system enable it to withstand capital outflow pressures without compromising financial stability. Supported by rising equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar—including demand arising from initial public offerings—the exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October onward (Chart 4.1). In December, this upward trend accelerated; from mid-December through February, the exchange rate stayed firmly on the strong side of the guarantee band. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar was driven both by robust IPO activity and by the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions due to tighter liquidity near year-end. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, causing the exchange rate to dip slightly; on 28 February, it closed at 7.7956 per US dollar. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained orderly throughout the review period. Since neither the strong-side nor weak-side exchange rate guarantee was triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at approximately HK$540 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate   Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs)  The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar largely mirrored movements of the US dollar, posting a marginal rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar largely tracked the trend of its nominal counterpart. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates  When assessing capital flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts: (1) Hong Kong dollar-denominated capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. Hong Kong dollar-denominated flows focus on the currency dimension of capital movements and help gauge monetary stability, particularly under the linked exchange rate system. Cross-border flows, on the other hand, pertain to the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong’s banking system, providing insight into the overall stability of the financial system. Each concept necessitates different monitoring indicators. In tracking Hong Kong dollar-denominated flows, attention must be paid to both the exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. Should the public or investors shift a substantial portion of their assets from Hong Kong dollars to foreign currencies, demand for the Hong Kong dollar would naturally decline, leading to a weaker exchange rate. Under the linked exchange rate system, should the exchange rate fall to the weak-side guarantee level of 7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to purchase Hong Kong dollars at banks’ request, thereby reducing the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained largely stable, and given that the exchange rate has stayed on the strong side of the guarantee band in recent months, no significant outflows of Hong Kong dollar-denominated capital were observed during the review period. For monitoring cross-border flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator; a substantial outflow of funds through the banking system would inevitably reduce deposit levels. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no notable cross-border capital outflows. The continued smooth and orderly functioning of Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets suggests that the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the local monetary environment remains limited. Nevertheless, we must remain vigilant regarding risks arising from the ongoing outbreak. Hong Kong boasts substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority thus possesses the capability, resources, and determination to manage capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained large, rising 4.0% since late June to reach HK$1,689.4 billion by end-January 2020 (Figure 4.4). As no trigger for the exchange guarantee mechanism occurred during this period, the total exchange fund assets remained largely unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base—including outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds, certificates of indebtedness, and currency notes and coins issued by the government—also saw steady increases. Figure 4.4 Components of the monetary base  During the review period, broad measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply remained largely stable. Broad money supply denominated in Hong Kong dollars (HKD M3) grew 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and then edged up 0.2% over the subsequent seven months from end-June 2019. An analysis of corresponding assets indicates that the growth in HKD M3 since end-June primarily reflects an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets as well as expansion of the monetary base, driven by higher levels of certificates of indebtedness and currency notes and coins issued by the government (Figure 4.5). Over the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits—the main component of HKD M3—remained largely unchanged (Figure 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to register modest growth, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Figure 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and corresponding assets  Over the seven months since late June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew modestly by 2.3% (Figure 4.6), primarily driven by US dollar deposits, which rose 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits declined 1.0% over the same interval; among them, Renminbi deposits denominated in Hong Kong dollars saw a slight decrease. Overall, total deposits held by authorized institutions increased steadily by 1.2% since late June. Supported by this growth in total deposits, Hong Kong’s overall broad money supply also expanded at a relatively steady pace: both M2 and M3 rose 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since late June (Figure 4.7). Given that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various transient factors—such as seasonal demand for funds related to initial public offerings, as well as business and investment activities—these figures should be interpreted with caution. Figure 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency  Figure 4.7 Broad money supply (M2)  Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates exhibited volatility. This reflected seasonal demand for liquidity as well as heightened capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the surge in initial public offering activity in the Hong Kong stock market, with overnight Hong Kong dollar interbank rates experiencing notable fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally increased. Large-scale IPO subscriptions exert significant pressure on overnight interest rates; as demonstrated by empirical analysis in Topic 4, market expectations regarding future IPO activity also influence the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. This occurs when market participants anticipate upcoming deadlines for large IPO subscriptions and proactively arrange medium-term funding in advance. Figure 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates  As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downward in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared to end-June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% by 28 February 2020 (Figure 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds dropped 50 basis points over the same period to reach 1.00%. Figure 4.9: Government bond yields, composite rates, and average mortgage rates for newly issued loans  On the retail front, the composite rate reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase was primarily driven by banks continuing to raise their preferred deposit rates to attract more deposits, thereby pushing up the weighted average Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following a cut to the target range of the US Federal Funds Rate at the end of October 2019, multiple retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, the Best Lending Rates offered by retail banks currently range between 5.00% and 5.50%. Regarding mortgage lending, for mortgages linked to Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), major banks raised the upper limit of interest rates calculated based on their Best Lending Rates. As a result, the average mortgage rate for newly issued loans climbed to approximately 2.63% in October. 45 Since November, the Best Lending Rates in the market have been lowered, leading to a slight decline in the average mortgage rate to 2.53% by January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus pandemic to US economic activity and to help the Federal Reserve achieve its policy objectives, the Fed cut the target range for the Federal Funds Rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25 on March 3 and March 15 (US time). Although HIBOR tends to follow movements in US interest rates over the long term, in the short run it may be influenced by local factors affecting demand for Hong Kong dollars, such as new stock listings in Hong Kong. The total balance of the banking system has been declining since April 2018; thus, HIBOR may become more sensitive to shifts in the supply and demand of Hong Kong dollar funds. Nevertheless, this does not imply that the current total balance of HK$540 billion is insufficient to meet interbank settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to function smoothly. Should liquidity become tight in the short term, banks can draw on liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid heightened Sino-US trade tensions, both offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019; on September 2, the offshore RMB fell to a ten-year low of 7.19 per US dollar (Figure 4.10). Entering October, expectations of renewed trade talks between China and the US reversed the RMB’s depreciation trend, and both offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter. Following the signing of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US, the RMB briefly surpassed the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since late January, the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic has once again exerted downward pressure on both offshore and onshore RMB. Between May and August, the offshore RMB generally traded at a discount relative to the onshore RMB; later in 2019 it mostly traded at a premium. At the end of January 2020, the discount widened briefly, yet the overall price differential remained modest by historical standards. Figure 4.10: Onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates  Despite fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market largely remained stable. During the review period, the 3-month CNH HIBOR continued to fluctuate within the 3–4% range (Figure 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to MSCI’s rebalancing of A-shares, as well as around the Lunar New Year holiday at the end of January 2020.

Due to increased uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profits of Hong Kong’s retail banks saw a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remain strong and robust by international standards. By historical standards, asset quality also remains at a healthy level. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed down in the latter half of last year, it still outpaced the growth of deposits during the same period. Consequently, both the average loan-to-deposit ratio across all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions rose. However, given that the aggregate liquidity in the banking system remains at a stable level and deposits have largely stayed flat, the liquidity situation in the banking sector continues to be sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will still face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social developments. Given the ongoing rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess how their loan portfolios’ asset quality might be affected under these potentially heightened risks. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks was 59, edging down 1.5% compared to the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets dipped slightly to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, down from 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Figure 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), net interest income continued to register modest growth during the review period. However, both loan loss provisions and operating expenses increased, resulting in a slight decline in overall profitability. Figure 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Figure 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three successive 25-basis-point cuts to the US Federal Funds target rate in the second half of 2019, no significant downward pressure has emerged in Hong Kong’s wholesale Hong Kong dollar funding market thus far. On the contrary, driven by various local factors—including seasonal demand for funds, heightened liquidity needs arising from major initial public offerings, and relatively tight interbank liquidity conditions—short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, over the review period, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained largely stable; the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate stood at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (the blue line in Figure 5.3). At the retail level, since Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remain near zero, retail banks had limited room to cut rates following the US policy rate reductions. 60 On the other hand, given the tightening of Hong Kong dollar liquidity within the banking system during the review period, banks continued to compete vigorously for long-term, stable deposit funding. 61 Reflecting the rising weighted cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite rate—a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks—gradually climbed from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% by end-2019; this remains at a relatively low level by historical standards (the green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3 Interest rates More broadly, given that the decline in US dollar funding costs for Hong Kong licensed banks offset the slight rise in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs for these banks dipped by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Figure 5.4). Looking ahead, multiple external and local downside risks will continue to cast a shadow over banks’ profit prospects. Relevant factors include uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future developments in Sino-US trade relations, and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could dampen already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank lending. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the current low-interest-rate environment worldwide is likely to persist, potentially exerting downward pressure on banks’ future net interest margins. Domestically, local social unrest since mid-2019 has continued to undermine business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already sluggish economic climate, if these conditions persist or worsen, they could adversely affect both the outlook for credit demand and the quality of banks’ assets. In terms of broader market developments, following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s issuance of eight virtual banking licenses, Hong Kong’s banking sector has begun rolling out virtual banking services. These new market entrants may seek to expand their market share by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, thereby potentially increasing funding costs for existing banks. Although the immediate impact may remain limited given the current modest scale of virtual banking operations, its long-term effects will likely hinge on whether existing banks accelerate their adoption of fintech solutions to maintain competitiveness. Findings from Topic 5 indicate a statistically significant correlation between the extent of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks and improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability levels. The capital position of Hong Kong’s banking sector remains robust, comfortably exceeding minimum international standards. By end-2019, the aggregate capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further rose to 20.7% (Figure 5.5). Meanwhile, the Tier 1 capital ratio climbed to 18.5%, of which 16.5% comprised Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.
