Against the backdrop of heightened Sino-US trade tensions, a slowing global economy, and ongoing local social unrest, bank lending growth rebounded modestly in the first half of 2019 before decelerating in the latter half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth—measured by changes in total loans and advances issued by all authorized institutions—rose by a modest 4.2% in the first half of 2019, then slowed to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 5.12). This slowdown was attributable to a concurrent easing in growth rates for both local loans (including loans utilized within Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans issued outside Hong Kong during the review period. In the second half of 2019, local loans and overseas loans grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively, both figures lower than the 4.5% and 3.5% growth rates recorded in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the full year 2019 still managed a moderate increase to 6.7%, surpassing the 4.4% growth rate observed in 2018.

The rollout of coronavirus vaccines has brought hope for economic recovery, bolstering global growth prospects. Coupled with ongoing fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. Nevertheless, global prospects remain clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. In the medium term, a disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high levels of debt, and the long-lasting economic damage caused by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly. The Hong Kong dollar stayed close to the strong-side convertibility guarantee level against the US dollar, driven primarily by demand related to equities. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Partly reflecting weaker economic activity and reduced credit demand due to recurring pandemic waves, total bank lending edged down in the second half of the year; however, it still posted a modest increase for the whole of 2020. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained largely stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong’s banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may impair the repayment capacity of firms and households, banks must remain vigilant regarding the impact of these downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but with coronavirus infection rates rising again from the fourth quarter onward, global growth slowed once more. Nevertheless, the breakthrough in vaccine development toward the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end, facilitating a return to normalcy and accelerated growth worldwide. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets climbed to new peaks in early 2021, despite emerging signs of a disconnect from the real economy. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be widely distributed. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing measures could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to scale back monetary easing earlier than anticipated and thus shattering market expectations of “prolonged low interest rates.” In the long run, policymakers must assess the costs and benefits of prolonging relief measures and address numerous economic after-effects triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt levels and lasting economic damage. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by rebounding export demand. With risk appetite on the rise, inflows of portfolio investment into the region picked up, and yield-seeking activities resumed. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global race to procure vaccines, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties regarding vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy—combined with deteriorating fiscal conditions among regional governments—could dampen market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. In mainland China, economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumer activity gradually returned to normal. For the whole of 2020, the mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will largely depend on the pandemic’s trajectory and developments in Sino-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts predict 8.4% growth for the mainland economy in 2021. After depreciating for several months at the start of 2020, the Chinese yuan strengthened for the remainder of the year, driven by faster economic recovery, a weaker US dollar, and robust capital inflows into the mainland bond market. Detailed analysis shows that during the COVID outbreak, fundamental factors—rather than market sentiment—played a more significant role in driving yuan exchange rate fluctuations (see Topic 1 for details). Hong Kong’s economy showed some improvement in the second half of 2020, yet real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. Supported by slightly stronger domestic demand and further expansion in goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rise in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed considerably, from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP declined by 6.1%, marking the steepest drop on record and representing the first instance in history of two consecutive years of contraction, following a 1.2% decline in 2019. The latest GDP figures by sector indicate that consumption- and tourism-related industries suffered even greater setbacks than the broader economy amid the pandemic. To combat the ongoing crisis, the government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the latter half of 2020, aimed at assisting industries and citizens affected by the pandemic while enhancing Hong Kong’s pandemic response capabilities. In its recent 2021/22 Budget, the government also announced extra countercyclical measures to stimulate the economy, including one-time HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and fully government-guaranteed preferential personal loans for unemployed individuals. In March 2021, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the “Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism,” announced an extension of the “Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme” until October of the same year and extended the repayment period for trade finance loans under this scheme. These extensions are expected to alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by certain corporate borrowers. The rollout of COVID vaccines offers hope for a return to normal economic activity; consequently, Hong Kong’s economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of this recovery hinge on numerous uncertain factors, including the pandemic’s evolution and the progress and efficacy of vaccine distribution. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy is anticipated to encounter significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, mainland China’s economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services; meanwhile, the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the success of their large-scale vaccination programs. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021, while international institutions and private analysts project an average growth rate of 4.4%. The labor market deteriorated further in the latter half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed steadily, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021; meanwhile, the underemployment rate rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. To address this worsening labor market situation, the government introduced the “Retain Employees Scheme” under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, offering time-limited (June–November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of this scheme, the government rolled out other targeted measures (such as lump-sum grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support industries severely impacted by the pandemic. In the short term, given the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Topic 2 examines the potential impact of fluctuations in Hong Kong’s tourism sector on the local labor market. Domestic inflationary pressures steadily eased over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate dropped significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively; in January and February 2021, it fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% respectively. Although the three-month annualized underlying inflation rate—a key indicator of inflation momentum—has fluctuated slightly in recent months, it remains at a low level. Given that both global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to stay subdued in the near term; in particular, the recent slowdown in private residential rent growth is expected to continue curbing local inflation. Market consensus forecasts an overall inflation rate for 2021 at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the government projects underlying and overall inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar remained close to the strong-side convertibility guarantee level against the US dollar, driven primarily by equity-related capital demand, including robust new share offerings and inflows of southbound funds via the Stock Connect programs linking Shanghai and Shenzhen with Hong Kong. Active fundraising activities in the first two months of 2021 further bolstered the Hong Kong dollar’s strength. During the review period, the strong-side convertibility guarantee was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in an inflow of HK$2,633 billion into Hong Kong. Throughout 2020, it was triggered a total of 85 times, bringing cumulative inflows to HK$3,835 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to proceed smoothly and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of substantial capital outflows from Hong Kong’s banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic’s trajectory, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the US may exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand such volatility. With the strong-side convertibility guarantee being triggered, the aggregate balance of the banking system rose, and Hong Kong interbank rates remained at extremely low levels. The composite rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, fell from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% by late February 2021. Thanks to these lower funding costs, the average interest rate on newly issued mortgages dropped from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the best lending rates offered by major retail banks remained unchanged throughout the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore RMB exchange rate strengthened, the offshore RMB (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore RMB traded at a premium relative to the onshore rate; in the fourth quarter, this premium averaged around 100 basis points, a level still considered moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to expand in the latter half of 2020; by end-January 2021, the total balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit had reached RMB826.3 billion. Regarding other RMB-related activities, RMB bank lending in Hong Kong declined, while RMB trade settlement saw growth; the daily average transaction volume on the CIPS (Cross-Border Interbank Payment System) remained robust at RMB1,191.5 billion throughout 2020. Hong Kong boasts highly efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous channels for cross-border capital flows to the Chinese mainland. With the gradual liberalization of the mainland’s capital account, rising global demand for RMB-denominated assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area plan, Hong Kong’s offshore RMB business is poised to benefit further. Supported by rising global equity markets and active buying of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors via the Stock Connect programs, Hong Kong’s stock market rebounded after experiencing a sharp correction at the start of the review period. Global equity markets rose due to unprecedented monetary easing measures implemented by major economies, positive market expectations regarding vaccine development as a catalyst for economic recovery, and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its 2020 losses, posting a 15.1% increase during the review period; in mid-February 2021, it briefly surpassed the 31,000-point mark, reaching a 32-month high. Backed by steady issuance volumes, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore RMB bond markets continued to expand in the latter half of 2020. After experiencing substantial net capital outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence rebounded swiftly following unprecedented economic stimulus measures introduced by governments worldwide; bond funds inflowing into the local market also saw a recovery. Although bond yields experienced a modest uptick during this period, global yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historic lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expects that the COVID-19 pandemic will eventually end, and the global economy will be able to accelerate its growth. Coupled with the expectation of a global monetary policy of “lower for longer” interest rates, investors were not deterred by the rebound of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the high expectations of the financial markets are disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. If the economic recovery is not as strong as expected, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than expected (for example, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices may become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support and address the many problems left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic scarring. The ongoing uncertainty of the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, where slower-developing emerging market economies may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programs could reverse the current optimism, leading to instability in capital flows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains uncertain and largely depends on the development of the pandemic and changes in Sino-US tensions. Therefore, the government has announced that it will continue to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the reopening of the economy, major economies mostly recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of new COVID-19 infections has risen again, prompting governments to resume lockdowns and social distancing measures, and the global growth momentum has weakened again. At the end of 2020, a more contagious variant of the virus emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use at the end of 2020, the market expects that the pandemic will eventually end, and the global economy will return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driving force supporting the global economic recovery comes from continuous policy stimulus measures, including the commitment of major central banks to a monetary policy of “lower for longer” interest rates amid weak inflation, and the continued fiscal easing measures of major advanced economies, especially the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than the forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020. In this context, market optimism has increased, and the stock prices of cyclical industries that usually benefit from economic recovery have risen, driving global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward P/E ratios of major stock indices. However, while the financial markets are performing strongly, the macroeconomic situation remains challenging, and the disconnect between the two may lead to volatility in the asset market in the face of multiple risks. First, the prospect of controlling the pandemic depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate was still low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote a more equitable distribution of vaccines, due to the limited supply of vaccines, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe. If the pandemic is not well controlled, various regions may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, which would in turn undermine the prospects for a global recovery. Chart 2.3 Percentage of the population that has received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is based on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the “lower for longer” monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures will be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have risen due to the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong currency and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing policies (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back the size of their monetary easing policies, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 US and Eurozone 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates. Third, there is significant uncertainty about the future of Sino-US relations. The wave of Sino-US “decoupling”, especially in the financial and technological fields, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. And given the increasingly tough attitude of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States towards Mainland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation of Sino-US tensions could trigger financial market turmoil in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to face the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While premature withdrawal of relevant measures could jeopardize the economic recovery and create a “cliff effect”, these measures are costly in the long run, including bringing financial burdens and delaying the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic, such as allowing “zombie companies” whose business models are no longer viable to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many problems left by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to falling corporate revenues and soaring government spending (Chart 2.5). Although the problem of soaring debt may not be imminent as global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors may raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt as a percentage of GDP. Another legacy issue involves the potential long-term economic losses or long-term scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may cause companies to reduce investment, while workers who have been unemployed for a long time may permanently withdraw from the labor market, leading to a large waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilized in the second half of the year after a sharp drop in the second quarter of 2020 (Chart 2.6). The momentum of the economic recovery mainly came from a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand for exports of electronic and technological equipment. At the same time, the hardest-hit service industries (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) continue to be in trouble. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020. Despite the uncertainty of the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have returned. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond fund inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields than bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the launch of vaccine production plans, equity funds also accelerated their inflow into East Asia in the last quarter of 2020. Currencies in the region also appreciated accordingly due to the inflow of portfolio funds, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its lowest point in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows. East Asia continues to face the ongoing uncertainty of the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the region's hard-hit service sector and economy, competition for early batches of vaccines around the world has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capabilities. As a result, slower-developing economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination among economies may prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investor optimism is largely driven by the rollout of vaccines, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination is far below expectations, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices may come to an end. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With the successful control of the novel coronavirus and the gradual recovery of consumption, the mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from the strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical equipment and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Throughout 2020, despite the unprecedented impact of the novel coronavirus pandemic on the economy, the mainland's GDP still recorded a growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution to GDP growth by demand component. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast shows that the mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economy can continue to recover still depends to a certain extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the mainland have normalized, the service industry is still partially disrupted as the pandemic has re-emerged in several northern provinces. In terms of the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to a new wave of outbreaks in most developed economies. In addition, the tense Sino-US relations are unlikely to ease in the short term, but the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the agreed-upon China-EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment will help China further integrate with other economies, which may partially offset the adverse effects of Sino-US decoupling on economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook is still full of uncertainty, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance will not change significantly in 2021 to support economic growth, while emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest government work report sets the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" prioritizes technological self-reliance and dual circulation, with the goal of reaching the level of a moderately developed country in terms of per capita GDP by 2035. The impact of the novel coronavirus outbreak on the repayment ability of bond-issuing enterprises seems to be limited, and the overall default rate of the mainland bond market remained at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp increase in bond defaults by state-owned enterprises, the total amount of defaulted bonds in 2020 increased (Chart 2.9). Although the increase in defaults by state-owned enterprises mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" of state-owned enterprises to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, the limited fiscal space of some local governments may also be one of the reasons, especially for local governments in less developed regions. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Onshore bond default size and ratio. In the second half of 2020, the financing costs of corporate issuers increased, especially for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalization of interest rates have to some extent led to an increase in financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default incidents in the last quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields. In terms of the real estate market, mainland property prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, especially in first-tier cities. In contrast, property prices in lower-tier cities rose at a much slower pace (Chart 2.11). As for the problem of oversupply of housing that plagued third-tier cities in previous years, it was basically under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid high market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, far below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remains well below pre-pandemic levels, Hong Kong’s economy showed some improvement in the second half of 2020, driven by a rebound in domestic demand and further expansion in goods exports. With hopes that COVID vaccinations will restore normal economic activity, the local economy is expected to return to growth in 2021, following the worst contraction on record in 2020. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of this recovery depend on numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollouts. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, Hong Kong’s economy is still expected to face significant challenges in early 2021. Consequently, the labor market is anticipated to remain under pressure in the short term, while domestic inflationary pressures will stay modest. Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3. A), yet economic activity remained far below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. Nonetheless, for the whole of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, marking the largest annual decline on record and representing the first instance in history of two consecutive years of contraction, following a 1.2% drop in 2019. Latest figures on sectoral GDP also indicate that economic activity in most sectors declined year-on-year in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related industries experiencing sharper contractions than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3. A and Figure 3.1). Private consumption turned positive in the 3rd and 4th quarters; however, consumer confidence remained weak amid the third and fourth waves of local infections, which prompted authorities to reimpose social distancing measures. With a brief improvement in business sentiment, overall investment spending also rose in the latter half of the year. Partly owing to stronger export performance—particularly to the Chinese mainland—Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). In contrast, services trade remained sluggish due to the ongoing stagnation of global tourism. Overall, net imports (a trade deficit) weighed on GDP growth in the second half of the year, partly reflecting slower growth in imports compared to exports. In its recent 2021/22 Budget, the government announced further countercyclical measures to stimulate the economy, including a one-time HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and 100% government-guaranteed loans for unemployed individuals. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, in collaboration with the “Banking Industry Coordinating Mechanism for SME Lending,” announced in March 2021 that the “pre-approved interest-only repayment” scheme would be extended to October of the same year; it also extended the repayment period for trade financing loans under this scheme. These extensions are expected to alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate borrowers. Novel coronavirus vaccinations are anticipated to facilitate a return to normal economic activity; consequently, Hong Kong’s economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole). However, the extent and pace of this recovery remain contingent upon various uncertainties, such as the pandemic’s trajectory and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollouts. Given that widespread vaccination will require time, the local economy is still expected to encounter considerable challenges in early 2021. On the external front, mainland China’s economy is forecast to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services; meanwhile, the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the success of their large-scale vaccination programs, thereby influencing both Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021, while international institutions and private analysts project an average growth rate of 4.4%. The labor market deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed to 7.2% in February 2021, reaching a 17-year high (Figure 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. The total number of employed persons stabilized after dropping to a low level (Figure 3.3), although government figures indicate a continued decline in the number of job vacancies. The nominal average wage index for employed persons, which reflects labor income, saw its growth rate slow to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020—the lowest level in nearly 11 years. To address the worsening labor market conditions, the government launched the “Retain Employees Scheme” under the second round of anti-pandemic relief measures, offering time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of this scheme, the government introduced additional targeted measures—such as lump-sum grants—under the third and fourth rounds of relief efforts to further support industries severely hit by the pandemic. In the short term, given the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, Hong Kong’s tourism industry has rapidly declined, prompting concerns over potential long-term adverse effects on labor market recovery. Accordingly, this special topic conducts an empirical analysis of how a thriving tourism sector influences the local labor market, thereby assessing the possible consequences of the current downturn in the industry. Since 2000, Hong Kong’s tourism sector has experienced significant fluctuations (Figure B2.1). Specifically, tourist arrivals declined during the SARS outbreak in 2003. However, following the launch of the “Individual Visit Scheme” in July of that year, tourist numbers surged. Under the initial scheme, mainland residents could individually apply for one or two trips to Hong Kong per year, with each stay limited to no more than 7 days. In April 2009, the scheme was expanded to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to obtain multiple-entry “Individual Visit” visas valid for one year. Consequently, the number of mainland tourists increased substantially. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure linking Hong Kong and mainland China, tourist arrivals reached record highs at the end of 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social unrest led to a 50% drop in tourist numbers during the second half of 2019; under the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the tourism sector has remained virtually stagnant since late January 2020. Figure B2.1: Tourist arrivals and related policies    We examine the impact of a flourishing tourism sector on local employment and income by focusing on the boost brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme. We consider this scheme, introduced in 2003, akin to a random economic shock, as its timing appeared largely exogenous and was unforeseeable to local residents. Our primary data source comprises population statistics drawn from Hong Kong’s population censuses or by-census surveys. Specifically, we utilize the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 censuses or by-census surveys. Additionally, we define tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hospitality, and transportation sectors. First, we employ a “difference-in-differences” analytical framework to compare employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the “treatment group” and older workers (aged 41–65) in the “comparison group.” We classify the younger group as the treatment group because they are still at the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment decisions in response to exogenous growth in Hong Kong’s tourism industry. Given that the impact of the tourism boom induced by the Individual Visit Scheme on the labor market may evolve over time, we also apply an “event study” approach to identify such time-varying effects. Our empirical findings indicate that, compared to their older counterparts, younger workers—particularly women and those with only secondary education—were more likely to enter tourism-related industries following the implementation of the scheme. Notably, the effect of the scheme on the probability of young women entering these industries was both pronounced and persistent; starting from 2006, this effect remained at nearly 5 percentage points above the average entry probability of older workers (Figure B2.2). We also employed a similar methodology to compare incomes between workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) and those in non-tourism industries (comparison group). The results show that after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme, wage growth among workers in tourism-related sectors outpaced that of employees in other industries. Moreover, compared to their counterparts in other sectors, female workers and those with lower educational attainment experienced even greater and steadily rising income increases—ranging from 3 to 20 percentage points (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2: Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on female employment   Figure B2.3: Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on income of female and low-education workers    These findings are largely consistent with international experience, underscoring that the tourism industry serves as a vital source of employment, especially for young people, women, and workers with lower educational levels. In the context of Hong Kong, our results align with prior analyses indicating that robust growth in tourism has heightened demand for low-skilled labor, thereby enhancing labor market stability among this demographic. However, as the tourism sector experiences a downturn, these worker groups may be disproportionately affected and thus warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was primarily driven by equity-related capital needs, including robust initial public offering activities and southward capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance rose to over HK$4500 billion, Hong Kong interbank interest rates declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the COVID pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the United States may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding such pressures. The proximity of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level was mainly driven by equity-related capital needs, including active IPO activities and southward capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects (Figure 4.1). Although some funds raised through IPOs were repatriated, buoyant sentiment in the local stock market and expectations of heightened capital demand toward year-end kept the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December. With continued robust fundraising activities in the first two months of 2021 (Figure 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at HK$7.7568 against the US dollar on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. During the review period, multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking led to an increase in the aggregate balance, indicating substantial capital inflows into Hong Kong. In September and October 2020 alone, the undertaking was triggered 47 times. Under the linked exchange rate system, the HKMA sold a total of HK$2,633 billion, raising the aggregate balance from HK$1,931 billion at end-August to HK$4,575 billion at end-February (Figure 4.3). Throughout 2020, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 85 times, resulting in cumulative capital inflows of HK$3,835 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from Hong Kong’s banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no abnormal capital movements observed. Figure 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate   Figure 4.2: Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange   Figure 4.3: Aggregate balance and Exchange Fund bills and bonds    During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally declined in tandem with the US dollar’s weakening against major currencies (Figure 4.4). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which has limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the latter largely mirrored the trend of the nominal index. Figure 4.4: Nominal and real effective exchange rates    Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the pandemic, economic recovery, and Sino-US tensions may further intensify capital flow volatility. As an international financial hub, Hong Kong hosts numerous fundraising activities, including IPOs, resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On one hand, these activities attract international investors to transfer funds into Hong Kong; on the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may later be transferred out of Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong’s ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system ensure that such capital flow fluctuations do not compromise financial stability. With continuous inflows of capital into Hong Kong dollars, the monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, Hong Kong’s monetary base expanded by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). This growth was primarily driven by multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking, which boosted the aggregate balance. Meanwhile, other components of the monetary base—including certificates of indebtedness, government-issued currency, and outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds—remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5: Components of the monetary base    During the review period, large-scale IPOs led to a surge in Hong Kong dollar deposits stemming from margin loans for share subscriptions. Consequently, Hong Kong’s broad money supply (Hong Kong M3) and its component of Hong Kong dollar deposits rose markedly between July and October 2020 and again in January 2021 (Figure 4.6). Following the conclusion of new share offerings and the repayment of IPO-related loans by clients, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money supply returned to normal levels by end-2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong M3 rose sharply once more, primarily driven by a major new share offering at the end of the month. Overall, over the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the January IPO, the growth rate stood at a more modest 9.1%. An analysis of corresponding assets indicates that, apart from IPO-related loans, the rise in Hong Kong M3 was mainly attributable to an increase in the monetary base triggered by activations of the strong-side convertibility undertaking (Figure 4.7). As a key component of Hong Kong M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; even after excluding the effect of the January IPO, they still increased by 9.1%. Although time deposits declined due to low interest rates, this drop was fully offset by robust growth in demand deposits and savings accounts, partly fueled by investment demand. Figure 4.6: Deposits held by authorized institutions, broken down by currency   Figure 4.7: Movements in Hong Kong M3 and corresponding assets    Overall, foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since end-June. With the aggregate balance rising, Hong Kong interbank interest rates remained at very low levels throughout the review period (Figure 4.8). Under the linked exchange rate system, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar rates; given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the US, Hong Kong dollar rates are expected to remain low, albeit subject to periodic fluctuations driven by capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demands. Due to the ongoing economic downturn caused by recurring COVID outbreaks, coupled with the effects of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong’s retail banks experienced further declines in profitability and a slight deterioration in asset quality during the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, given their still-strong capital and liquidity positions, the banking sector in Hong Kong remained resilient. Throughout the review period, to continue supporting the broader economy through these difficult times, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority decided to extend various relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines offers hope that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties, along with persistent geopolitical tensions, are likely to hinder business activities and continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong’s banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may impair the repayment capabilities of both businesses and households; thus, banks must remain vigilant regarding how these downside risks affect their asset quality. During the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared to the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets dropped to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, down from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% during the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.2). This led to a decline in net interest income, which outweighed the modest rise in non-interest income, ultimately resulting in lower overall profitability. For the full year of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 29.4%, while their return on assets fell to 0.77% from 1.19% in 2019. The Composite Rate—a measure of the average HKD funding cost for retail banks—followed a similar trend, dropping significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% by the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). These risk factors are expected to continue affecting loan quality and profitability within the banking sector in the near term. Entering 2022, the global economy performed weakly, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify globally, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of a large-scale pandemic outbreak and the possibility that the pace of monetary policy tightening may exceed expectations if U. S. inflation proves more persistent and widespread than anticipated. If the Federal Reserve significantly tightens monetary policy and leads to tighter global financial conditions, it will pose pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong Dollar exchange rate softened, but transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For the full year 2021, the growth in total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the continued economic recovery, coupled with the possibility that the pace of U. S. monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected; these risk factors will pose challenges to the credit risk management of banks. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, with weakness continuing into 2022, as the highly infectious Omicron variant led to increased global movement restrictions and persistent supply bottlenecks continued to pressure production. At the same time, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify amid supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, spreading to a wide range of commodities and services in major advanced economies (especially the United States). Recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the sharp rise in commodity prices may further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while increased financial market volatility may cause global financial conditions to tighten less ideally, making the global monetary policy outlook more complex. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties. In the short term, if a large-scale pandemic outbreak occurs, the re-implementation of lockdown measures and the further worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and widespread than expected grows, the Federal Reserve's stance has become hawkish, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning discussions on shrinking the balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to significantly tighten monetary policy, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt repayment abilities, and disorderly capital outflows will pose pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may cause global commodity prices to face risks of continuous increases, aggravating shortages in industrial goods supplies and increasing financial market volatility. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressure on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Topic 1 will discuss whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds when markets are under pressure, and discuss the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, though the recovery momentum of some Southeast Asian economies was temporarily slowed as they re-implemented strict epidemic prevention measures in the third quarter, while technology product exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the short-term economic outlook in the region faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants still pose a hidden concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and tight public health resources. Second, the Fed's accelerated policy normalization may trigger capital outflows within the region and exacerbate currency depreciation pressure; meanwhile, regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery will find it more difficult to strike a balance between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activities. Third, the slowdown of major economies, combined with the potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually restarts, will weigh on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will transmit to regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decisions of regional central banks regarding monetary policy normalization will become more complex. Some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and higher sensitivity to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs for their central banks. In the long run, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater importance on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Topic 2 studies the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk, as well as how such sensitivity is influenced by a company's environmental performance. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of coronavirus outbreaks, power rationing measures, and property market tightening measures. Looking ahead, due to the continued slump in the property market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term. Therefore, mainland authorities have made stabilizing growth their top priority for this year and have launched a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. The total amount of onshore bond defaults and state-owned enterprise (SOE) onshore bond defaults both decreased in the second half of 2021; Topic 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk of the banking sector remains manageable, as mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, low non-performing loan ratios, and high provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real local production GDP grew moderately, as merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the continued global economic recovery, improving local labour market conditions, and the government's launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, economic growth in the second half of 2021 was 5.1%, compared to 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, total economic growth was 6.4%, the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local outbreaks and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures posed pressure on Hong Kong's economic activities. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the "2022-23 Budget" to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "Personal Concessionary Loan with Full Loan Guarantee" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with the maximum loan amount increased and the application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, will also extend the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which also applies to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme."  Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery in 2022, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown of global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of several basic and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2022 will range between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organisations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are affected by several uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of the normalisation of US monetary policy. With the economic recovery, the labour market further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by the end of the year. Total employment rebounded somewhat but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged under a new wave of local pandemic cases. Additionally, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local pandemic cases and tightening epidemic prevention measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the short term (especially in industries involving face-to-face contact). In the longer term, the labour market situation will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have increased slightly in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate rose slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the 3rd and 4th quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The headline inflation rate, which reflects inflationary dynamics and is calculated on a three-month year-on-year basis, also rebounded slightly in recent months, partly due to rising prices for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term as import prices rise and logistics are disrupted by the pandemic. However, soft rents and moderate local labour cost pressures should suppress overall price pressures. Market consensus predicts that the overall inflation rate in 2022 will reach 2.4%, while the government expects the overall inflation rate in 2022 to be 2.1%, with the headline inflation rate at 2.0%. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar briefly rebounded slightly in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak southbound net buying funds through the Stock Connect schemes and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalises its monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained at the strong side of the exchange rate band for most of the period, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. The Hong Kong interbank market continued to trade smoothly and orderly. As banks had ample liquidity, the Hong Kong interbank lending rate remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continues to flourish. In particular, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow, with the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB1,113.5 billion as of the end of January 2022. Although the renminbi loan balance decreased, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. The average daily transaction volume of the renminbi real-time payment settlement system in 2021 rose to RMB1,522.6 billion. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from Hong Kong’s efficient financial infrastructure and the bidirectional Stock Connect schemes (Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong), Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continuing liberalisation of Mainland’s capital account, increasing demand for renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial co-operation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and robust corporate earnings drove major global equity markets to continue their upward trend overall in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to reach a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. However, growing concerns over the tightening stances of major central banks in advanced economies amid rapidly rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict have led to some consolidation in major global equity markets since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of virus variants—Delta and Omicron—and persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy significantly slowed in late 2021, with growth momentum remaining weak into 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify, spreading to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Heightened inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to adopt a more hawkish monetary stance, raising the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions might weigh on currently elevated asset valuations and hinder the recovery in emerging markets where economic rebound remains generally lagging. Recently, the Russia-Ukraine conflict drove up energy and other commodity prices while triggering volatility in global financial markets, thereby exacerbating several of the aforementioned risks.  In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant, the regional economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021; major tech-exporting economies within the region continued to perform better than others. Although the Omicron variant is not expected to severely impede the regional economic recovery at present, any uncertainties related to this new variant will continue to cast a shadow over the economic outlook. Additionally, the normalization of U.S. monetary policy may prompt adjustments in regional asset prices, while slower growth in major economies could dampen export growth in Asia. On one hand, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has led to higher commodity prices and heightened inflation risks; on the other hand, it has dampened consumer demand and increased global economic uncertainty, thereby complicating monetary policy normalization efforts by regional central banks.  In mainland China, economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 infections, power rationing, and tightening measures in the real estate sector. Looking ahead, the domestic economy may continue to face downward pressures stemming from cooling property markets and the spread of the Omicron variant. In light of this, the government has prioritized stabilizing growth this year, and macroeconomic policies are expected to provide greater support.  Global economic recovery noticeably decelerated in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly contagious Omicron variant, combined with ongoing Delta transmission, triggered a new wave of infections and prompted countries worldwide to reimpose mobility restrictions. Moreover, supply chain issues—such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production materials like semiconductors—continued to constrain output. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global real GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the U.S. and other major advanced economies, and slower growth momentum in mainland China offsetting expected rebounds elsewhere in Asia (Chart 2.1).  Chart 2.1 IMF forecasts for global real GDP growth  Concurrently with the slowdown in global growth, inflationary pressures also continued to rise during the review period. Core inflation—excluding food and energy prices—increased notably in major advanced economies, especially in the U.S., which implemented relatively large-scale policy stimulus since the onset of the pandemic. Driven by supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have now spread across a broad spectrum of goods and services (Chart 2.2). Furthermore, the recent Russia-Ukraine military conflict has driven up prices of multiple commodities, potentially intensifying already elevated global inflationary pressures. (2) “Advanced Asian economies” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) The “emerging Asian economies” comprise mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook remains highly uncertain, with significant downside risks. It will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and any subsequent disruptions to supply chains, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, as well as the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have thus far implemented targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared to previous lockdown policies, these relatively relaxed measures should help mitigate supply chain disruptions; indeed, since late 2021, there have been initial signs of improvement in this regard (Chart 2.3). Nevertheless, should a large-scale outbreak occur, lockdowns might be reinstated, potentially worsening supply bottlenecks once again. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index – sub-index for supplier delivery times Assuming the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually ease, providing some relief to commodity inflation. However, several factors could prolong the current elevated global inflation levels beyond expectations: the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on Russian energy imports drive up commodity prices; the lagged effect of rising production costs on final selling prices; the likelihood that earlier sharp rises in global housing prices will lead to higher rents in the future; tight labor markets posing upward pressure on wage growth; and rising inflation expectations. Notably, given that U.S. inflation hit its highest level in decades, the Federal Reserve adopted a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer describing high inflation as “transitory.” It also doubled the pace of asset purchases tapering from $15 billion to $30 billion per month, aiming to conclude its asset purchase program by March 2022 and began discussing balance sheet reduction. Recent market pricing suggests the Fed may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, given the eurozone’s closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face greater policy dilemmas. Against this backdrop, and with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated due to prolonged accommodative policies, if inflationary pressures compel the Fed to tighten policy faster than anticipated, borrowers’ debt repayment abilities could deteriorate, triggering financial market volatility. Recently, heightened geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have spurred risk aversion in financial markets, with signs of dollar shortages emerging, such as widening cross-currency swap spreads. Should global financial conditions tighten prematurely, emerging economies with weaker fundamentals and still reeling from the pandemic may face renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility could also prompt redemption pressures on open-end funds, heightening their liquidity risks. Topic 1 examines whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-end funds—can mitigate such risks during periods of market stress, as well as its potential limitations. In emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021; however, the spread of the Delta variant dampened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as key exporters of technology products in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from robust global demand for such goods, further accentuating regional disparities in the recovery. Inflationary pressures, however, remained moderate across most emerging Asian economies. Figure 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index  The market generally anticipates a broad recovery across Asian emerging markets in 2022. However, the short-term economic outlook in the region faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread across the region since late 2021, its economic impact remains relatively mild compared to previous infection waves. Nevertheless, in certain economies where vaccination rates lag and public health resources are limited, there remains a risk of new variants emerging. Second, the normalization of U.S. Federal Reserve policy could trigger capital outflows and exert downward pressure on regional currencies. For economies still needing accommodative monetary policies to support recovery, striking a balance between curbing capital outflows and sustaining economic activity will prove increasingly difficult. Given the historically strong correlation between U.S. and Asian long-term yields (Figure 2.5), any sudden spike in U.S. long-term yields could also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, heightening the risk of adjustments in regional asset markets.  Figure 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding U.S. Treasury yields  Third, the outlook for regional commodity trade is clouded by the prospect of a slowdown in major economies and a potential shift in global demand from commodities to services as the global economy gradually reopens—factors that could dampen export growth in the region.  Figure 2.6 United States: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP  Fourth, although economic and financial ties between regional economies and Russia and Ukraine remain limited, the surge in commodity prices triggered by the conflict is likely to fuel inflation regionally while curbing consumer spending. Coupled with heightened global economic uncertainty, this makes it more challenging for regional central banks to decide on monetary policy normalization. Central banks in economies with weaker growth momentum and greater sensitivity of inflation to energy prices face particularly difficult policy choices. The pandemic also underscores the long-term need for regional economies to develop more sustainable and resilient growth models capable of withstanding other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors must place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment decisions. Box 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance.  The COVID-19 pandemic inflicted a severe shock on global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, certain open-end funds experienced substantial capital outflows (Figure B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management.  Figure B1.1 Capital outflows from select open-end funds during the March 2020 crisis  Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another possible reason for these large outflows is investors seeking a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming their shares early to avoid potentially higher redemption costs amid market stress. To curb outflows driven by this first-mover advantage, some open-end funds employ swing pricing—a pricing mechanism designed to reduce such advantages for investors. Although many open-end funds utilized swing pricing during this crisis, no empirical research has yet demonstrated whether it effectively reduces fund outflows. Against this backdrop, this Box conducts an empirical study to determine whether swing pricing helped mitigate capital outflows from open-end funds during the March 2020 crisis, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. It also seeks to identify factors that might limit the effectiveness of swing pricing under market stress. Based on these findings, we offer policy recommendations aimed at enhancing financial stability. The “first-mover advantage” refers to investors redeeming their shares ahead of others, thereby shifting the associated costs onto later investors. The first-mover advantage primarily exists in open-end funds that follow traditional pricing rules. Under this mechanism, the costs associated with investor subscriptions and redemptions—such as transaction costs incurred from portfolio adjustments—are reflected in the fund’s price only after the transactions take place. Consequently, investors who redeem their shares first are not required to bear such costs. This serves as an incentive for them to redeem their holdings early, particularly when substantial redemption costs are anticipated. Thus, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to expectations of rising redemption costs. This, in turn, heightens the redemption pressure and liquidity risks faced by open-end funds.

Driven by continued growth in merchandise exports and private consumption, Hong Kong’s economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021, posting positive annual growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local COVID-19 infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on economic activities in Hong Kong. Overall, the economy is expected to remain on a recovery path throughout 2022; however, the extent and pace of this recovery will be influenced by various uncertainties and risks, including the pandemic situation and the normalization of U.S. monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the labor market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the short term due to higher import prices, weak domestic rent levels and labor costs should help contain overall price pressures.  Hong Kong’s economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew by 5.5% in the third quarter and 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), though the growth rate slowed compared to the first half of the year. For the whole of 2021, real GDP expanded by 6.4%, marking the first annual positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities rose modestly by 0.6% in the third quarter and 0.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.1). Domestically, improving labor market conditions and the Government’s consumption voucher scheme contributed to higher private consumption. However, after two consecutive quarters of strong rebound, overall investment spending declined in the final quarter. Externally, as the global economy continued its recovery, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remained robust, while trade in services stayed weak, partly due to the continued stagnation of inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). On a net basis, external trade weighed on GDP growth in the third quarter but provided support in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Volume of imports and exports  A new wave of local COVID-19 infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on economic activities in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to bolster the economy. To ease cash flow constraints, enhancements were made to the “100% Guaranteed Personal Special Loan” and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme; these included raising maximum loan amounts and extending application and repayment periods. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, in collaboration with the banking sector, also extended the “Pre-approved Interest-only Repayment” scheme until the end of October 2022. Under this scheme, borrowers were given a one-year option to repay only part of the principal, which also applied to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.  Hong Kong’s economy is expected to continue its recovery throughout 2022, though at a slower pace than in 2021, reflecting slower global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion, while various infrastructure and construction projects promoted by the Government will also provide economic support. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2022 to range between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth estimate by international organizations and private-sector analysts stands at 1.6%. Nevertheless, the extent and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties and risks outlined in earlier chapters. In particular, recent developments regarding the pandemic, the accelerating pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization, and heightened geopolitical concerns—such as the situation between Russia and Ukraine—have cast a shadow over both Hong Kong’s and the global economic outlook. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could provide a boost to local economic growth. With the economic recovery, the labour market further improved in the second half of 2021; the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 3.9% by year-end (Chart 3.3). The total number of employed persons in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, though it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures resurfaced amid a new wave of local COVID-19 infections. Additionally, a decline in the number of online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the latest wave of local infections and tighter anti-pandemic measures are expected to exert some pressure on the local labour market in the short term, particularly on industries involving face-to-face interactions. In the longer run, labour market conditions will depend on the evolution of the local pandemic situation and the pace of economic recovery.
