On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively; it remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, as local demand rebounded and external prices rose (Chart 3.5), prices for dining out and certain energy-related items have been rising at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby dampening overall inflationary pressures (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remain weak, they have edged up in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). However, weak rent trends and moderate labour cost pressures should help keep overall price pressures in check. Consensus forecasts predict that the overall inflation rate in 2022 will reach 2.4%, while the Government forecasts an overall inflation rate of 2.1% and an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the same year.

Under the atmosphere of hedging in the local stock market and concerns over the normalization of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong Dollar (HKD) exchange rate softened during the review period. Due to ample liquidity of the HKD, the Hong Kong interbank offered rate remained at a low level. Overall, HKD foreign exchange and money market transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties regarding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, which are capable of withstanding the shocks brought by capital flow volatility. Overall, the HKD remained on the strong side of the convertibility undertaking for most of the period, and transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the HKD has gradually softened against the US Dollar (USD) under the hedging sentiment in the local stock market (Figure 4.1). Although the HKD rebounded slightly in October 2021 due to improving market sentiment, its upward momentum subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak southbound net buying funds through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Figure 4.2), as well as market expectations that the USD would strengthen as the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, new share capital raising activities continued to provide support for the HKD (Figure 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there were no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. At the same time, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no signs of abnormal cross-border capital flows. Figure 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Figure 4.2 Southbound Net Buying through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Figure 4.3 Stock Capital Raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)  Despite the strengthening of the USD during the review period, the HKD nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable due to the appreciation of the Renminbi (RMB) against the HKD (Figure 4.4). Given that the inflation rate gap between Hong Kong and its trading partners is very small, the HKD real effective exchange rate index largely followed the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding US monetary policy, the development of the pandemic, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As USD interest rates rise, the outflow of HKD funds (the speed and scale of which will depend on market conditions at that time) may lead to a weakening of the HKD and trigger the weak-side convertibility undertaking under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Hong Kong also possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without affecting financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained loose. The HKD monetary base rose by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in certificates of indebtedness. Reflecting the continuous demand for foreign exchange fund notes by banks in response to ample liquidity in the banking system, the issuance of notes was increased; during the review period, foreign exchange fund notes and bonds increased by HK$1,197 billion to HK$11,887 billion, while the Aggregate Balance (before Discount Window activities) correspondingly decreased by HK$1,199 billion to HK$3,376 billion (Figure 4.5). Meanwhile, the banknotes and coins issued by the government remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5 Total Reserve and Foreign Exchange Fund Notes and Bonds During the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while HKD deposits increased slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering (IPO) related funding demand as well as business and investment related activities. Therefore, it is more appropriate to observe the longer-term trends. In 2021 as a whole, total deposits and HKD deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The specific category loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. With robust capital and liquidity, the Hong Kong banking industry remains resilient. During the review period, the HKMA continued several support measures to further assist the economy through difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to economic recovery, coupled with the risk that the pace of normalization of US monetary policy may be faster than expected; both factors will pose challenges to the credit risk management of banks. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to do their part to mitigate its impacts. To this end, the HKMA has invested significant effort in advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA’s Annual Report last year, we are publishing our Sustainability Report as a separate publication for the first time this year. I hope this report provides readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategies and priorities in strengthening the banking system's ability to cope with climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and a sustainable development institution. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's major functions. Readers will learn about our specific measures and initiatives in this report, with key highlights as follows:  Banks' daily operations face climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken specific measures to strengthen the ability of banks to cope with climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into regulatory procedures and researched how to leverage technology to assist banks in assessing the impacts of physical risks. In view of the increasing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we also shared best practices with the industry on how to properly manage these products to facilitate banks in enhancing their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative projects related to addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance development. Locally, we are working with other financial regulatory authorities through the "Inter-agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance" (the Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy; the framework will increase transparency in the financial markets and bring green finance policies closer to consistency. Internationally, we are actively participating in several different international organizations to assist in formulating policies to address climate change and assessing its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet the demand for green and sustainable financing in the Asia region. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for the global bond market, the amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth, with an increase of 42% and a total issuance amount rising to US$805 billion, making it the largest hub in the Asia region for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². Relevant issuers include the People's Government of Shenzhen Municipality and the People's Government of Hainan Province, whose issuances once again demonstrate Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable finance between the Mainland and the international market. The flourishing of Hong Kong's green bond market is partly attributed to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds worth nearly US$160 billion, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recycling, energy efficiency, and energy saving. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts," including assisting the Government in issuing the first batch of government green retail bonds worth HK$200 billion in May 2022, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at that time. Additionally, we assisted the Government in issuing the first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. This was the first batch of tokenised green bonds issued by a government globally, and this issuance also marked a milestone as we successfully combined our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for the healthy development of the climate finance ecosystem, and they rely on the efforts and cooperation of different sectors to be established. To this end, the HKMA primarily works with the Supervisory Team, other relevant government departments, regulatory bodies, academic institutions, and the financial industry to expand the aforementioned elements. In addition to the development of a local green taxonomy as mentioned above, the Supervisory Team also promotes industry skills training and improves Hong Kong's data resources through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Centre" established under it. Furthermore, the Supervisory Team has made good progress in other areas, such as the mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the work of the Exchange Fund in terms of responsible investment, specifically setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we have optimized risk management to enhance the climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns of the Exchange Fund. Additionally, to fully seize the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investments for the Exchange Fund, identifying investment opportunities that help support climate transition and mitigate climate change to improve the long-term returns of the portfolio. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to 2017 levels. In fact, the Exchange Fund's risk exposure to high-carbon assets remains consistently lower than that of the overall market. In the future, we will continue to move towards the net-zero emissions target by constantly strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, continuing to cooperate with all stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonization and transition of the investment portfolio. At the HKMA, the "Institutional Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee," chaired by me, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility. In terms of the environment, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and promoting more environmentally friendly markets to the general public; in terms of employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively create a healthy and inclusive working environment; and in terms of social responsibility, we are committed to improving the public's level of financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to society. Compared to the levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage in 2022 achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope One emissions and, using 2015 as a baseline, reduce Scope Two emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development requires continuous efforts and cooperation from all parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must lead by example and work together with like-minded peers and international organizations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and work priorities in responding to climate change under each major function. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a daunting task, and we will do our utmost to achieve this goal. We are confident that with the collective efforts of all colleagues, the financial industry, and the general public, we can successfully respond to future climate challenges. Chief Executive, Yu Wai-man

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable institution. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking industry, we will work to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements for climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the Common Assessment Framework for the banking industry's "Greenness Baseline". At the same time, the HKMA will support banks' work in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as exploring different measures and technical solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing as part of the regular supervisor-led stress testing for the 2023 to 2024 cycle. Participating banks will be required to assess their resilience to climate risks based on an enhanced stress testing framework that covers a variety of stress scenarios, including extreme climate events and adverse economic environment. To foster the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, and maintain communication with the industry to provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the development of the green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements for developing a local green classification framework. On market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance size of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA is also assisting in the implementation of the Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme, which is funded by the Government, to expand Hong Kong's talent pool for green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of combining green finance and tech. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other institutional departments on cross-sectoral issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various special initiatives in Asia with the International Finance Corporation, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps for making green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will also enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead project initiatives in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or before, as part of its commitment to participating in global climate response efforts and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social, and governance factors into its investment management process, strive to achieve the goal of net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate response efforts. As a responsible and sustainable institution, the HKMA cares for its staff as well as the community and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to participating in global decarbonisation and climate response efforts. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon reduction and encourage staff to give their full support in saving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into the procurement process. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency while minimising potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change represents a significant risk for the financial system. The HKMA has been striving to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system to foster a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue fulfilling their vital role in the financial system and to channel more funds toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places special emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, as well as accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their ability to detect environmental crimes, and participates in the recently released Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks, addressing common questions and clarifying how existing Basel frameworks encompass such risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA remains committed to integrating climate-related factors into its regulatory framework. Following the issuance of Module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in its Regulatory Policy Manual in 2021, the HKMA has maintained ongoing dialogue with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges related to implementing relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen oversight of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has devised a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into banking supervision procedures, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of this two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised version of Module SA-1 “Risk-Based Supervision” in its Regulatory Policy Manual, enhancing the CAMEL rating system by integrating climate risks into risk-based supervision processes. Meanwhile, drawing on lessons learned from a pilot programme in 2021, the HKMA has refined climate risk stress test scenarios and evaluation frameworks. The HKMA also plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress tests into regular supervisory stress tests, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year plan, the HKMA is also strengthening its green assessment framework for banks to reflect recent developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Concurrently, the HKMA is reviewing its supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar Two capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to enhance their risk management frameworks to address climate change and risks associated with the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing popularity of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing on banks’ development and ongoing management of such products. During this review, several best practices were identified; these were shared with the industry via a circular issued in December to help banks gradually improve their climate risk management capabilities. Technological applications can improve data availability and strengthen banks’ ability to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. Additionally, in collaboration with other central banks and regulators, the HKMA completed a project under the Innovation Hub of the Bank for International Settlements, exploring how technological solutions can facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices; this involves utilizing advanced analytics and compliance technologies, supported by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined its anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce administrative burdens and paper usage for banks. To enhance transparency across financial markets and ensure greater consistency in green finance policies, the HKMA is working with other financial regulators to develop a local green taxonomy. Commonly referred to as a green classification catalogue, this taxonomy categorizes economic activities as green or sustainable, providing authorities and market participants with a reference point to determine whether a particular activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA maintains close contact with industry players and other relevant stakeholders to thoroughly discuss the features and challenges of such a framework, and intends to put forward proposals and conduct consultations on its structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. The HKMA fully recognizes that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system. Therefore, it incorporates a broader range of climate-related factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research, thereby enhancing its ongoing monitoring efforts. In its continuous monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account and includes analyses of climate-related risks in all its financial stability reports. By actively participating in the Working Group on Scenario Design and Analysis under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the HKMA carried out multiple applied research projects in 2022, focusing on two main topics: greenwashing practices within the corporate green bond market,3 and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risks.4 The findings from these studies are instrumental in formulating policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Locally, these studies help the HKMA continuously monitor and assess the effects of climate risks on financial stability. Internationally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with various stakeholders through multiple channels, including international central bank research seminars and its semi-annual “Monetary and Financial Stability Report.” The HKMA’s “Liquidity Arrangement Framework” is a collateralized standby funding mechanism designed to provide timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is currently exploring the possibility of incorporating sustainability considerations into the evaluation of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions aimed at addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance as a mainstream practice. Through such participation, it helps foster policy dialogue on climate change and its implications for financial stability at both international and regional levels, while also gaining valuable insights to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system’s resilience to climate-related challenges.

To strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA has stepped up efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide necessary infrastructure and incentives, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates responses within the financial sector to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategy1. The Steering Group’s work is guided by its strategic plan, which sets out 6 key focus areas and 5 action pillars aimed at strengthening Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and fostering a greener, more sustainable future (Figure 1). These include: strengthening climate-related financial risk management to reinforce Hong Kong’s status as a global risk management hub; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation, and investor protection; enhancing relevant skills among industry professionals and raising public awareness; encouraging product innovation and research initiatives to channel funds toward green and sustainable projects; seizing business opportunities arising from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance hub within the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. To date, the Steering Group has made good progress in advancing sustainable finance in Hong Kong. Its current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre (see below), the development of a green taxonomy (see “Establishing a green classification framework to facilitate green financing” in the chapter “Building a sustainable financial system” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as opportunities in the carbon market. Specifically, in March the Steering Group released a preliminary feasibility assessment on opportunities in Hong Kong’s carbon market, pledging to support Hong Kong’s development as a regional carbon trading hub—including the creation of a high-quality international voluntary carbon market—and to capitalize on collaboration opportunities within the GBA. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP2 to improve data availability in Hong Kong and enhance sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, both parties developed a questionnaire on climate and environmental risks targeted at non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This tool not only facilitates corporate sustainability reporting but also helps financial institutions collect and analyze company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks a significant step by the Steering Group in expanding its data initiatives to include SMEs—an important yet previously under-served segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre in July 2021 to coordinate efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and academic institutions in training and policy development, while also building resource platforms and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three information portals, focusing respectively on 3 themes—data, training resources, and internship opportunities—to help the financial sector and other industries access relevant data and learning materials on green and sustainable finance. One of these portals provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To support talent development, the Centre assisted the Government in December in launching the “Pilot Scheme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training,” which offers financial assistance to practitioners, students, and graduates participating in relevant training and skill enhancement programs. Additional measures to promote skills development include the “Sustainable Finance Internship Scheme,” which creates more internship opportunities for students, and the introduction of a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the HKMA’s “Professional Qualifications Framework for the Banking Industry”3 for banking professionals. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance throughout the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance”4, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry associations, research bodies, and technology providers to foster collaboration in green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to help commercial banks and other financial institutions fully realize their potential in making green finance a core component of their operations, thereby encouraging greater participation of the financial system in efforts to address climate change. The Alliance operates as a one-stop learning platform for financial institutions, enabling them to access essential knowledge, tools, and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transition into credible green financial institutions. It also serves as a gathering place for green finance leaders, connecting green finance institutions across emerging markets to facilitate communication and discussions on cutting-edge issues, thereby advancing the global green finance agenda and unlocking countless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became founding members of the Alliance. They collaborate closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices in green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities—all contributing to the transition toward a green economy. Additionally, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 pledged in 2022 to provide climate expertise in areas such as innovation, standardization, and academic research. Detailed information on the Alliance and its membership structure can be found on its official webpage (English version): Founding Members. Meanwhile, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA signed a Memorandum of Understanding. Since March 2021, the Alliance has organized 18 training sessions and roundtable discussions, attracting over 6,000 participants from across the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. In June 2022, the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Research Institute7, released its first research report on a cutting-edge topic: “Climate Risks: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices, and Regulation.” The HKMA has consistently promoted the issuance of green and sustainable debt while fostering a local ecosystem of related professional services. In 2022, the total value of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong—including bonds and loans—reached USD 805 billion, marking a 42% increase. +42% Value of green and sustainable debt issued (USD 805 billion) To demonstrate its commitment to tackling climate change and to promote green finance while striving to develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the issuance of related green bonds. To date, the Government has issued green bonds equivalent to nearly USD 160 billion, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects covering areas such as green building, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report” detailing how funds raised through green bonds are allocated and their anticipated environmental benefits. To enable the general public to participate in Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment and share in its benefits, the first batch of retail green bonds worth HKD 200 billion was issued in May. These bonds received enthusiastic response from the public, making them the largest retail green bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance also expanded the range of green and sustainable financial products available in Hong Kong, further cementing its status as a leading green finance hub both regionally and internationally. During the 2022–23 fiscal year, the Government continued its regular issuance of institutional green bonds, issuing bonds equivalent to USD 57.5 billion in January 2023. This multi-currency issuance involved USD, EUR, and RMB, with maturities ranging from 2 to 30 years, thereby providing an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the wider region. The issuance was well received by global investors and successfully attracted new investors who had not previously participated in any Government green bond offerings, reflecting strong confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term creditworthiness and economic fundamentals. Responding to investor demand, the Government doubled the RMB-denominated bond issuance volume to RMB 100 billion. Both international investors and Mainland investors participating via the Bond Connect “Southbound Channel” saw their share increase, underscoring Hong Kong’s role as a premier offshore RMB hub and further reinforcing its position as a leading international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing tokenized institutional green bonds, serving as a test case for utilizing distributed ledger technology in bond issuance and settlement. These were among the world’s first tokenized green bonds issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis via a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes—including coupon payments, secondary market transactions, and redemption at maturity—also digitized. The Government’s experience with this issuance serves as a valuable reference for other market participants interested in similar bond offerings in the future. To provide the industry with credible and accessible market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on Hong Kong’s and the region’s green debt markets. According to the report by the International Capital Market Association, Hong Kong emerged in 2022 as the leading hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances. The total value of bonds issued through Hong Kong reached USD 278 billion, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB 5 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022; this issuance included RMB 2.6 billion worth of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also made its debut in Hong Kong by issuing RMB 5 billion in offshore bonds, which comprised blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlight Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable financing between the Chinese mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as the region’s premier fundraising platform. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Subsidy Scheme” launched in 2021, utilizing it to attract more relevant professional service providers—including financial institutions, green consultancy firms, and external review agencies—to establish or expand their operations in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been widely welcomed by the industry. By the end of 2022, it had subsidized external review costs for over 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments, both prior to and following issuance, thereby helping these issuers ensure compliance with market best practices and international standards. Starting in March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan amount threshold for eligibility for external review subsidies from HKD 200 million to HKD 100 million, thereby facilitating access to green financing for smaller enterprises. Following the successful completion of a proof-of-concept for tokenized retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Hong Kong Centre of the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub collaborated once more under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitizing mitigation outcome benefits (MOI), with the aim of enhancing transparency, objectivity, and environmental integrity within the green bond market. This project was completed in October 2022, resulting in the development of two prototypes capable of tracking, delivering, and transferring digitized MOI by leveraging blockchain and related technologies.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having spearheaded investments in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015. It required its outsourced investment managers to adopt the "Principles for Responsible Ownership" issued by the Securities and Futures Commission and to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently according to the principle of "capital preservation first, long-term appreciation," believing that prioritizing ESG factors can unlock long-term sustainable value and mitigate relevant risks for investments. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "2050 Net Zero Emissions" target in 2022 and optimizing risk management strategies to enhance the resilience of its asset portfolio, thereby seeking more ideal risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organizations to formulate ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a crucial role in managing climate risks. To fulfill its commitment to the "Glasgow Declaration" and the greening of the global financial system, published by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 UN Climate Change Conference, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures  The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Secretary for Financial Services, established the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to prioritize ESG investments with risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to other items to achieve the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Further details regarding the HKMA's responsible investment framework can be found on the HKMA website. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and is responsible for monitoring the ESG and climate-related risks involved in the Exchange Fund's investment projects. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management policies, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the ESG status of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Supervision Department of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and monitoring various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions and work progress discussed by the ESG Committee at each meeting are reported to the Chief Executive of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Monitoring and Governance Framework for Responsible Investment: A dedicated team within the Risk Management and Supervision Department works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on the integration of ESG factors and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities of various investment projects: Public Market Investments. The Credit, Regulation and Supervision Committee, composed of senior management from the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed-income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Supervision Department. In addition, the Risk Management and Supervision Department also participates in the selection, appointment, and supervision of external investment managers for the equity portfolio from an ESG perspective (see the section "Striving to Actively Exercise Ownership Rights" in the "Risk Management" section on page 27). For private market investments, the Investment Committee, chaired by the Governor of the Monetary Authority, considers the ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Supervision Department and the private market investment team for each investment proposal. Specific evidence² continues to show that the impacts of climate change and related risks are significant. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming that the "Nationally Determined Contributions" (NDCs) announced by various regions are fully implemented, the global temperature rise is estimated to reach as high as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement goal of keeping the global average temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more ambitious policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and the market's repricing of assets based on projected future trends, combined with inherent physical risks, will intensify pressure on asset valuations. Given the updates to global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the Monetary Authority, leveraging the expertise of external consultants, has further assessed the resilience of the Foreign Exchange Fund's "investment portfolio" under a "Rapid Transition" scenario (Figure 2), following its 2021 assessment of other scenarios. The "Rapid Transition" scenario includes higher transition risk factors in the short, medium, and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are abruptly divested to maintain the average global temperature rise below 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario is broadly consistent with the disorderly scenarios suggested by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "investment portfolio" can remain resilient in the medium to long term because a larger proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds, which have lower sensitivity to transition impacts. Industry distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets can benefit from relevant transitions. Transition risks and asset repricing may cause shocks to performance in the short term (especially for equity assets). The "investment portfolio" as a whole will be subject to increasingly intensifying impacts from physical risks that manifest gradually over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable industries. Like analysis of other modeling methods, climate scenario analysis has its limitations. The relevant analysis is based on the market benchmark industry distribution at the strategic asset allocation level and does not consider the effects of actively selecting specific securities within an industry. Deeper research shows that the investment items within the "investment portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or experience milder impacts compared to the market benchmark of strategic asset allocation. This result reaffirms that the Monetary Authority's responsible investment, focused on countering climate change, can enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio. Climate change trajectories remain uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve with improving data quality and policy developments. The Monetary Authority will periodically review the relevant scenarios and optimized assessments to more clearly confirm the resilience of the Foreign Exchange Fund facing climate change. As a long-term investor, the Monetary Authority fully understands the risks and opportunities that climate change can bring. The Monetary Authority is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities for climate transition, climate risk mitigation, and enhancing long-term portfolio returns. In 2022, the Monetary Authority continued its positive momentum by increasing its holdings of green, social, and sustainable bonds by another fifty per cent. Regarding equity investments, the Monetary Authority invests in an active equity portfolio with a governance theme and adopts a decarbonization strategy for passive equity portfolios by tilting towards companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring the establishment of a dedicated private equity fund with the dedicated partners of the Foreign Currency Fund's "Long-term Growth Portfolio" to promote green and sustainable development in the Asian region (Illustration 3). Illustration 3: Ongoing measures to increase ESG investment. The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to producing clean energy, places great importance on social and biodiversity factors. Before the establishment of the wind farm, local villagers used poison bait to prevent predatory animals from preying on their livestock, but this action unintentionally harmed certain vultures, some of which are endangered species. Livestock are important assets for local villagers. To assist villagers in protecting their livestock, the operator constructed livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the animals from natural predators. Furthermore, the operator employed a bird surveillance team to issue warnings when vultures were spotted being attracted by animal carcasses accidentally left by predators, in order to shut down the wind turbines and prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win situation: it protects the livelihoods of the villagers while simultaneously reducing the number of vultures killed by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities and open up new revenue sources for enterprises, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operation. The investee company is a comprehensive logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China, specializing in cold chain pharmaceutical, chemical product, and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continuously rising ESG operational standards, primarily driven by multinational corporate clients requiring their service providers to meet high carbon reduction targets in line with the Paris Agreement. In response to these demands, the company hired external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive carbon reduction plan yielded significant results in 2021 alone. The aforementioned ESG measures led to the company being awarded the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" by the China Logistics and Procurement Association. These achievements and accolades enabled the company to secure numerous business opportunities from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical product sectors who place particular importance on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully hosted the 4th annual ESG workshop, where it exchanged good ESG practices with 9 participating private market institutions (including dedicated partners, limited partners, and corporations) and promoted sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public market, the HKMA urged trading partners (mainly investment banks) to expand their ESG manpower and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr. Li Dazhi, Chief Executive of the Foreign Currency Fund Investment Office, delivered the opening remarks at the HKMA ESG Workshop in 2022. On an international level, the HKMA actively participates in the work of formulating industry ESG investment standards and practices: as one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a joint action coordinated by the PRI to develop standardized responsible investment due diligence questionnaires (5 and 6) for private equity and venture capital investments, to assist private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of dedicated partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in multiple working groups to support the research work of FCLTGlobal; the relevant research aims to explore the main market practices for long-term investment portfolios and for decarbonizing private assets, as well as the application of relevant practices for long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the drafting of the NGFS "Climate-related Disclosure Guidance for Central Banks" to demonstrate its commitment to adopting best practices in ESG. The HKMA also leads a working group under the NGFS "Net Zero Central Banking" working group, participating in the formulation of sustainable and responsible investment policies within the central banking sector. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars to share insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. Lau Wai-kuen (middle), Chief Risk Officer of the Foreign Exchange Fund Investment Office, spoke at the ESG Investment Opportunities Sharing Session, stating that building internal capabilities is crucial for continuing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging employees to take relevant sustainability courses and obtain related qualifications, the HKMA has also gained knowledge and practical experience from the process of seeking advice from external consultants on major industry practices for the climate transition of asset portfolios since 2021. On the other hand, the HKMA utilizes ESG data compiled by reputable external information providers to supplement its ongoing analysis of asset portfolios, thereby helping to strengthen the ESG resilience of the Foreign Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own carbon footprint, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s overall climate objectives. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also fulfills its commitments to safeguarding employees’ physical and mental well-being, promoting financial inclusion, and fulfilling its social responsibilities. The HKMA endeavors to conduct its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, it implements the principles of sustainability under three key pillars: the environment, employees, and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee leads the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategies. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives as well as representatives from the Risk Management and Supervision Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department; it also submits regular reports to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under its guidance, multiple teams and working groups are tasked with planning and executing measures within their respective areas. In 2022, the Committee approved the HKMA’s climate targets for its operations and reviewed the transition roadmap aimed at achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. Throughout the year, it continued to monitor progress on the HKMA’s green initiatives, including proposals to strengthen its sustainable procurement policies, procedures, and practices. **Governance framework for sustainability**   In recognition of the HKMA’s dedication to environmental protection, employee welfare, and broader societal well-being, The Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the “15 Years and More of Caring” badge for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to its own carbon footprint and has formulated internal “Green Office Guidelines” to manage the environmental impact of its operations. Environmental considerations have been integrated into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, BEAM Plus awarded gold certification to certain renovated office areas of the HKMA. This was the second green building certification received by the HKMA, following its LEED Gold certification in 2021. The HKMA has implemented various energy-saving measures. In 2022, total energy consumption stood at 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per person), representing a 24.4% decrease compared to 2015 (Figure 1). In 2022, total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions amounted to 2,996.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e)8 (1.7 tCO2e per person), a reduction of 38.2% from 2015 levels (Figure 2). **Figure 1**   **Figure 2**   *Greenhouse gas emission intensity (Scope 1 and Scope 2)*  The HKMA encourages paperless operations within the organization. It has also implemented a print management system requiring employees to log in to printers to confirm each print request, thereby minimizing unnecessary printing and toner usage. When printing is unavoidable, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are strongly encouraged. Additionally, the HKMA is currently preparing to implement an internal electronic record-keeping system. In 2022, total paper consumption was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per person), a 65.3% drop compared to 2015 levels (Figure A). **Figure A:** *Paper consumption intensity*  The HKMA continues to adhere to the “4R” principles in its waste management efforts. Apart from conventional waste, it also seeks to reduce electronic waste by adopting technical solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external firm for the first time to conduct a waste audit, analysing the composition of waste generated in its offices. The audit revealed that food waste constituted a significant proportion of total waste; consequently, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme (see “Enhancing waste management” on page 41). The total volume of non-hazardous waste generated in 2022—including general waste and recyclables—was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per person), representing a 4.8% decrease compared to 2015 (Figure 3). This fluctuation in trends can be attributed to the implementation of work-from-home arrangements during the peak period of the pandemic, as well as the subsequent return to office operations after the fifth wave of infections. Figure 3: Density of non-hazardous waste  The HKMA places great emphasis on waste reduction at the source, striving to minimize waste generation, promote reuse, and encourage recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a consultancy firm to conduct a waste audit for the first time, aiming to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste generated in its daily operations—such as plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood, and electronic products—and to obtain recommendations for further waste reduction. Based on the audit findings, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, installing food waste collection bins in all staff kitchens. The collected food waste is transported daily to an organic waste recycling centre in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy. The residual matter produced during this process can also be turned into compost for landscaping and agricultural purposes. Additionally, recycling bins have been conveniently placed throughout the office premises. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and pays greater attention to improving source segregation of recyclables, as well as providing guidance on proper handling of recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles. The HKMA also continues to organize various activities aimed at raising staff awareness of environmental protection, explaining waste management policies, and encouraging staff to make full use of available recycling facilities. The HKMA operates two data centres—one for regular operations and one as a backup. Given that these centres account for a significant portion of the organisation’s total energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green design principles and multiple energy-saving measures, including rack-mounted air conditioning systems, LED lighting, and 24-hour round-the-clock monitoring of energy efficiency. Following the completion of a consultancy study on enhancing the environmental performance of these data centres in 2022, the HKMA is now preparing to implement the recommended measures to further improve overall energy efficiency. It has also begun preparations for obtaining green data centre certification. Recognising the importance of fostering a culture of sustainability, the HKMA regularly introduces various programmes and activities to educate and motivate staff to adopt sustainable habits and green, digital working practices. The HKMA shares tips on green living and publishes annual statistics on office-wide energy consumption and paper usage, reminding staff of their individual roles in addressing environmental issues; it also welcomes suggestions from staff regarding sustainability initiatives. Under the leadership of a Senior Manager from the Administration Division, a task force comprising staff from various departments collaborates to generate ideas and concrete measures for promoting a greener working environment. Members of this task force also serve as ambassadors when new green initiatives are rolled out. The HKMA encourages broader adoption of environmentally friendly practices across society, implementing multiple measures to enhance operational efficiency within the HKMA, the financial industry, and the wider economy while minimising resource consumption. The HKMA’s “System for Transmitting Electronic Returns” (STET) serves as a one-stop platform enabling banks to submit various periodic reports—weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually—electronically. Another system, “e-Delivery”, provides a secure electronic communication channel through which the HKMA disseminates circulars, guidelines, and other information to banks. Both systems contribute to substantial paper savings each year. In handling bank complaints and enforcement activities, the HKMA has also taken steps to support paperless document submission; bank customers can now lodge complaints via electronic channels by filling out online forms. Additionally, the HKMA is currently developing a next-generation management information system to streamline complaint handling and facilitate the transition from paper-based records to digital ones. To reduce paper usage, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU)9 has adopted digital signatures in its daily communications with participants, including circulars, account opening and closure notices, and responses to audit confirmations. Moving forward, the CMU will continue exploring additional green initiatives, such as implementing automated electronic processes for both internal and external communications. The HKMA promotes the use of the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored-value payment instruments to encourage the public to adopt electronic payment methods as alternatives to cash and physical cheques. Further details on FPS and stored-value payment instruments can be found in the “Hong Kong’s Status as an International Financial Centre” chapter of the HKMA’s Annual Report. Sending electronic red envelopes is simple and convenient; it also reduces reliance on physical envelopes and cash, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s sustainable development. To this end, the HKMA continues to actively promote electronic red envelopes via various social and traditional media platforms, encouraging the public to use FPS or other e-wallet services to send them during the Lunar New Year. Major banks and e-wallet providers have also launched various campaigns to attract users, such as offering festive-themed user interfaces, enhancing usability, and running prize draws or cash rebates. For those who still prefer to give physical red envelopes during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA encourages them to use “new-old” banknotes—notes that are technically old but still in pristine condition—for this purpose. Using such notes helps minimize the need for printing new banknotes, thereby reducing environmental impact. Feedback from note-issuing banks indicates that the public has increasingly embraced the use of new-old notes in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts to promote coin recycling. Coins collected through this programme are returned to circulation to meet public demand, improving coin circulation efficiency and reducing minting requirements. The programme operates two coin collection vans; to date, they have served over one million people, collecting more than 800 million coins worth approximately HK$1.3 billion in total. In 2022, around 78% of users chose to convert part or all of their collected coins into credit for stored-value payment accounts. The HKMA maintains close collaboration with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, deploying coin collection vans on the day of the NGO Flag Day to support social welfare initiatives. Launched in 2014, the Coin Collection Programme is the world’s first systematic coin collection programme utilizing mobile vans; it has received numerous local and international awards for its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin processing. Each of the two vans is equipped with two high-speed coin counters to collect coins exchanged by the public. Participants may opt to receive cash in exchange, add the value to their stored-value payment accounts (such as Octopus cards or e-wallets), or donate it to charitable causes. Besides coin collection, the vans are occasionally used for educational activities, such as school visits.

The purpose of this verification was to confirm whether the Climate Targets were developed in compliance with the SBTi Corporate Handbook. The verification was carried out in accordance with the “Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information” provisions of the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised) issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to provide reasonable assurance through the issuance of an opinion and conclusions. The verification process followed all requirements outlined in the SBTi Corporate Handbook. The HKMA was responsible for data collection and reporting. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency can provide reasonable assurance and concludes that:   • The Climate Targets were formulated in accordance with the SBTi Corporate Handbook. Shen Xiaoyin   Head of Assurance   Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency   March 2023    The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency also conducted an independent verification of the HKMA’s environmental data for 2022 (“2022 Data”). The 2022 Data includes total energy consumption in 2022, greenhouse gas emission intensity under Scope 1 and Scope 2, paper consumption intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rates, as well as changes in these figures compared to 2015 levels. The HKMA’s greenhouse gas emission data was compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol jointly developed by the World Resources Institute (“WRI”) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (“WBCSD”). The verification covered data from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2022, as well as relevant data from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2015, used for annual performance comparisons. The verification scope covered a total of 6 office and warehouse assets: 4 offices at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place, and 4) Kowloon Trade Centre, and 2 warehouses at 5) Lok Sing Industrial Centre and 6) Chong Lee Centre, located in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The purpose of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance regarding the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data, as well as to assess the adequacy of the HKMA’s data collection mechanisms. Within the verification scope, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency examined representative data and supporting evidence drawn from 6 assets. This verification was conducted in accordance with the “Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information” provisions of the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised). The procedures were designed to yield reasonable assurance through the issuance of an opinion and conclusions. The verification process adhered to all requirements stipulated in the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. To test data integrity and accuracy, the process involved tracing selected sample data back to their sources; it also evaluated basic procedures related to data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checks, while conducting reliability tests. Additionally, the internal data collection and management mechanisms were assessed, and interviews were held with personnel responsible for preparing the 2022 Data; representative data and documentation were then examined. All relevant raw data and supporting evidence underwent thorough review during the verification process. The HKMA remained responsible for data collection and reporting. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. The verification team from the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency had no involvement whatsoever in the preparation of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency can provide reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The 2022 Data is substantially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA’s overall data collection mechanisms for the 2022 Data are adequate.
