Scaling up and accelerating climate action has become the most urgent task at hand. Nearly half of the critical 10-year period for addressing the climate crisis has already elapsed. To keep global warming within 1.5 degrees Celsius, we must reduce global carbon emissions by over 40% during this 10-year period. Yet greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach new highs. Recent climate science research indicates that the window of opportunity to limit global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius is rapidly closing. The effects of a 1.1-degree increase in temperature are already evident worldwide: record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, as well as severe flooding and storms, are occurring more frequently and with greater intensity across the globe. Hong Kong is no exception; last September, following a powerful super typhoon, we experienced a once-in-a-century downpour. Despite having robust infrastructure and rapid disaster-response capabilities, the impact was still severe—widespread flooding, disrupted transportation, and extensive road damage. All these events serve as a stark reminder that decisive and proactive climate action is imperative. Asia faces particularly significant challenges in its low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that appropriately reconcile climate action with economic growth and social inclusiveness. This is no easy task. Given the region’s rapid economic growth and burgeoning population, it accounts for over half of global carbon emissions. Moreover, Asia-Pacific’s high population density and geographical characteristics render it highly vulnerable to rising sea levels and extreme weather events. As economies within the region develop at varying paces, while low-carbon transition offers new opportunities for some, it poses a major challenge for others in securing the necessary funding. Market estimates suggest that Asia-Pacific will require over $3 trillion annually in low-carbon transition investments over the next 30 years. As an international financial hub, Hong Kong possesses both the capability and responsibility to leverage finance to support low-carbon transition across Asia. As a banking regulator, market facilitator, and responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has consistently dedicated substantial efforts to advancing the sustainability agenda. Readers will find details of specific measures and initiatives undertaken by the HKMA over the past year in the subsequent chapters of this report. To strengthen internal governance and better coordinate sustainability efforts across various functions, we established the Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee last year. Further information on this committee can be found in the newly added chapter on “Governance of Sustainable Development.”  Hong Kong’s banking sector plays a pivotal role in supporting Asia’s transition to net-zero emissions. Beyond fulfilling its traditional regulatory duties by ensuring banks properly manage climate risks, the HKMA also acts as a facilitator, helping the banking sector provide financing for low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green taxonomy designed to assist banks and other financial institutions in identifying environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate goals. In May, we released a prototype of this taxonomy for public consultation, and we are currently refining it based on feedback received. Additionally, given the growing demand for higher-quality and globally comparable sustainability disclosures, the HKMA is collaborating with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards issued in June by the International Sustainability Standards Board—a comprehensive global benchmark for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator extends beyond crafting frameworks and rules; we also strive to address practical challenges faced by the industry. Currently, many banks struggle to conduct physical risk assessments due to data limitations. To address this, the HKMA will soon launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform. By simply entering a property address, banks will be able to evaluate how physical disasters might affect residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under various climate scenarios, thereby aiding them in managing related climate risks. As a leading international financial center and hub for sustainable finance in Asia, Hong Kong continues to serve as a bridge, channeling international investment toward sustainable development projects in the region and supporting its low-carbon transition. In recent years, international green and sustainable bonds issued in Hong Kong have accounted for over one-third of the total volume in the Asian market, placing us well ahead of other regions. Notably, in 2023, the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong for the 3rd and 2nd consecutive years respectively, reaffirming Hong Kong’s vital role as a green gateway linking the Chinese mainland with the rest of the world. The robust growth of sustainable bond activities in Hong Kong can be partly attributed to the exemplary role played by the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds worth approximately US$250 billion, which were sold to both institutional and retail investors. We have seized every issuance opportunity to continuously innovate and expand the features of green bonds—including currency options, tenors, and distribution channels—thereby laying the groundwork for other public and private green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bond in 2022, we launched the world’s first batch of tokenized government green bonds in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the issuance of a second batch of tokenized green bonds; denominated in four major currencies and issued in a digital-native format, these bonds represent the world’s first multi-currency digital green bonds. Simultaneously, we have proactively introduced various measures to enhance the vibrancy and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem. These efforts span multiple areas, including skills training, data enhancement, green fintech, and transition finance. In particular, regarding talent development, we introduced a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Banking Professional Qualifications Framework in 2023, offering bank professionals systematic training to deepen their understanding and expertise in this field. Transition finance constitutes another key priority area; it aims to provide funding for decarbonization efforts in high-carbon and hard-to-abate industries, thereby preventing these sectors from being left behind due to lack of financial support. To foster the healthy development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand its Green Taxonomy to include transition activities. We will also broaden the scope of the Green and Sustainable Finance Subsidy Scheme—which provides financial assistance to eligible bond issuers and borrowers—to cover transition bonds and loans, thereby encouraging regional enterprises to raise transition financing in Hong Kong. Furthermore, we will strengthen engagement with relevant stakeholders, leveraging public-private partnerships and blended finance models to attract private investment toward sustainable development projects that have historically faced financing difficulties. Certain aspects of these initiatives necessitate cross-sector collaboration and are primarily coordinated by the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional cooperation remains equally important. Beyond our long-standing partnership with the International Finance Corporation under the Green Commercial Banking Alliance, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office became a founding member in 2023 of both the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance and the Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership. Additionally, the Glasgow Net Zero Financial Alliance has announced plans to establish a regional chapter in Hong Kong. Through these collaborations, we aim to promote skills development and knowledge sharing, ultimately facilitating the flow of capital toward sustainable projects both regionally and globally. To foster new business opportunities and knowledge exchange, the HKMA helped organize the inaugural “Hong Kong Green Week” earlier this year, attracting over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 regions, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial communities. The event served as a platform for discussing ways to expand climate financing in the region and forging new partnerships. In his keynote address at the “Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum”—a flagship event of the Green Week—Mr. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive of the HKMA, emphasized that as custodian of Hong Kong’s official reserves and a major global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of investing in green and sustainable assets, gradually expanding the Exchange Fund’s ESG and green portfolios in both public and private markets. In pursuit of its goal to achieve net-zero emissions across its portfolio by 2050, the HKMA launched last year an active global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition, while also extending the application of a customized low-carbon equity index to another public market portfolio. Moreover, the HKMA’s investments in green, social, and sustainability bonds have consistently outperformed benchmarks, embodying the principle of “doing well by doing good.” In the private markets, we continue to pursue green-related investment opportunities, having become an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. By end-2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had declined by 6% and 46% compared to 2021 and 2017 levels respectively, remaining consistently below the overall market average. As a sustainability-oriented institution, the HKMA remains committed to continuous improvement, setting our sustainability goals and initiatives based on three core pillars: the environment, employees, and social responsibility. Specifically, on our journey toward a low-carbon transition, we continually strengthen our capacity to address climate change by evaluating our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures encompass emissions reduction, energy efficiency enhancement, and waste management, all aimed at fulfilling our commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We have formulated plans to completely eliminate Scope one emissions in the near term, and we are making good progress toward our mid-term target of reducing Scope two emissions by 2030. To attract and retain top talent for fulfilling the HKMA’s vital functions, we also prioritize promoting employees’ physical and mental well-being alongside our green objectives. Additionally, through collaboration with various stakeholders, we strive to advance financial inclusion, improve public financial literacy, and raise awareness of financial fraud prevention, thereby contributing to the creation of a caring society. The challenges posed by climate change are immense and highly urgent. Economies worldwide are moving toward a more sustainable future, a transition expected to bring profound changes to financing activities and asset allocation. While this shift entails considerable risks, it also presents unprecedented opportunities. As a leading global hub for sustainable finance, Hong Kong bears the responsibility of spearheading efforts to tackle these challenges. We are also well-positioned to capitalize on this trend. The HKMA will fully support the industry in financing the low-carbon transition; as a responsible investor and sustainability-focused institution, we will lead by example and collaborate with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

Climate change risks and other sustainability-related issues are of global concern. The HKMA’s objective in its sustainability efforts is to play a leading role through its policies and operations, ensuring that Hong Kong’s financial system and the HKMA itself are resilient to climate change risks, while supporting the transition to a more sustainable economic development path. By actively participating in international and regional organisations, the HKMA also aims to contribute to the formulation of regional and global policies and standards for green and sustainable finance. As a banking regulator, the HKMA will further strengthen the banking sector’s capacity to adapt to climate change and manage climate risks. Specifically, key priorities include: conducting a new round of thematic reviews on banks’ climate risk management practices, as well as holding further consultation sessions as part of the assessment of banks’ progress in complying with regulatory requirements on climate risk management; continuing efforts to integrate climate considerations into the HKMA’s regulatory review processes; completing the second round of industry-wide climate risk stress tests, providing guidance to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing insights and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures by aligning relevant regulations with the International Sustainability Standards Board’s sustainability disclosure standards, which serve as a global benchmark, and preparing for the implementation of Pillar 1 of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s framework on climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidelines on best practices for transition planning with the industry. To foster the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will continue to monitor local and international market and regulatory developments, while maintaining close contact with the industry to ensure banks adopt appropriate sales procedures. Additionally, the HKMA will act as a facilitator, promoting the growth of the green finance ecosystem and supporting banks in financing the economic transition. We are set to publish a local green taxonomy and will continue expanding its scope to include transition activities and other relevant initiatives. Meanwhile, we will also explore the application of technological solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their exposure to climate risks; one example is an upcoming cloud-based platform designed to facilitate banks’ physical risk assessments. To enhance staff expertise, we will also introduce a professional-level module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the “Banking Professional Qualifications Framework” in 2024. Hong Kong is well-positioned to serve as a regional and international hub for sustainable finance. To fulfil this role, the HKMA is assisting the Government in implementing the proposals outlined in the 2023–24 Budget, namely expanding the scope of the Government Green Bond Programme to cover sustainable finance projects, thereby further developing Hong Kong’s green and sustainable bond market; it is also working to attract more green financing activities, including transition finance, to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Subsidy Scheme. We will continue to encourage more government entities, institutions, and enterprises to raise green funds in Hong Kong, while exploring potential synergies between green finance and technology. Furthermore, we will continue to support the implementation of the Government-funded “Pilot Scheme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training” to expand Hong Kong’s pool of green finance talent. As co-chair of the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, we will continue to collaborate closely with other government departments to coordinate cross-sectoral policies and initiatives aimed at advancing green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In 2024, the Steering Group will focus on three key areas: sustainability disclosures, the application of technology, and transition finance. As another key priority, through the Green Banking Alliance, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will continue to jointly launch various initiatives in Asia. These initiatives include conducting research on green finance, providing insightful market analyses, offering targeted professional training for banks, and delivering practical guidance to help financial institutions develop their own distinctive green transition pathways. In 2024, we will also strive to deepen our collaboration with the Glasgow Net Zero Finance Alliance, the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance, and the Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership. As a responsible investor, the HKMA is committed to achieving net-zero emissions across its Exchange Fund portfolio by 2050 or earlier. We will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund investments through a three-pronged approach to responsible investing, ensuring the resilience of our asset portfolio throughout the transition to net-zero. Recognizing that achieving the goals set out in the Paris Agreement requires an overall economic transformation, we are refining our net-zero strategy to focus on assets that deliver positive climate benefits to the real economy, while still meeting the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. As an environmentally conscious organisation, the HKMA’s decarbonisation strategy will be continuously updated to reflect the latest developments in the market, regulatory frameworks, technology, and other climate-related areas. To further strengthen our climate resilience and risk preparedness, we will explore the feasibility of utilising technological solutions to assess the impact of physical risks on our operations. Additionally, we will continue to actively encourage staff participation in our sustainability efforts, including launching campaigns to foster sustainable habits and optimising office processes and practices. The HKMA will also maintain consistent, efficient, and sustainable procurement practices, which include evaluating suppliers’ ESG practices during contract selection and renewal. Building on our achievement of Green Data Centre certification in 2023, we remain committed to upholding the stipulated certification standards. When updating our data centre facilities, we will not only keep pace with technological advancements but also incorporate green design and operational practices. Meanwhile, we will continue to minimise electronic waste through technological applications and convergence efforts, while actively modernising our internal systems to improve efficiency and mitigate potential risks. Lastly, in terms of social responsibilities, the HKMA will seek additional community service opportunities for our staff and collaborate with industry stakeholders to promote financial inclusion, enhance financial literacy, and raise public awareness regarding financial fraud prevention.

Climate change affects every aspect of human life, and everyone can contribute to mitigating its impact. Through its multiple roles as a central banking institution, banking regulator, market facilitator, responsible investor and sustainable development institution, the HKMA contributes to promoting and accelerating the transition to net-zero emissions in Hong Kong and across Asia. The HKMA has put in place a robust governance framework for sustainable development to lead the formulation of relevant strategies and policies, oversee the implementation of corresponding measures, and ensure that sustainability considerations are embedded in the HKMA’s own operations and practices. In striving to uphold good institutional governance, the HKMA has established a sound sustainable development governance framework with clear accountability arrangements and high transparency for its sustainability-related work. This governance framework ensures that sustainability considerations are effectively integrated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, and that there are effective mechanisms to monitor and assess the progress and effectiveness of its sustainability efforts.  The HKMA’s sustainable development governance framework comprises: the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant sub-committees, which oversee the work of the HKMA, including its efforts on sustainable development, and provide advice; the Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee (Steering Committee), chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, which leads the HKMA’s overall environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategies and policies at the management level; in respect of responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, which is responsible for coordinating and overseeing ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office; and, for other functional areas, the relevant teams and working groups, which are responsible for planning and implementing sustainability measures relating to banking and market development as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), jointly initiated by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the work of financial regulators, government bureaux and departments, industry stakeholders and other parties, with a view to accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong.  Given the significant expansion in the scope of the HKMA’s sustainability work in recent years, we established the Steering Committee in October as a new central platform to lead and more effectively coordinate all sustainability initiatives across the HKMA’s different functional areas. The Steering Committee provides guidance on the formulation of strategies, policies and plans for ESG-related matters in four functional areas: the banking sector, market development, Exchange Fund investment and internal operations; oversees the implementation of ESG-related plans by the HKMA’s various functional departments; assesses the HKMA’s performance and effectiveness in achieving its ESG objectives; and supervises external communication strategies. The Steering Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with the three Deputy Chief Executives as standing members. In addition, we will invite the Executive Directors in charge of major functions relating to green and sustainable development to attend Steering Committee meetings to report on the key achievements and future plans of their work. The Steering Committee meets regularly and is supported by the HKMA’s Banking Department, Corporate Services Department, External Department, and the relevant working groups under the Exchange Fund Investment Office.  Apart from formulating and implementing its own sustainability measures, the HKMA and the SFC jointly launched the Steering Group in May 2020. As a cross-agency platform, the Steering Group provides strategic direction and coordinates cross-sectoral efforts by the financial industry in addressing climate and environmental risks, thereby consolidating Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance centre in Asia and globally. For details of the work of the Steering Group, please refer to the chapter “Strengthening the Green and Sustainable Finance Ecosystem”.

Climate change represents a significant risk for the financial system. The HKMA has been working to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system in order to foster a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue fulfilling their vital role in the financial system and to channel more funds toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places special emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, as well as accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA is committed to devising various policy measures to enhance the banking system’s ability to cope with climate risks. In August, the HKMA issued a circular on net-zero transition planning, outlining high-level principles to help banks remain safe and sound during the transition to net-zero emissions. Following this circular, in the fourth quarter we conducted a questionnaire survey among selected banks to gain insights into their transition planning efforts. Based on the survey results, we will share observations and best practices regarding transition planning with the industry, and organize seminars or workshops to facilitate the exchange of experiences among banks. Regarding disclosure requirements, in light of recent international developments—including the International Sustainability Standards Board’s International Sustainability Reporting Standards released in June, and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s consultation on a third pillar disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks launched in November—the HKMA is intensifying its efforts to refine Hong Kong’s sustainability-related disclosure framework for banks. Specifically, the HKMA is collaborating with local authorities and stakeholders to develop a comprehensive roadmap for Hong Kong that aligns with the International Sustainability Reporting Standards. Throughout the year, the HKMA strengthened its supervision of banks’ climate risk management and provided guidance to help them further enhance their climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA has made substantial progress in implementing its two-year plan to integrate climate risk considerations into banking supervision procedures. Climate risk management has now been included as a permanent agenda item in prudential supervisory meetings with bank management. Banking supervisors also employ a revised CAMEL rating system that incorporates climate risk factors, to assess banks’ risk profiles and risk management practices. As part of this two-year plan, the HKMA revised its “green” assessment framework to focus on banks’ transition planning efforts. Additionally, the HKMA is reviewing its supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address climate risks. Following the conclusion of the 12-month implementation period stipulated in Guideline GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” of the Supervisory Policy Manual under the 2023 two-year plan, the HKMA launched a thematic review on climate-related risk governance in the second quarter. This thematic review covered 4 main areas: governance structures for climate-related risks, oversight of climate strategies, supervision of climate risk management practices, and organizational culture, awareness, and communication. The HKMA also made several enhancements to its climate risk stress testing framework, including introducing a new 5-year scenario to evaluate the potential impact on banks when economic and climate shocks occur simultaneously. Following these improvements, and as part of its regular supervisory-led stress testing program, the second round of climate risk stress tests commenced in June. This exercise aimed to comprehensively assess banks’ exposure to climate risks and further strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. A total of 44 banks participated in this stress test, representing an increase of more than sixty percent compared to the initial pilot program conducted in 2021. The HKMA also hosted a Climate Risk Stress Testing Forum in November, which attracted up to 300 banking professionals. By facilitating the exchange of experiences among banks, the event helped deepen the industry’s overall understanding of climate risk measurement. The HKMA also conducted a series of consultation meetings to review banks’ progress in implementing Section GS-1, “Climate Risk Management,” of the HKMA’s Supervisory Policy Manual. Meetings were held with bank management to discuss their efforts in climate risk management and shared challenges facing the industry; the HKMA also examined information provided by banks and other publicly available data to assess their progress. Targeted recommendations were issued to encourage and support banks in further strengthening their climate risk management capabilities in line with regulatory expectations. Given the growing global focus on climate change and related mitigation efforts, the HKMA has observed rising demand for green and sustainable investment products, with some banks already offering such products to meet customer needs. In response, the HKMA completed a thematic review on banks’ sale of green and sustainable investment products and issued a circular in November outlining the standards it expects banks to meet, as well as sharing observed best practices. Covering areas such as product due diligence, disclosure, governance and controls, staff training, and record-keeping, the circular aims to reduce potential greenwashing risks and enhance investor confidence, thereby promoting the sound development of such investment activities. The HKMA will continue to monitor emerging trends and market developments. The HKMA is committed to promoting the application of technology in green and sustainable banking. For instance, technology can improve data availability and risk analysis, thereby strengthening banks’ ability to manage climate risks. The HKMA is set to launch a pilot cloud-based platform enabling banks to assess the impact of physical climate risks on residential and commercial buildings under various climate scenarios. Additionally, the HKMA continues to collaborate with other central banks and regulators to explore how technological solutions can aid in physical risk assessment. On another front, the HKMA encourages the adoption of sustainable anti-money laundering practices through advanced analytics and artificial intelligence, thereby reducing compliance-related resource consumption. In 2023, the HKMA launched an online shared data submission platform that fully automates the collection of financial crime risk data, streamlining banks’ processes for submitting anti-money laundering data in a sustainable manner. In September, the HKMA held a “Green Fintech Competition” aimed at identifying market-ready solutions to help the banking sector address challenges in: (i) net-zero transition or transition planning; (ii) climate risk management; (iii) green and sustainable finance; and (iv) sustainability or climate-related disclosure and reporting. The competition attracted over 85 entries from some 70 companies. In December, the HKMA organized a “Green and Sustainable Banking Symposium” to provide a platform for the banking and technology sectors to discuss the role of low-carbon technologies and green fintech in Hong Kong and Mainland China’s net-zero transition; the results of the Green Fintech Competition were also announced at the event. Approximately 400 participants from banks, tech firms, regulatory bodies, and academia attended the symposium. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green and sustainable financial decision-making, the HKMA, with assistance from consultants, developed a local green taxonomy framework. In May, the HKMA published a discussion paper titled “Prototype of Hong Kong’s Green Taxonomy Framework” to solicit stakeholders’ views on establishing and implementing a green classification system. Based on the consultation outcomes, the HKMA is currently fine-tuning the prototype framework and identifying further areas for development in the next phase. The HKMA participates in the work of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), which has identified environmental crimes as predicate offences for money laundering. Given the close link between anti-money laundering efforts and environmental, social and governance (ESG) considerations, this area is attracting increasing attention from regulators worldwide. The HKMA fully recognises that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system; therefore, it incorporates broader climate-related factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its ongoing monitoring efforts. In its continuous assessment of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account and includes analyses of climate-related risks in all its financial stability reports. By actively participating in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps to further develop climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. As a member of the Transition Planning Working Group under the Financial Stability Board, the HKMA contributes to analysing the interaction between transition planning by financial and non-financial firms and financial stability, thereby helping policymakers adopt a forward-looking and dynamic perspective when assessing climate-related financial risks. In terms of research, the HKMA conducts multiple applied research projects to explore the impact of climate change and broader ESG issues on the financial sector and the economy. Research topics include the climate risk exposure of banks and investment funds, the flow of ESG-related funds, the effect of climate change on property prices, and the ripple effects of corporate ESG performance across global supply chains. These research findings enhance the HKMA’s understanding of how climate change and ESG issues affect financial stability, thereby aiding policy formulation. Locally, these studies help the HKMA continuously monitor and evaluate the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Internationally, the HKMA shares its research outcomes with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including climate-related international forums and its Research Memoranda. The HKMA’s Liquidity Arrangement Framework is a collateralised standby liquidity facility designed to provide timely liquidity support to banks in need. In line with NGFS recommendations, the HKMA now incorporates sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively engages in international and regional discussions aimed at addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, it helps foster policy dialogue on climate change and its implications for financial stability at both international and regional levels, while also drawing valuable insights to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a leading regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA is committed to raising market awareness and participation, providing necessary infrastructure and enabling factors, and supporting international initiatives to align with global standards. Throughout the year, the HKMA worked closely with local and international partners to foster a richer ecosystem and further advance green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategy. Since its establishment, the Steering Group has made notable progress. In January 2024, it announced key measures aimed at helping Hong Kong seize opportunities in sustainable finance; these include sustainable disclosure, ecosystem development, transition finance, and green fintech. Specifically, a Sustainable Disclosure Working Group has been set up to develop a roadmap for Hong Kong’s adoption of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. This roadmap will cover 4 key areas: sustainable reporting, verification, data and technology, and skills training. Additionally, a Transition Finance Working Group was established to explore ways of supporting financial institutions and enterprises in transition planning and reporting. The Steering Group also works to strengthen the sustainable finance ecosystem through cross-sectoral skills training and data enhancement. In particular, we continue to promote the use of the Climate and Environmental Risk Questionnaire for Non-Listed Companies, jointly launched by the Steering Group and CDP in 2022 (version 2). Moving forward, the Steering Group will stay abreast of latest developments in green and sustainable finance, further cementing Hong Kong’s role as a regional and global hub in this field. In January 2024, the Steering Group unveiled three new key initiatives designed to capitalise on investment and financing opportunities arising from the low-carbon transition in the Asia-Pacific region. To facilitate skills development within the industry, the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre under the Steering Group implements the Government’s Pilot Scheme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training, providing financial assistance to practitioners, students, and recent graduates undertaking relevant training or pursuing qualifications. As of December 2023, 46 international and local training programmes or qualifications had been recognised under the scheme, with over 560 funding applications approved. The HKMA has also introduced a foundational level module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the Banking Professional Qualifications Framework; this module aims to nurture talent within the banking sector and enhance overall professional capabilities. In 2024, the HKMA will continue collaborating with the banking industry to develop an advanced level of this module, addressing the growing demand for specialised professionals in green and sustainable finance. To help financial institutions and enterprises—particularly SMEs—better understand key climate and sustainability-related issues such as climate risk management, sustainable reporting, greenhouse gas emissions calculation, and transition planning, the HKMA partnered with relevant government bureaux and departments, as well as global partners including CDP, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ)3 and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF)4 to organise a series of seminars and workshops throughout the year, attracting participants from both the financial services and corporate sectors. For students, following the launch of the Sustainable Finance Internship Programme in 2022, training sessions were held in January and February 2023 to deepen interns’ and university graduates’ understanding of sustainable finance. Recognising technology’s potential to bridge climate-related data gaps and improve data quality, the HKMA is committed to making such data more accessible and reliable, thereby supporting sound decision-making and effective climate action. In February 2024, the Steering Group rolled out a series of website optimisation measures to provide financial institutions, enterprises, and the general public with a one-stop source of information on green and sustainable finance. Key optimisation initiatives include an electronic platform for sustainable disclosures, tools for calculating and estimating greenhouse gas emissions, as well as more consolidated, easy-to-navigate, and searchable data and resources. During Hong Kong Green Week, the Steering Group, in collaboration with Cyberport and Invest Hong Kong, also hosted the event “Leveraging Technology to Catalyse Sustainable Finance”, which showcased leading green innovation solutions and Hong Kong’s strengths in green technology. Held from 26 February to 1 March 2024, “Hong Kong Green Week – Finance Theme” saw over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 regions attend various sustainability-themed activities. These included representatives from financial institutions, enterprises, central banks, international organisations, government agencies, academia, and consultancy firms. The flagship event of Hong Kong Green Week was the “Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum”, co-organised by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). The forum brought together more than 400 participants, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial sectors, to discuss ways to unlock climate financing in the Asia-Pacific region. Over the two-day event, a wide range of topics were covered, including energy transition, decarbonisation in heavy industries, the circular economy, the future development of sustainable finance, and emerging climate technologies in Asia-Pacific emerging and developing markets. The forum also prompted public and private sector entities to co-host over 10 roundtables, workshops, and other networking events on subjects such as climate financing, carbon markets, the electric vehicle supply chain, net-zero transition financing, green finance taxonomies, and green development financing in the Belt and Road region. Additionally, on 29 February 2024, the HKMA and the International Monetary Fund jointly organised the “Asia Climate Finance Roundtable” to explore key measures for scaling up climate financing and the roles of central banks and regulators in climate risk management. All these activities form part of the HKMA’s broader efforts to foster and enrich Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance ecosystem. They serve as valuable platforms for participants to develop new business opportunities, share knowledge, and explore fresh avenues to address climate financing challenges in the Asia-Pacific region. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance across the region. In November 2020, IFC and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance”5 as a collaborative platform to bring together financial institutions, banking industry bodies, research institutes, and technology innovators in the region to advance green commercial banking. Since March 2021, the Alliance has held 22 training sessions and roundtables, attracting over 7,300 participants from across the globe, including Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. In October, the Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB jointly released a cutting-edge research report titled “Developing Ambitious Climate Strategies for Green Banking: Case Studies”. Throughout the year, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office joined the newly established “Capacity Building for Sustainable Investment Alliance” (CASI) and the “Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership” (GIFP) initiated by the Belt and Road Green Development International Alliance. Collaboration with CASI and GIFP will facilitate capacity building, knowledge sharing, and channel more funds towards green and sustainable projects in Asia and beyond. In August 2023, the Global Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ) announced the establishment of its Hong Kong chapter, which will support net-zero efforts by local and Mainland financial institutions. The HKMA serves as an advisor to GFANZ in its work. To demonstrate its commitment to addressing climate change, promoting green finance, and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority assisted in the issuance of green bonds under this programme. To date, the Government has issued green bonds for institutional and retail investors equivalent to approximately US$250 billion; the proceeds have been allocated to over 70 green government projects, including green building, waste management and recycling, as well as energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing how the funds raised are allocated and their expected environmental benefits. In the 2023–24 fiscal year, the Government continued its regular issuance of green bonds for institutional investors, issuing green bonds equivalent to around US$6 billion in June. This triple-currency offering, covering bonds denominated in US dollar, euro and renminbi with various maturities, attracted a wide range of investors; the total subscription amount reached nearly US$30 billion. The issuance volume of renminbi bonds was increased from RMB100 billion in January to RMB150 billion this time, and for the first time, 10-year renminbi bonds were introduced. This move helps extend the Government’s renminbi yield curve and further diversify offshore renminbi products. The strong response from global investors to these green bond offerings reflects their recognition of Hong Kong’s efforts in promoting green and sustainable development. In October, the Government issued a second batch of green retail bonds with a total value of HK$200 billion, further fostering market development and advancing inclusive finance. This issuance provided members of the public with an investment opportunity offering stable returns, enabling them to participate in and benefit from Hong Kong’s green finance development.

As a major global asset owner and manager, the Monetary Authority plays a pivotal role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate agenda. The Monetary Authority has long been a pioneer in responsible investment. Since 2015, it has been spearheading investments in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to actively exercise asset ownership rights and integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Guided by the principle of “preserving capital first, achieving long-term appreciation”1, the Monetary Authority invests prudently, believing that thorough consideration of ESG factors helps mitigate investment risks while unlocking the long-term sustainable value of investments. As one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and set a “net-zero emissions by 2050” target2 for its portfolio, the Monetary Authority remains committed to advancing its responsible investment journey, with a strong emphasis on sustainability—particularly the urgent issue of climate change—to enhance the resilience of the Exchange Fund and achieve better risk-adjusted long-term returns. As a responsible investor, the Monetary Authority contributes to building a robust green and sustainable finance ecosystem by collaborating with like-minded investors, regulators, and international organizations to develop industry standards and promote the adoption of responsible investment practices within the financial sector and central banking community. Through oversight and collaborative efforts, it strives to foster a future where finance and sustainable development go hand in hand. Illustration 1: The responsible investment journey of the Exchange Fund  Comprehensive and reliable ESG information is essential for integrating sustainability considerations and devising credible climate transition plans aimed at achieving net-zero targets. To fulfill its commitments under the Glasgow Declaration of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS)3 and the strategic plan of the Multi-Agency Task Force on Green and Sustainable Finance, the Monetary Authority has taken proactive steps by preparing this chapter on responsible investment for the Exchange Fund in accordance with recommendations from the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes the framework and guiding principles for responsible investment, which are then implemented by the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund in its investment management activities. The primary guiding principle sets the tone for how the Monetary Authority balances responsible investment practices with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority, oversees ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. It reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management policies, monitoring their implementation through regular reports submitted by the Sustainable Investment Unit within the Investment Office. As illustrated in Illustration 2, the ESG Committee under the Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Strategy Officer, coordinates and supervises all ESG-related activities within the Office. Proposals and progress updates discussed during its quarterly meetings are reported to the Chief Executive of the Investment Office. Additionally, the Green and Sustainable Oversight Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority and comprising the Chief Executive of the Investment Office and the Chief Strategy Officer, meets semi-annually to provide guidance on ESG policies and measures across various functions of the Monetary Authority, including the Investment Office, in pursuit of its overall ESG objectives. Illustration 2: Governance structure for responsible investment at the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund  As shown in Illustration 1, the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund embarked on its responsible investment journey in 2016, initially focusing on managing ESG risks that could affect the Fund’s financial performance. As sustainability evolved rapidly and became a strategic priority for major institutions worldwide—extending beyond mere risk management—the Investment Office re-evaluated its approach to responsible investment. July 2023 marked another milestone: the Office established a new Business Strategy Division led by the Chief Strategy Officer, tasked with coordinating and steering its strategic development; this division incorporated the former Responsible Investment Unit under the Risk Management and Oversight Department, now renamed the Sustainable Investment Unit. This strategic realignment reflects the Monetary Authority’s shift in emphasizing responsible investment from a risk-based perspective to a more proactive and forward-looking stance in addressing sustainability-related issues in investment practices. The Sustainable Investment Unit collaborates closely with various teams within the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund to integrate ESG factors into investment practices. It also assists senior management at the Investment Office in managing ESG-related risks and opportunities—particularly those related to climate change—across all investment portfolios:    **Public market investments** – The Credit, Regulation, and Oversight Committee, composed of senior officials from the Investment Office, reviews how ESG factors are incorporated into credit risk models, taking into account inputs from the Sustainable Investment Unit. Meanwhile, the Risk Management and Oversight Department regularly reports on the ESG performance of the fixed-income portfolio. Additionally, the Sustainable Investment Unit contributes from an ESG perspective to the selection, appointment, and oversight of external investment managers managing the equity portfolio (see Section 40, “Risk Management,” under “Promoting active ownership” for details). **Private market investments** – The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority, considers ESG-related assessments provided by both the private market investment team and the risk management team for each proposed investment. The Monetary Authority recognizes that physical and transition risks4 stemming from climate change, as well as associated opportunities, can significantly impact the long-term performance and value of the Exchange Fund’s investments. According to the United Nations Environment Programme’s *Emissions Gap Report 2023*5, unless greenhouse gas emissions are further reduced worldwide, global average temperatures are projected to rise by 2.5°C to 2.9°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. The urgent need for more aggressive policies, technological innovation, or behavioral changes to curb this temperature rise may exacerbate transition risks such as asset devaluation or stranded assets. Concurrently, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events pose additional physical risks to investments. The Monetary Authority believes that investing in a greener future aligns with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives; hence, it places special emphasis on climate-related considerations when integrating ESG factors. In 2022, it set a target for its investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, underscoring its commitment to global climate efforts. The Authority continues to strengthen its three-pronged approach, with a clear focus on carbon reduction and transition. The following sections elaborate on these measures. **Illustration 3**: The Monetary Authority’s three-pronged approach to responsible investment    In pursuit of its net-zero goal, the Monetary Authority prefers proactive engagement over outright exclusion or divestment from potential investments. First, maintaining a diversified and robust portfolio is vital to fulfilling the Exchange Fund’s primary investment objectives. Excluding entire sectors or industries would narrow the pool of investable opportunities, potentially affecting both returns and risk profiles. Through an inclusive approach, the Monetary Authority can identify opportunities to invest in companies—including those in high-emission industries—that are undergoing transition and possess advanced technologies and sound corporate governance to adapt to evolving global climate trends. Second, addressing climate change necessitates the transition of core “brown” industries. Merely divesting from such sectors fails to resolve the underlying carbon emissions problem. Instead, the Monetary Authority supports these industries by deploying strategic capital and actively exercising asset ownership rights, thereby encouraging them to adopt sustainable and low-carbon practices—benefiting both themselves and the global community. In response to market developments, the Monetary Authority is refining its net-zero investment strategy to adopt a holistic approach that yields transition outcomes aligned with both the Exchange Fund’s goals and global net-zero targets, while adhering to its guiding principles for responsible investment. By integrating ESG factors into investment decisions, it continues to seek sustainable investment opportunities that foster climate transition and enhance the long-term resilience of the Exchange Fund’s portfolio (Illustration 4). In 2023, the Monetary Authority sustained its momentum in responsible investment. In public markets, it launched a new actively managed global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition, overseen by an external investment manager; it also expanded the use of a customized low-carbon equity index to another portfolio managed externally. Meanwhile, green, social, and sustainability bonds prioritized by the Authority outperformed their benchmarks, exemplifying the principle of “doing good while generating returns.” In private markets, the Monetary Authority actively built a resilient long-term growth portfolio, seizing investment opportunities expected to benefit from long-term economic trends such as climate and energy transition. For instance, this year the Monetary Authority invested in two Asia-focused transition investment funds, demonstrating its commitment to addressing Asia’s climate transition needs. Illustration 4: Ongoing measures to promote ESG investing. The Monetary Authority has invested in a company specializing in producing eco-friendly thermoplastic materials from non-recyclable household waste—including organic matter such as food scraps—and materials that cannot be recycled. Unlike conventional chemical recycling processes, which rely on energy-intensive high-temperature environments to produce plastics, this company has pioneered a low-temperature production method powered entirely by solar arrays. This plastic material, derived entirely from waste, can serve as a sustainable, versatile alternative to oil-based resins commonly used in retail, durable consumer goods and other industries. It is also compatible with existing standard manufacturing processes and cutting-edge technologies such as 3D printing. The company is a staunch advocate of the circular economy. The following diagram illustrates the positive environmental outcomes resulting from its advanced plastic production process: Managed by the International Finance Corporation, the MCPP is an innovative initiative that combines funds from institutional investors with IFC’s own capital to expand sustainable financing for private companies in emerging markets. In 2017 and 2019, the Monetary Authority committed to two tranches of investments under MCPP, each worth USD 10 billion. It further collaborated with IFC to launch “MCPP One Planet,” a new global climate-related investment platform in 2021; this platform is the world’s first cross-sectoral emerging market loan portfolio aligned with the Paris Agreement. Through the MCPP program, the Monetary Authority has pledged to provide financing for 80 sustainable development projects across 38 developing countries, spanning 19 sectors including infrastructure, agriculture, real estate, and manufacturing. The International Finance Corporation has compiled data on MCPP loans. According to IFC’s reports, the Monetary Authority’s loan commitments have provided support to emerging markets and developing countries in various areas such as economic transition and human resource development. Specifically, projects financed by the Monetary Authority are projected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 560 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent annually—equivalent to the emissions generated by an average gasoline-powered car traveling 140 billion miles. The green and sustainable finance ecosystem serves as a cornerstone for global sustainable development in the future. The Monetary Authority actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investing and enhance industry capabilities.

The HKMA is committed to becoming a sustainable institution and is adopting a multi-pronged approach to reduce its carbon footprint, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In addition to promoting environmental sustainability, the HKMA also focuses on the physical and mental well-being of its employees and its social responsibilities, striving to promote financial inclusion and enhance the financial literacy of the public. As a responsible institution, the HKMA sets sustainability goals under three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility. The Green and Sustainability Steering Committee (Steering Committee)1, established in October and chaired by the General Manager of the HKMA, is the primary decision-making body for the institution's sustainability measures. The predecessor of the Steering Committee was the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which was responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating the vision, strategy, and policies for corporate sustainability and social responsibility. At the departmental level, the Deputy General Manager (Corporate Development and Operations) oversees the implementation of sustainability activities and submits regular progress reports to the Steering Committee. The Green Office Task Force and the Volunteer Service Group provide support for coordinating the institution's sustainability work; the former serves as a platform for discussing how to create a green working environment to pool ideas, while the latter aims to cultivate a culture of participating in volunteer activities. The HKMA has formulated a roadmap to guide its transformation. The work focus is on implementing carbon reduction strategies in its daily operations, including operating green buildings and data centers, practicing green travel, adopting energy-saving measures, digital tools, and more eco-friendly operating models, waste reduction, and establishing a sustainability culture. The HKMA also plans to utilize carbon embedding tools within its own value chain to reduce emissions, while adopting carbon offset measures for emissions that are difficult to reduce. In addition to the aforementioned environmental commitments regarding its daily operations, the HKMA continues to roll out more eco-friendly operating schemes for the wider public, covering channels applicable to banks for submitting electronic documents and communication, as well as electronic payment and coin collection schemes for the general public. To strengthen and maintain its operational capabilities, the HKMA employs a professional team, establishes a talent pool, and focuses on the physical and mental well-being of its employees. In terms of social responsibility, the HKMA encourages employees to participate in volunteer and charitable activities; considers selecting social enterprises (SEs) in procurement; promotes financial services consumer education; and collaborates with the banking industry to ensure that all sectors of society have fair access to basic banking services. The remainder of this chapter lists the details of the above strategies. Under the HKMA's overall corporate risk management framework, the Risk Committee2, chaired by the General Manager of the HKMA, considers the potential risks and threats the HKMA faces in its daily operations, including those caused by climate change. The physical impacts of climate change, such as more extreme weather causing flooding or other damage, may affect the HKMA's offices and hinder employee travel. To manage physical risks, the HKMA regularly updates its business continuity plans to respond to extreme weather conditions. The HKMA also regularly conducts evacuation and backup facility activation drills to ensure employees are prepared to execute business continuity measures at any time. The design of the office also incorporates several measures to mitigate potential risks. Transition risks may affect the HKMA's energy use, air travel, and waste disposal. The HKMA has been monitoring the transition risks it faces by tracking its own greenhouse gas emissions, waste generation, energy consumption, and paper usage. The HKMA's climate goal is to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions across all scopes (Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 for air travel) in all aspects of institutional operations by 2050 or earlier. As a recent emission reduction target, the HKMA plans to completely eliminate emissions from its own vehicles by converting all of its existing vehicles to electric vehicles; and, using 2015 as the base year, to reduce the intensity of purchased electricity emissions by 63% in 2030 or earlier through various decarbonization and offset strategies. Despite challenges in determining emissions from other activities in its value chain, the HKMA will still take a multi-pronged approach within a practically feasible scope to minimize greenhouse gas emissions from these activities (e.g. paper consumption, waste generation, and air travel). The HKMA's long-term and short-term emission reduction targets were formulated with reference to the "Science Based Targets initiative" methodology, which has also been verified by the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau. The HKMA has appointed the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau to verify the emissions, energy consumption, paper consumption, and waste data disclosed in this report.6 The scope and base for verification are set out in the "Verification Statement" section of this report. In 2023, in addition to publishing the "Annual Report", the HKMA also published its "Sustainability Report" independently for the first time. The HKMA's efforts to strengthen ESG reporting were recognized with an ESG Award in the "Public Sector" category of the "Best Corporate Governance and ESG Awards 2023" by the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants. The HKMA is the first financial regulator to receive an award in this category. The judging panel praised the HKMA for achieving good ESG standards, noting that the "Sustainability Report" is clear and easy to read, and that the appointment of an independent body to verify its target-setting methodology and the environmental data disclosed in the report reflects its commitment to making high-transparency and accountable reporting. Furthermore, the HKMA received the highest rating of Gold Award in the "Not-for-profit and Charitable Institutions" category in the "Best Annual Report Awards 2023" by the Hong Kong Institute of Management Professionals. The judging panel praised the HKMA's annual report for clearly presenting comprehensive financial information and making good use of infographics, demonstrating the HKMA's determination to enhance financial literacy and promote financial inclusion. In recognition of the HKMA's commitment to caring for the environment, employees, and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Society of Services has awarded the HKMA the "15+ Years of Heartfelt Care" logo for 17 consecutive years since 2006. The HKMA is committed to properly managing the environmental impact of its operations, and its internal "Green Office Guidelines" provide guidance to employees on resource utilization and office waste generation. The HKMA has integrated environmental factors into the design, operation, and maintenance of its owned and leased offices. When renovating offices, existing furniture and decoration materials are reused as much as possible to reduce waste, and eco-friendly building and decoration materials are prioritized. The HKMA has consistently followed this practice, thus obtaining LEED7 and “Green Building Environmental Assessment for Interior”8 Gold certifications respectively in 2021 and 2022 for parts of its offices renovated in the International Finance Centre Phase II. Adopting new technologies and making good use of existing technologies to improve energy efficiency remains one of the HKMA's focus areas. In addition to promoting good habits, such as turning off unnecessary lighting fixtures within the work area outside of office hours to save electricity, other energy-saving measures include using LED lighting equipment, motion sensors, setting air-conditioning room temperatures at appropriate levels, and making good use of energy in information technology network infrastructure. The HKMA's energy consumption has continued to decrease, reaching 2.59 MWh per person in 2023, a 29.7% decrease from the 2015 base (Figure 1).9 Based on the nature of the HKMA's daily operations, its greenhouse gas emissions primarily stem from the greenhouse gas emissions caused by the electricity consumed, which is generated from fossil fuels. In 2023, the combined intensity of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from purchased fuels and electricity was 1.48 tCO2e per person, a 45.2% decrease from 2015 (Figure 2). In addition to standardizing equipment, office software, and meeting facilities, the HKMA has adopted digital tools and technologies, and automated and streamlined workflows to build a digitalized work environment and strengthen online collaboration within the organization. 11 Paperless meetings have become the primary meeting format for the HKMA. To further reduce paper consumption and improve efficiency, all internal administrative matters are primarily handled through electronic processes. Furthermore, the HKMA encourages employees to integrate green and digital work modes, replacing paper documents and communications with digital methods. At the same time, the implementation of an electronic record storage system is underway. The aforementioned green and digital measures have yielded positive results. The HKMA's paper density in 2023 was 11.55 kg per person, a significant reduction of 64.8% compared to 2015 (Figure 3). Since the COVID-19 pandemic, most international activities have returned to physical formats; meanwhile, to promote the development of Hong Kong's status as an international financial center, it is inevitable that some HKMA employees need to travel overseas for official business. To reduce carbon emissions from air travel, the HKMA encourages employees to take direct flights or combine different official trips where feasible when participating in overseas activities. At the organizational level, the HKMA reduced its emissions by 126 tCO2e in 2023 by purchasing sustainable aviation fuel. Additionally, the HKMA participated in the "Gold Standard"12 carbon offset program to offset the remaining carbon emissions from air travel; the program involves waste-to-energy, solar power generation, and providing efficient and cleaner cooking facilities in developing countries. The HKMA will continue to make similar arrangements in 2024. The HKMA's procurement process takes sustainability and environmental factors into account. As part of a comprehensive review of the organization's procurement policies and procedures, the current practice of procuring green products has been established as a formal system, following the environmental specifications of the government's "Green Procurement List," particularly in the procurement of electrical appliances and office consumables. Furthermore, tender evaluation criteria have included ESG factors and innovative suggestions that help enhance productivity and efficiency. At the same time, all suppliers must commit to complying with environmental regulations. In accordance with the "4R" principles—Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle—the HKMA adopts a three-pronged approach to minimize waste generation and manage waste disposal. Additionally, the HKMA conducted two waste audits in 2022 and 2023 to assist in formulating targeted waste management strategies. Details regarding the non-hazardous waste generated, including general waste sent to landfills and various types of recyclable waste, are included in the "Performance Summary" on page 56. In 2023, the HKMA participated directly for the first time in the red packet recycling program of the International Finance Centre Management Company. Employees submitted approximately 3,000 used but still pristine red packets. These red packets were subsequently handed over to an environmental organization for distribution to the public for use in the following year's Lunar New Year. Given that the HKMA's operations and backup data centers account for the main portion of the organization's total energy consumption, the two data centers have been upgraded to meet the highest standards set by the "Green Building Environmental Assessment" for existing data centers, achieving optimal Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE)13. In 2023, the HKMA's two data centers received "Gold" and "Platinum" ratings respectively, based on the 2021 assessment guidelines for "Green Building Environmental Assessment for Existing Data Centers"; the HKMA is the first and only organization in Hong Kong to obtain these ratings. Improving the energy efficiency of the two data centres has always been a key focus of the technical team. To this end, the team adopted green designs during the renovation works and employed good operational practices that comply with energy efficiency standards to reduce PUE and achieve relevant targets, including 24-hour monitoring of the data centre's environmental facilities and continuous improvements to environmental factors such as airflow and air temperature settings. As the technical team continuously improved the energy utilization of the data centres, the HKMA commissioned an external consultant in December 2021 to conduct a review to comprehensively assess the green level of the data centres and formulate recommendations to further enhance performance in various aspects. The study was completed in mid-2022. Shortly after the completion of the study, the HKMA also began preparations to obtain "Green Data Centre" certification under the "BEAM Plus" certification scheme. The certification process is very comprehensive and rigorous. Throughout 2023, the technical team launched optimization measures based on the consultant's report recommendations to improve energy performance as well as health elements of the working environment within the data centres.

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau has conducted an independent verification of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s ("HKMA") 2023 environmental data ("2023 Data"). The 2023 Data includes total energy consumption in 2023, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, greenhouse gas emissions from business aviation travel, paper consumption, non-hazardous waste generated (including general waste and recyclable waste sent to landfills), their respective intensities, and the changes in these figures compared to 2015 levels. Additionally, the 2023 Data includes the volume of food waste generated during the year, its intensity, and the changes compared to the levels when the HKMA launched its food waste recycling scheme in November 2022. The HKMA's greenhouse gas emission data is prepared in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol ("GHG Protocol") jointly published by the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development. The scope of verification covers data related to the period from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2023, as well as relevant data from the period from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015 used for annual performance comparison (excluding food waste volume). The scope of verification covers a total of 5 office and warehouse assets, of which 4 offices are located at 1) International Finance Centre Phase II, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) Taikoo Place Phase I, and 4) Kowloon Trade Centre; the warehouse is located at 5) Loke Sun Industrial Centre in Kwai Chung. The purpose of the verification is to provide reasonable assurance on the accuracy and reliability of the 2023 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA's data collection mechanism. Within the scope of verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau reviewed representative data and supporting evidence selected from the 5 assets. This verification work was performed in accordance with the "International Standard on Assurance Engagements (Revised) 3000 (Other Assurance Engagements besides Assurance Engagements on Historical Financial Information)" issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to provide an opinion and summary to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process is determined according to the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tests the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing selected sample data back to their sources, and also reviews the basic procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checks, and performs reliability testing. The verification process also includes verifying internal data collection and management mechanisms, interviewing representatives responsible for preparing the 2023 Data, and selecting representative data and information for verification. Relevant raw data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of data. Our verification work is absolutely independent and impartial. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau verification team was not involved in the preparation process of the 2023 Data. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau provides reasonable assurance on the 2023 Data and concludes: the 2023 Data is substantially accurate and reliable; the HKMA's overall data collection mechanism is adequate. Reviewed by Shen Xiaoyin, Supervisor, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau, April 2024

The threats posed by climate change are imminent, and accelerating global climate action has become a matter of urgency. The World Meteorological Organization confirmed that 2024 was the hottest year on record, and also the first year in which global temperatures exceeded the critical threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. At the same time, although global greenhouse gas emissions eased slightly during the COVID pandemic, they have recently hit new highs, highlighting the inadequacy of current climate change mitigation measures. In the process of addressing global warming, the emergence of climate-related risks will intensify, and their impact on the economy and financial markets is difficult to predict. Furthermore, current geopolitical tensions, an increasingly fragmented global economic landscape, and the potential for exacerbated energy security issues, coupled with an uncertain economic outlook, all present greater challenges for countries in responding to climate change. The transition to a low-carbon economy requires substantial and sustained funding support. Across the globe, the transition challenges faced by Asia are particularly severe. As noted by the World Economic Forum, Asia is not only an engine of global economic growth but also the region most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Therefore, Asia plays a pivotal role in whether the global community can successfully achieve net-zero emission targets. As a leading international financial center in Asia, Hong Kong needs to strengthen its leading role and fully leverage the power of finance to support and drive the region's transition. To this end, the HKMA published the "Sustainable Finance Action Plan" last year, outlining our vision and roadmap for gradually integrating sustainable development concepts into the core of the financial system. Our work focuses on both enhancing the ability of the financial industry to cope with climate-related risks and assisting the industry in seizing relevant new opportunities. At the same time, we also lead by example and play a guiding role. The HKMA's sustainable development work includes four areas: supporting the banking sector towards net-zero emissions, investing in a sustainable future, promoting net-zero financing, and advancing more inclusive sustainable development. The banking system plays a key role in the net-zero transition in Hong Kong and Asia, but it also faces numerous risks during the transition process.
